articles.title: HYDE PARK AND THE GARIBALDIAN COMMITTEE.
articles.text:
HYDE PARK AND THE GARI-
BALDIAN COMMITTEE.

TIIE disgraceful ruffianism which took place
in Hyde Park on Sunday, the 30th ult.; was
repeated last Sunday, on a scale of greater mag-
nitude, and attended with more serious conse-
quences. The persons composing the Work-
ing Men's Garibaldian Committee, who con-
vened the meeting on the 30th of September,
are far from blameless in this matter. They
incurred a heavy responsibility without due
consideration. Like Frankenstein, they created
a monster which they were unable to control.
They used the power and the prestige of an
illustrious name, to "-raise the whirlwind,"
but they lacked the necessary knowledge, and
courage to "direct the storm." They assumed
a leadership, and with„a:a responsibility, which
subsequent events have shown them totally-
unfitted to sustain. By the absence of organisa-
tion, and a want of moral courage, they allowed
what would otherwise have been one of the
'most glorious demonstrations of working class
opinion, to degenerate into a display of ruffian-
ism and violence happily unknown of late
years in working class movements. There
may be a difference of opinion as to the pro-
priety of holding the meeting, but there can be
none as to the wretched management of its
conveners. I was one of those who concurred
with the meeting, believing it to be promo-
ted by men who understood what they were
about, and who would take care that it was not
directed from its legitimate object. But what
turns out to be the fact? This committee
convened a meeting, the object of which, and
the time and place at which it was held, they
must have known and expected would draw an
immense mass of people together, and
*ley must, or ought to have been, aware,
that it was likely to meet with opposition
from the more ignorant and bigotted
Irish Catholic party; but did they take any
measures to keep this opposition within legiti-
mate bounds, or to make the meeting efficient
for its purpose? None whatever. They were
evidently inexperienced in the management of
popular demonstrations, and an overweening
confidence blinded them to eventualities. I
have no personal knowledge of the members of
the committee, and am acquainted with the
names only of a few of its members, but from
inquiries I have made I find that though they
are all honest, well-meaning, and enthusiastic
men, nearly the whole of them are unknown
to the working classes at large, and therefore
do not possess that prestige and experience
requisite to control and keep in order a large
mass of excited people. What, then, if they
felt it necessary and desirable to hold this
meeting, was their obvious duty? Why, to have
called into their councils the knowledge and ex-
perience of those well-known men who, for
years, have been in constant communication
with the working men of London, who are
known to and trusted by them, and who have
gone through many political and social cam-
paigns within the last few years. But no; they
did not do this; they convened an open air
demonstration, at which it was certain thou-
sands of all classes—friends and enemies—
would attend, with as little preparation and '
organization as they would have called a meet-
ing of their 'own members in their own club-
room, and the result has been what any man of
experience might have foreseen—the great and
glorious cause they intended to uphold and
advance has been covered with ridicule, and
disgraced by violence. I hold the Garibaldian
Committee responsible for the humiliation to
which the workmen of London have been sub-
jected, and the failure of the meeting. By the
showing of the chairman who was to preside
at the meeting—a man respected. by all who
know him—in a letter he published last week
in the daily papers, far from possessing any
control over the meeting itsQlf, the committee
had no control over the speakers who were to
move their resolutions, one of whom, without
waiting for their arrival on the ground, began to
address the meeting on his own account, and
commenced the proceedings before any chair-
man was appointed.! This, of itself, was suffi-
cient to create confusion; and if they were
powerless to keep in check the ambition or im-
patience of their own friends, it is not surpri-
sing they were unable to curb the violence and
ruffianism of their opponents. Although sup-
p6eted by at least four-fifths of the assembled
thousands, their own disorganisation compelled
them to succumb to the comparatively few
blackguards who opposed the object of the meet-
ing; and the elite of the working men of Lon-
don, after having nobly responded by thousands
to the call made upon them to do honour to the
"defeated, wounded, and imprisoned." Italian
pariot, found themselves in the hands of ineffi-
cient leaders, by whose carelessness and want of
foresight they were exposed to the bludgeons
of a brutal, ignorant, and hired. mob of
Irish blackguards, at once a disgrace to them-
selves, their country, and their creed. The
forbearance of the people under this disap-
pointment and insult was of the most exem-
plary character. The committee, or those of
them that could be found, were pressed. on all
sides to adjourn the meeting, with an assurance
that on the following Sunday a sufficient num-
ber Of their friends would be in attendance,
prepared to maintain order, and allow the
legitimate object of the meeting to be carried
out. This advice was at last acted upon, and
after a show of hands had been called for from
those who felt spmpathy with Garibaldi, and
responded to by thousands, a member of the
committee declared the meeting adjourned
until the next Sunday.

,If, however, the committee were blameable
for their disorganisation and consequent weak-
ness on the 30th of September, their subse-
quent conduct and proceedings—displaying a
want of judgment, and lack of moral courage,
unprecendented among working-class leaders—.
lays them open to the severest censure. They
their responsibility in a cowardly man-
ner ; they inflicted: in\ich injury on the cause
they were no doubt desirous to uphold; they
neglected the duty they owed to themselves;
and, by their pusillanimity and disorganisa-
tion, betrayed those men who had responded
to their Can into the hands of a band of ruf-
fians, who made the cry of religion a cloak for
their outrage and violence. They must now,
and for ever, renounce all idea of becoming
leaders of th.e working men of London. The
meeting having.been adjourned by one of their
own body, and great publicity having been given
to that announcement in the press, they were
bound at all . hazards to have held such ad-
journed meeting, taking all proper precautions
to repress disturban?e, early in, the week,
have announced their intention of foregoing
:their duty. But they did neither of these
things; and they must be held responsible for
the proceedings of Sunday-last. Had they held
the meeting, and avoided the mound of rubbish,
all would have passed off peaceably; or had they
sufficiently early, and with proper publicity,
made, known their intention of abandoning
the meeting, the concourse of respectable peo-
ple would not have assembled, and the

articles.text:

But they lacked the moral courage to do the
one thing, and knowledge and experience
enough to perform the other, and hence the
unfortunate result. The committee may, and
probably will, say, that the announcement of
an adjournment of the meeting was the act of
one member of the committee only, and not
the act of the whole body. I will at once con-
cede that it was so, and for a good reason; the
general body of the committee were, like the
" nick " of horses in a Derby race, "no-
where." But they all, on Monday morning,
saw by the papers the announcement was
made, and they should immediately have either
sanctioned that announcement, or taken the
other course suggested. Their having done
neither, throws a responsibility Upon them
which they cannot easily shake off; nor can
they avoid it by making the excuse, that they
issued a circular towards the end of thesweek, for
which they obtained admission into the
columns of one or two papers. This was not
a publicity sufficient, nor was it made early
enough to be of any effect; in proof of which
the great bulk of the people assembled in
Hyde Park last Sunday were entirely ignorant
of any abandonment of the meeting until they
arrived on the pound: this should not, and
ought not, to
,have been so, and would not,
if the committee had done their duty. -
It is with considerable reluctance I feel
compelled to use the lash to a body of well
meaning working men; but they have brought
the punishment on themselves, by assuming a
position they were unequal to. As a jour-
nalist, writing in the interest of working men,
in a working man's paper, I am bound to take
notice of these, shortcomings of their would-be
leaders, and -hold them up as warnings to
others; and as a working man, jealous of the
honour and dignity of my class, I believe it

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE.
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE.

MANHOOD SUFFRAGE.
TO TFIE EDITOR OF THE BEEIIiVE.

Stit,—ln your impression of the 13th ult. a corre-
spondent of yours asks for a definition of manhood
suffrage, and. concludes with saying that universal
suffrage is a delusion and a snare.' 1 had hoped
that Scourge' would have given him an answer; but
I will apply my poor abilities to convince him that he
is labouring under a delusion. First, I would advise
him to write a letter to the town-clerk, or to the
treasurer, or to the mayor of the nearest ancient free-
man's borough, asking them to let him know on what
day of the month they swear young men in as freemen
(the borough that I belong to admits them the first
Monlay in every month of the year), so that he may
attend and see with his own eyes and hear for himself
the burgess oath, then he will be a living witness of
manhood suffrage. It might happen at the time that
a son of a mason's labourer, from birthright, an
apprentice of a chimney sweep, from seven years'
apprenticeship, and an alderman's son, all admitted
to their freedom from mathood suffrage alone
but they must be unconvicted of crime, and if any
freeman is convicted of felony he is' disfranchised
for life. Now, sir, you will carry out these enquiries
to other boroughs of which there are above 100. I
have no doubt but that you will find upwards of 2,000
burgesses for life enrolled annually: This perhaps will
satisfy you at present for the term Manhood Suffrage.
The next point, is .Universal Suffrage a part of the
Constitution?' I answer it is! In the reign of
Edward the Third, the majority of boroughs were
incorporated under the names of the Mayor and
Aldermen and free burgesses, and in their charters
every male of the age of twenty-one unconvicted of
crime, swearing loyalty to the sovereign, and to
defend his rights and the right.; of the borough, was
to be admitted into the Corporation, and the charter
provides that their sons and apprentices, when they
arrive at twenty-one years of age, unconvicted of crime,
shall be admitted as freemen; but, Sir, some of the
borough charters go a step further, and provide
that if any non-freeman marry the daughter of a free-
man, this qualifies him for all the privileges of the
freeman after taking his burgess oath. Grimsby is one
of the latter class. There was another class of free-
men called scot and lot voters. Their charters gave
the vote to [all the inhabitants of these boroughs for
the time they occupied, or, as the charter words it,
smoked a chimney. This was Household Suffrage, and
you must own that this was Universal Suffrage to
all these boroughs, both to the life freeman and the
scot and lot freeman. This last class of voters the
Reform Bill of '32 swept away-and gave their rights
to tenpounders only providing they paid the Poor
Rates. Arr OLD FREEMAN. -
No. 72, Watery-street, Sheffield.

articles.title: HOW CABMEN ARE TREATED.
articles.text:
HOW CABMEN ARE TREATED.

- TO THE* EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
Sru,—;-A few days since I carried two ladies, with
children and a box, from the Waterloo Station to the
Castle Tavern, Portugal-street, Lincoln's-inn-fields.
My legal fare was 2s. which was refused me, and
ls. 6d. offered, which I declined to accept. I sum-
moned Mr. R. Muston, the landlord of the tavern and
husband of one of the ladies, to Bow-street, and the
summons was heard before Mr. Henry, on Tuesday. I
proved my case, and the defendant was oriered to pay
the extra sixpence, but the magistrate refused me my
costs. I therefore lost the price of the summons, 2.5.,
and experienced much loss of time, which to me was
money. In face of this treatment we cabmen are ex-
pected to be all that is good and virtuous, patient and
long-suffering.
Yours, Bce., THOMAS MILES.
Mile-end, Oct. 8.

articles.title: TO THE EDITOR OF THE REEHITE.
articles.text:
TO THE EDITOR OF THE REEHITE.

SIR-I was engaged at the Easton Railway Station
to drive a Mrs. Nelson, of 33, Montpellier-square,
Brompton, with her two servants, to her residence.
When I arrived there she give me 3s, I demanded
38. 6d.., which was my legal fare. She refused to pay
any more, and gave me her name. I then summoned
her before the magistrate at Hammersmith Police-court
for the 6d. On the day of hearing the case the lady
appeared personally, and swore before the magistrate
that I demanded 48. - The magistrate said I was en-
titled to the 3s. 6d., and ordered the lady to pay the
6d. without any costs

WILLIAM REID.
ItoberVe Mews, Tlampatevi-road,

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, OCTOBER, 11, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, OCTOBER, 11, 1862.

TIIR PROPOSED CITY GARIBALDI

MEETING.

A numerous and influentially
.attended meeting of
the general committee of gentlemen who have interested
themselves in getting up the City requisition to the
Lord Mayor for convening a public meeting of the citi-
zens of London at Guildhall to express sympathy with
Garibaldi, and to protest against the French occupation
-of Rome, was held on Monday evening at the Guildhall
Coffee-rooms, King-street, Cheapside, Mr. J. M. Parry,
Q.C., in the chair.
Mr. Richardson (one of the hon. secretaries) read
letters approving the objects of. the meeting, several
enclosing subscriptions, from a large number of gentle-
men including Mr. Western Wood, M.P., Mr. .LoAe,
MX:, the Rev. Dr. Spence, Mr. Montague Chambers,
Dr. RosS, Mr. S. Morley, Dr. Epps, and -severat mem-
bers of the Common Council. He said.the.Lord Mayor
had consented:on the receipt of a numerously-signed
requisition, to grant the use of the Guildhall for the
meeting.
S-3veral gentlemen having expressed an opinion that
it would add greatly to the weight of the meeting if
the Lord Mayor would preside, it was iesolvedi on the
motion of Mr. Morris, seconded by Mr. Lawrence, that
the committee wait upon the Lord Mayor, for the pur-
pose of requesting him to Occupy the chair at the pro-
posed meeting.
It was also resolved, on the motion of Mr. Barker,
seconded by Mr. Bennett, that the meeting be held at
the Guildhall of the City, at two o'clock, on Tuesday,
the 14th inst., subject to the approval of the Lord
Mayor.

articles.title: DEPUTATION TO THE LORD MAYOR.
articles.text:
THE DEPUTATION TO THE LORD MAYOR.

On Tuesday morning the committee met at the
Mansion House for the purpose of having an interview
with the Lord Mayor. On assembling in the ante-
room' Mr. Richardson, addressing the members, said
he had received a note from the Lord Mayor on the
subject of the deputation, with which he thought they
should be made acquainted. The note was as fol-
lows: • _ _

'Mansion-house, October 6,

Dear Mr. Richardson,—Garibaldi being now libera-
ted (or to be so soon) no longer requires our sympathy,
and it seems to me that there is nothing to gain for
him by holding the proposed meeting. A soldier, such
as he undoubtedly is, would not willingly accept
sympathy for a moment, nor would he willingly have
it supposed he lost a bAttle. Ile, like a truly loyal
subject, deprecated a conflict with the troops of
his sovereign. His loyalty has been appreciated, and
the amnesty may well satisfy his friends. If you and
those with whom you are acting concur with me in all
this, you will perhaps not press me to give orders for
the hall being prepared.—Yours sincerely,
"WILLIAM CIIIIITT."

After a few minutes' conversation the deputation
determined to see his lordship and carry out the object
for which they'attended.
The members of the deputation having been intro-
duced to his lordship,
Mr. Parry said—My lord, we are a deputation from a
committee of gentlemen interested in the welfare of
Garibaldi and in the speedy evacuation of Rome by
the French troops. The meeting which your lordship
has sanctioned to be held in the Guildhall has a double
object in view, in the first place to express the sympa-
thy of the citizens of London with Garibaldi and his
cause, and in the second place to protest against the
continued occupation of Rome by the troops of the
French Emperor, an occupation which aye deem dan-
gerous to the peace of Europe. We desire to see Rome
become, as she ought to be, the capital of free Italy,
an Italy which had been acknowledged by all the
principal powers of Europe. The deputation trust,
therefore, your lordship will add to the weight of the
meeting by consenting, as chief :nagistrate of the cizy
of London, to preside over its proceedings, and a copy
of the resolutions to be proposed will be submitted for
your lordship's approval.
The Rev. Dr. Worthington, as a minister of the
Church of England, deeply sympathising withltaly and
Garibaldi, trusted his lordship would accede to the
wishes of the deputation.
The Lord Mayor said he must reiterate the senti-
ments contained in his letter to Mr. Richardson. The
situation of affairs with respect to that illustrious
patriot Garibaldi had been much changed within the
last few days. He had been recognised by his King as
a loyal subject, and sympathy was no longer required.
He thought the second subject ailuded to by the
learned gentleman (Mr. Parry) hardly came within
the scope of the requisition. Had the Roman question
been alluded to, he thought the requisition would not
have been so numerously signed, and certainly he
should have hestitated before granting the use of the
Guildhall. He thought it incompatible with his posi-
tion to take the chair as requested, even had the meet-
ing been confined to its original object. He was
anxious not to take any step in his official position to
compromise the Government. Holding these views,
he must decline to take the chair, and indeed, in the
altered circumstances, he thought the meeting should
not take place, and hoped the deputation would not
press him for the use of the hall, as he thought he
ought not to grant it. His sompathies, however, were
entirely with Garibaldi, had he required them.
Mr. Parry said they were entirely in his lordship's
hands. He would remind his lordship that it had
gone forth to the world that he had granted the use of
the Guildhall for the meeting, and any hesitation or
retractation of such permission would have a bad effect.
The committee had made their arrangements on the
faith of that promise, and he trusted his lordship would
well Consider before he recalled it. The deputation
thought that an expression of sympathy with Garibaldi
and his cause from the citizens of London was as much
called for as ever, and it would be given.
The Lord Mayor said_he must positively decline to
.take the chair, and would send an answer to the depu-
tation in a day or two, as to whether he would grant
the use of the Guildhall for the meeting.
The deputation then retired.

articles.title: REFUSAL OF THE GUILDHALL BY THE LORD MAYOR.
articles.text:
REFUSAL OF THE GUILDHALL BY THE
LORD MAYOR.

A numerous and influentially attended meeting of
the Garibaldi City Meeting Committee, also attended by,
a large number of the requisitionists, was held on Thurs-
day evening at the Guildhall Coffee House; Mr. Ser-
jeant Parry in the chair, to receive the reply of the Lord
Mayor as to whether be would grant the use of the
Guildhall for the proposed meeting. It having become
known that his lordship had refused the use of the hall
for the meeting, considerable excitement prevailed,
and much ill-feeling was displayed towards his lordship.
Mr. Richardson, the secretary, read the letter he'had
received from the Lord Mayor, in which his lordship
declined to grant the use of the Guildhall on the
double ground that the amnesty to Garibaldi did away
with the necessity for sympathy, and that the intention
to discuss the question as to the French occupation of
Rome did not come within the scope of the requisition
, presented to him. Several speeches, anything but com-
plimentary to his lordship having been made, in which
he was accused of yielding to undue influences, a reso-
lution was adopted that the meeting should take place
on Wednesday next, at 2 o'clock, at the London
Tavern, under the chairmanship of Mr. Western
Wocd, M.P., who had placed his services at the dis-
posal of the committee. Some routine business having
been transacted, and a sub-committee appointed to
attend to. the, details, the meeting concluded..

articles.title: BRISTOL IVO /LEIN-U. HEN'S BEII– ITHY WITH GARIBALDI:
articles.text:
BRISTOL IVO /LEIN-U. HEN'S BEII-
- ITHY WITH GARIBALDI:

On Friday, the 3rd inst., an immense and most en-
thusiastic meeting of the work;ng classes of Bristol
was held in the Broadmead Rooms, to express their
sympathy with Garibaldi. The worthy and highly.
respected mayor, John Hare, Esq., presided, who after
delivering an extremely able speech, called on Mr.
Butcher to move the first resolution, which expressed
admiration of the noble and lofty patriotism that had
characterised the life of the wounded patriot. This was
seconded by Mr. James Bastowe, and supported by
Mr. H. Cassham and Mr. J. G. Shaw' each of whom
was much cheered during their remarks. The second
resolution, moved by Mr. Henry Way, stated that the
meeting felt convinced that the present occupancy of
Rome by the French troops tends to keep alive feelings
dangerous to the peace of Europe, and subversive of
the best interests of the industrial classes. In the
course of his speech he observed that the meeting
might depend upon it that the outspoken voices
of Englishmen would have great weight with
Napoleon the Little,' and that it was something for
him to know that he was held in disgust by many
thousands of honest men. He concluded an address
which throughout elicited great enthusiasm, by ex-
pressing a hope that Rome would yet be obtained for
the Italians, Hungary for the Hungarians, and Poland
for the Poles. The resolution was seconded by Mr.
Naylor in an able speech; and Mr. James rose to sup-
port it, but he had not proceeded far with his remarks
when a most tumultous scene ensued, tho. speaker's
language being of a most unpalatable character to the
tastes of the meeting—such as Neapoleon's policy
supported one of the most damnable systems in the
world, and that he (the speaker) would drain his heart's
blood to dethrone such a hellish monster. Mr. James,
after vainly endeavouring to be heard amidst general
uproar, resumed his seat; and when the chairman put
the resolution to the meeting, with Mr. James's name
attached as a supporter, another uproarious scene was
theresult, the meeting not being satisfied till his name
was withdrawn, after which it _was carried amidst loud
and protracted cheering. Mr. Alfred Rudd moved that
a petition be sent to Earl Russell praying that the Go-
vernment should do all in its power for the reparation
of the injuries inflicted on' the people of Rome, and
endeavour to put an end to the present occupa-
tion of the Roman States by the Government
of France. During the reading of the petition, which
embraced several points, much alarm was caused,
several lighted crackers being thrown about the room,
exploding amongst the crowded assembly, but the
matter was generally treated as a joke. An ironical
cry was also raised of 'Three cheers for his Holiness
the Pope,' which produced loud laughter only; and
throughout the proceedings Victor Emmanuel, the
French Emperor, and the Pope came in for a full mea-
sure of disapprobation. Mr. Howell having seconded
the adoption of the petition, it was agreed to; after
which, a vote of thanks was proposed, and carried, to
the worthy Mayor for presiding, amidst enthusiastic
cheering; and his worship, after briefly responding,
called for Three cheers for Garibaldi,' when a round
of deafening cheers was given for the Italian patriot,
upon which the assembly broke up, the meeting alto-
gether being worthy of the working men of the great
city of Bristol.

articles.title: BRISTOL REFORM UNION.
articles.text:
BRISTOL REFORM UNION.

On Wednesday, Oct. 1, a lecture was delivered at
the society's rooms, Castle-green, by Mr. W. Mqt-
thews, on The Principles of Liberty and the Public
Duties of Life.' After some introductory remarks the
lecturer spoke at great length on the educational ele-
vation and the development of the faculties of the
people, as among the first and leading elements of that
true manhood necessary for the fullest exercise of
liberty, and which he thought should be the primary,
aim of all movements for the elevation of a commu-
nity. He said that a great want was a more
definite and decisive knowledge of the charac-
teristics of independence. In discoursing on the
theory of national laws, he observed that the
welfare of the public should be the supreme ele-
ment, and the liberty of the subject the
supreme result, and this should be the object of the
laws of every free country. He illustrated the nature
of the laws respecting the accumulation of private
property, and spoke at length on various other
branches of his subject, concluding by exhorting all
present to take an active interest in the welfare of
their country. The lecture was diversified by quota-
tions from Shakespere, Milton, Tennyson, Mackay,
&c., delivered in a clear and forcible manner, and was
listened to with marked attention throughout. At the
oonclusion, a Tote of thanks was unanimously accorded
to Mr. Matthews for his able and instructive lecture.
Mr. Gaylen, wild presided, announced that in con-
sequence of the lecture on Financial Reform being
fixed for the 15th, the usual fortnightly meeting would
not be held on that date, in order that members might
be able to attend the lecture.

articles.title: PLANET PERMANENT BUILDING AND INFESTMENT SOCIETY
articles.text:
THE PLANET PERMANENT BUILD-
ING AND INFESTMENT SOCIETY

The fourteenth annual meeting of the members of
the above society was held a few days since in the
large room attached to the society's offices, 30, Wilson-
street, Finsbury; Dr. Ingoldby, of 11, Finsbury-
square, chairman of the board of directors, and one of
the trustees of the society, presiding on the occasion.
The attendance was very numerous, and included
many of the influential members from different parts
of the kingdom.
Mr. Edmund W. Richardson, the secretary, then
read the annual report and financial statement. We
gather from the former that the year just closed has
been by far the most prosperous of any' since the for-
mation of the society, and that, whilst the directors
had to report in 1860 that during the then preceding
year the business had been doubled, they had on the
present occasion the satisfaction of stating that during
the past year the business had increased in a similar
ratio. About twice as many investment shares had
been issued during the year, and in the same period
the large sum of £,27,025 had been advanced to the
members upon mortgage of freehold, leashold, and
copyhold property in different parts of England and
Wales. other sources of the society's income
appear likewise to have proportionately increased.
It was remarked, however, that notwithstanding such
greatly augmented business, the withdrawals had
been less than in the previous year. The different
sources of profit realised during the year had enabled
the directors, after adding £5 per cent. interest to all
existing accounts, to carry, in the shape of bonus, a
further sum of £5 per cent, to the credit of all shares
entitled to profits, making the total interest on all
such accounts for the past year £lO per cent. The
total income from all sources during the year have
exceeded £36,000.
The report was adopted, the retiring directors re-
elected, and votes of thanks to the officers having been
carried, the meeting concluded.

TILE C.AI3MEN' S DELEGATE
MEETING.

The fifth -delegate meeting of cab-drivers represent-
ing the metropolitan districts was held at the BEEHIVE
Office, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet.street, on Tuesday
evening last. The following delegates were present :
South London: Messrs. Cook, Smith, Wellman,
Towel. Highbury: Messrs. Lovell, Sibley, Eison,
EArle, Wood. Paddington: Messrs. Harris, Wakelin,
G.)od, Griffin. Westminster: Messrs. Wise, Walton.
Est End: Messrs. Goodwin, Hayes, Quin, Bates.
EAstern Counties: Mr. T. Miles.

Mr. Wise (Westminster) was called to the chair, and
having briefly addresser] tat) meeting,
Mr. Lovell brought under the notice of the meeting
the subject of proprietors signing the licences of
drivers, which he contended was a gross injustice. The
law stated that all licences should be thus signed, but
Proprietors only occasionally did .so and this system
had acted very injuriously to many drivers who might
have their licences thus written upon out of spite. He
moved that the present law, requiring proprietors to
sign zell licences be adhered to, and a penalty of £5 for
omission.
Mr. Miles seconded the motion.

Mr. Cook moved an amendment, which Mr. Well-
man seconded, that the clause be erased from the act.
The amendment was carried.

Mr. Wakelin introduced the question of the length
of time which often elapsed before drivers were called
upon to answer any charges brought against them,
owing to delays in serving the summons.
A long discussion ensued, and eventually the follow-
ing resolution was proposed by Mr. Quin, and seconded
by Mr. Griffin: 'That every driver shall be served
with the summons for misconduct, &c., within seven
days after the alleged offence may have been com-
mitted, and three clear days before the day of hearing.'
This resolution was adopted.
The appeal question wasthen considered. Some dele-
gates thought that an appeal to the quarter, sessions
would be sufficient, while others advocated an appeal
to the superior courts of law. -
The Chairman suggested that they should decide
upon whether they thought an appeal from the contrary
and vexatious magisterial decisions necessary, and if
so, they should take legal advice before coming to any
decision as to the mode or plan on which the appeal
should be made. •
Mr. Towell moved and Mr. Wakelin seconded the
following resolution That the power of appeal from
magisterial decisions be granted, such appeal to be
cheap and effectual.' Agreed to.
The Chairman said he wished to throw out a sugges-
tion, that all those seven-day proprietors who now hold
more than one plate, should be compelled to have half
six-day and half seven-day plates. Cabmen were now
working 365 days in the year, and it was high time
some action was taken to procure more time for rest.
He was aware, however, that this was a question as
much for proprietors as drivers and he only mentioned
it that the subject might not be lost sight of.
Mr. Lovell moved, "That on any driver proving
his case before a magistrate, such magistrate shall
allow him his costs and expenses.' _ .

Mr. Miles seconded the motion, and alluded to a
case in vrhich he had that day been concerned at Bow.
street, where, although the magistrate acknowledged
he was right, yet refused to allow him anything for
costs.

The resolution was agreed to.
Mr. Towell moved, 'That all clauses relating to
the Metropolitan Stage Carriage Act be expunged
from the Hackney Carriage Act, which should stand
by itself.
Agreed to.
Mr. Goodwin moved, 'That district meetings be
called, when the delegates shall report their proceed-
ings, and that the proprietors be requested to attend
these meetings.
The motion was adopted, as was also one that
these district meetings should all be held within the
present month.
Messrs. Wise (Westminster), Wakelin (Paddington),
Cook (South London), Goodwin (East End), Lovell
(Highbury), and Miles (Eastern Counties), were then
appointed as a sub. committee to arrange the mi-
nutes of the delegate meetings, and prepare them
for the use of the district meetings.
It was then resolved that the sub-committee should
meet on Wednesday next, and that the delegate meet-
ing should stand adjourned until the first Wednesday
in November.

articles.title: CHURCH-RATE CONTEST AT .DORKING.
articles.text:
CHURCH-RATE CONTEST AT
.DORKING.

A vestry meetinc, to make a church rate was held at
Dorking on the 37d inst., when the. chairman (the
vicar of the parish) refused a resolution moved by Mr.
C. Rose and seconded by Mr. T. Marsh, proposing the
adjournment of the vestry till the 7th of November
next to allow an opportunity of investigating and re-
porting on the liability of the ecclesiastical districts
into which the parish is divided. On the proposal of a
motion to adopt the churchwarden's estimates, an
amendment was moved by Mr. Cole and seconded by
Mr. W. A. Marsh to expunge some of the items and
reduce others. The amendment, on being put to the
vestry, was declared to be carried, and a poll was then
demanded by the churchwardens. A rate of 23. in
the pound was then proposed, when Mr. Rose
protested against the irregularity of the chairman's
allowing such a resolution to be made before the esti-
mate was disposed of. On the motion for the rate
being put to the vestry, the chairman declared it to be
lost, and a second poll was demanded by the church-
wardens. The polling commenced at the vestry, and
was resumed on Monday. At the declaration of the
poll in the afternoon on that day, the numbers stood as
follows :—For the rate—Persons, 100; votes, 201.
Against the rate—Persons, 120; votes, 146. Majority
in favour of the rate, 55. Mr. C. Rose protested against
the chairman's declaring the poll before the estimate
had been decided upon. The chairman then declared
the amendment on the estimate to be lost, whereupon
Mr. Rose moved, and Mr. A. W. Marsh seconded:
'That the vestry do adjourn till the 29th inst., to give
the churchwardens an opportunity of amending their
estimate. The Chairman refused to put the amend-
ment to the vestry, and hastily signing the
poll book and declaring the proceedings terminated,
left the chair. Mr. Rose again protested, and con-
tended that the former amendment on the estimate
being negatived the original resolution to adopt it was
now before the vestry. It was perfectly competent
for him, therefore, to move another amendment. A
suggestion that another chairman should be appointed
brought the Vicar back to the front of the chair, which
he claimed to occupy. Mr. Rose now moved another
amendment as follows: That the item for lighting
and warming the church, £2l, be expunged, and that
the item for incidental expenses, £25, be reduced to
£ll. Mr. Abel seconded the amendment. The Vicar
still remained inexorable, whereupon Mr. Rose once
; more protested, and called upon all present to witness
' the Vicar's refusal to put the amendments. The rate,
though ostensibly carried, is clearly invalid. The ir-
recoilarity of the proceedings, the excessive character
of rate, the excess being one-third of the amount
of the estimate, its retrospective nature also, and other
vitiating components, render it hopelessly illegal. A
considerably larger number voted against the rate on
the present occasion than at any previous contest.

articles.text:
IT A.LY.

GARIBALDIAN SOLDIERS CONDEMNED
TO BE SHOT.

The court-martial on five of the Garibaldiau
soldiers, who were made prisoners at Aspromonte,
and who deserted from their tegiments, was com-
menced on the 21st ult. The charges against them
were desertion and treason in bearing arms against
the state. The court was composed of six captains
of infantry, artillery, and engineers, Col. Cavalchini
being president. The trial lasted the whole day,
and a great many persons were present. The ac—
cused were defended in an eloquent speech by
Gatti de Forsano, an officer, but they were con-
demned to be shot. They will appeal, it is sup-
posed, to the royal clemency.

TURIN, OCT. 6.

This morning the king signed a decree granting
au amnesty to all persons concerned in the acts and
attempts which took place lately in the Southern
provinces, with the exception of those who deserted
from the Royal army.—[The text of this decree

will be fonnd n another Column.] The number of
those excepted from the amnesty does not exceed
100, two of whom are commissioned officers, and ten
are non-commissioned officers.

OCT. 7.—The Diritto of today publishes a
telegram from Naples, announcing that Deputies
Mordini, Fabrizi, and Calvino, have been set at
liberty.
The Discussione of to-day states that the visit
of Prince Napoleon to Naples has been undertaken
with the object of inquiring into the political con-
dition of the countty, and of reporting it to the
Emperor. The same paper says that the institution
of a great military command in Sicily was intended
immediately to precede the raising of the state of
siege, but that this measure has been postponed on
account of the recent outrages.

OCT. B.—According to intelligence received from
Varignano, Garibaldi is suffering from slight then-
matism in the joints.
The Italia of this evening states that nothing
has yet transpired to justify the rumour of an ap-
proaching visit to Paris of Signor Ratazzi.

PRUSSIA.

BERLIN, OCT. 7.

In the Chamber of Deputies to-day the debate
on the resolution proposed by Herr Forkenbeek was
continued. The Chamber, after some further dis-
cussion, rejected with large majorities all the amend-
ments, and adopted by a special vote the resolution
of Herr Forkenbeck by 251 against 36. The Min-
isters were thus signally defeated by the party of
progress.

ST. PETERSRURG, OCT. 8.

The Czar has requested Count Zamoyski, the
Polish patriot, recently summoned to St. Petersburg
on account of his permitting a meeting of Polish'
noblemen to take place in his house at Warsew, to
travel for the benefit of his health. He is expected
to remain absent from the Russian empire for some
time, as under present cirlumstauces the Emperor
considers the return of Count Zamoyski to Warsaw

inconvenient.

CHINA, JAPAN, AND AUSTRALIA.

CANTON, AUGUST 27.

The rebels are again moving and obstructing the
conveyance for silk. Colonel Ward has capturel
three cities. A fierce engagement was fought on
the 22nd inst. resulting in the capture of Quyaon (11),
thus clearing a large portion of the canal. A treaty
has been concluded between the Imperial Govern—
ment and the Belgian Consul.
Intelligence from Japan states that affairs were
somewhat quieter, but an outbreak against the party
favourable to foreigners was considered imminent.
The Government at Yeddo was doing its utmost to
maintain order- The guard of the British and
French Legation had been increased. The repre-
sentative of the Daimios at the Imperial Court had
committed suicide.

3/lELBOUINE, AUGUST 26.

Frightful inundations have occurred all over the
country, doing an immense amount of damage. Mr.
Limburg, the explorer, has returned, after having
successfnlly crossed the Australian continent, He
has made a favourable report. Trade at Melbourne
dull. •

articles.text:
AMERICA..

NEW YORK, Sept. 27.

A. special Provost Marshal General has been ap-
pointed, with head-quarters at Washington. Pro-
vost Marshals will be nominated in all the States,
and will receive their instructions from the Provost
Marshal General at Washington. They will arrest
deserters and all disloyal persons, and inquire into
treasonable practices. :Ninety-seven of General
Pope's officers have been released from Richmond
on parole.

ATTEMPT TO DESTROY A FAMILY BY GUNPOWDER.—
A person named James Anstey, a stationer, residing;
at Sheerness, was brought up before the county magis-
trates at Sittingbourne, on Friday last, charged with
causing an exptosion of gunpowder in his house, with
intent to murder his wife and family. According to
the evidence of the wife, who seemed greatly affected,
she and the prisoner had latterly lived on very bad
terms. She had considered her life in danger from his
conduct. On Saturday, the 27th ult., he talked about
a divorce. He went out about half-past nine in the
evening of that day, and returned after a short time,
behaving in a very strange manner. No words, how-
ever, passed between them, and witness went up stairs
to retire to rest; their five children all being in bed,
two in witness's room, and three in an adjoining one.
In about five or six minutes afterwards witness was
lifted from her feet, and heard a loud report, which
shook everything in the room. She immediately rushed
down stairs, the smoke coming from the shop
(which was under her bed room), nearly stifling her.
The smoke appeared to be from an explosion of gun-
powder. She went into the street, and raised an
alarm. Wirness believed the explosion was caused by
the prisoner, with the intention of injuring her and
her children, from the expressions he had used. The
prisoner, in reply to the charge and the evidence given
in its support., said he knew nothing of the matter. He
was fully committed for trial at the assizes, bail being
refused.

CONVICTION AT YORK 'UNDER THE NEW GAME ACT.
—On Saturday, at York, before G. Lloyd, L. Thomp-
son, and G. Agar, Esq., three North Riding magis-
trates, James Kidd was summoned for having had un-
lawfully in his possession sixteen partridges and two
nets. At half-past six o'clock on Friday morning two
policemen, named Ryder and Eden, were on duty on
the Malton-road, about a mile from York, when they
stopped the defendant, and took from him the partridges
and nets. He did not give any account as to how they
came into his possession, and he was not asked. lir.
Breary, who appeared for the defendant,- submitted
that there was not a tittle of evidence td-support the
charge nor to show how the birds had come into the
possession of his client. The magistrates fined Kidd
£5, including the costs, ordered the nets to be de-
stroyed, and directed that the partridges should be sold
and the proceeds paid to the clerk to the justices. The
fine was paid, but notice of appeal against the decision.
' was given.

2IIE HYDE-PARK RIOTS.

Hyde-park on Sunday last was the scene of a -riot
far exceeding in magnitude that which took place on
the previous Sunday. The committee who convened
the first meeting, so disgracefully interrupted on the
previous Sunday, determined to abandon their inten-
tion to hold the second meeting, and during the week
'issued a •notice to that effect. The publicity given
through -the press to previous proceedings, combined
with. the fact that the abandonment of the meeting ,
bad not become generally known, caused an immense
assemblage in the park on Sunday last. Before two
o'clock all the principal thoroughfares leading to I
Byde-park were crowded with persons proceeding to-
wards it, many of them carrying sticks, and by three
o'clock the police on duty estimated that at least 100,000
persons had passed through the par: gates. As on
the previous Sunday, the mound of earth near the
Marble-arch was the centre of attraction, and at an
early hour of the afternoon it was taken possession of
bra body of about 200 leish labourers, armed with
, bludgeons, who at once raised the cry of 'Three cheers
for the Pope, and down with Garibaldi.' Immediately
surrounding this mound were stationed about 500 more
of the same class similarly armed, and who openly ex
pressed their intention to oppose by force any meeting
being held in favour of Garibaldi. It soon became
rumoured through the crowd that the committee did
not intend holding any meeting, and while many
approved of this decision, by far the greater number i
impressed much disappointment. On the abandonment
ef the meeting becoming known to the Irish party on
and about the mound, they set up a loud shout, and '
began taunting the Garibaldian party for thei,
cowardice. A working man, who, unperceived by the
Irish, had made his way on to the mound, here rushed
to the front, and, waving his hat, and holding aloft a '
board with the name of Garibaldi painted upon it,
called upon the vast mass of people in front and around
the mound to give three cheers for the Italian patriot,
whieh appeal was responded to by a tremendous burst
of cheering from the assembled thousands. In an
instant a dozen of the Irish bludgeons rattled aboutthe
bead of the Garibalditm champion, and he was hurled
from theniound bleeding profusely. This was the first
act of violence committed, and was followed by a
desperate rush of the Garibaldians upon the Irish-
men, woo, from the advantageous position they hell
their determination, and the free use of their cudgels,
succeeded in beating back their assailants, but few oi
whom. had • anything but nature's weapons at then
command. Just at this time a body of powerful Irish
labourers and others came upon the ground, ail armee
with sticks, and fought their way up to their country
men, who, thus reinforced, and emboldened by then
recent triumph, with loud hurrahs for the Pope, mad.
a desperate rush amidst the crowd, knocking down in-
discriminately mere women, and children, among&
others two or three soldiers of the Guards, who seeme.
an-especial object of dislike to the Irishmen. The Gari
baldians, irritated at this cowardly and ruffianly attack,
and headed by about twenty soldiers, who had rushee
to the aid of their comrades, then fought their way ui
to the mound, and after a severe struggle witi
the Irishmen ranged around its base, succeeded ii
obtaining- ty tooting upon it. The scene now becam,
one of great excitement. The soldiers, who were
armed with sticks supplied them by the crowd, amid th,
cheering of the Garibaldians and the yells and shout
ing of the Irish, laid about them with unsparine
vigour. The blows • from the sticks resounded on al,
aides, and blood began to flow freely from the heads o
both parties.- Each, soldier had at least a dozen assail-
ants to contend with, many of whom were evident')
expert at the use of their weapons, and possessed o,
sufficient buildog ferocity to make them most fortnid•
able opponents. At least-a-dozen men were lying al
this time bleeding and senseless on the top of tb.
mound, and the soldiers were on the point of being
overpowered by numbers, when about half-a-dozen o ,
the Life Guards, about the same number of the 3r.
Buffs, followed I.y a body of least fifty working me,
with sticks paid umbrellas, rushed .on to the mound,
and turned the tide of victory. After a territi
melee of about five minutes the Irish gave way
and made a precipitate retreat from their position
,
One• soldier of the 3rd Buffs, . a short, thick-se
raln, armed eith a p.ece of park rail, knocked dowi
NIX of the Irishmen in succession, receiving in retur,
a severe wound in the forehead. As the Irishme,
-were beaten from the 'mound; the people seized upoi
those who hart made themselves most conspicuous, an(
dragged them to the outskirts of the crowd, and gay.
them in charge to the policemen several of whorl
were there stationed, but with orders not to interfer,
unless under the personal orders of the commissioner.
Those who were identified as having taken pert in the
first ensfaught upon the people, were taken off to th,
station-house. The Garibaldians and the soldier,
being now in possession of the mound, one of the sol
diets was hoisted on the stroulders of his comrades
and said if any of the committee were present who hat
called the meeting last Sunday, and wished to propoa
a resolution in favour-of Garibaldi, the soldiers woul,
form a circle round the mound, and guarantee them ,
hearing. No one responded to this appeal, but it gave
rise ;to one of the greatest bursts of cheers that eve,
resolended in- Hyde-park, followed by cheers for the
a e... The Irish, now driven from the mound ant
re. . ered perfectly infuriate by their defeat in that
4 e quarter, forme .t themselves into several detachee
, ~.., bodies of about 200 each, and forcing their way int,
thestrowd in different directions, began striking- at al.
within their reach. It was estimated that there was
at this time 200,000 people assembled, and the
rushing of one portion of the crowd to escape
the blows of these ruffians, the determined steam,
made against them by other portions, the shouts of the
men, the shrieks of the women and the cries of the
juveniles, presented a scene of the most &arming de-
scription. Sticks were being used and stones wer.
flying iu all directions, and at least 2,000 people
were battling in diffe:rent parts of the park. . In
• some cases knives were used, and several persons
were tatzen off the ground who had been stabbed
About 500 scaler i were now mixed up in the crowd,
great numbers of whom were fighting against the
Irishthen, who at last were overpowered, and fled in all
directions, many of them meeting. with the knots of
Garibaldians, by whom they were severely nialtreated.
Sir. R. Mayne and Captain Harris, the Commissioners
of Police, now came upon elle ground, and it getting
dusk, and seeing the alarming state of affairs,
despatched a constable to Wellington Barracks for a
strong picket of Fusiliers, about fifty of whom, under
the command of an officer, but without arms, weedily:
- . attended, one party taking possession of the mound,
and the other ordering the soldiers into barracks. A
strong body of the D division of police, who had been
kepi in reserve in the Marble-arch, were also brought
_ oia the ground under the command of Captain Harris.
These measures, combined with the retreat of the
Irishmen' and the approach.of dusk, put a stop to
- the proceedings, and the people gradually left the
park, which became quite cleared by eight o'clock. A
large number of persons were severely injured during
the afternoon, and the various surgeries in-the neigh-
hood were crowded with parties waiting to have their
wounds dressed.
On Thursday morning a number of workmen were
employed in Ilyele-park,, by. order of the Hon W.
Cowper,. her Majesty's Commissioner of Works,
revelling the mounds from which the orators who
assemble in the park are in the habit of addressing
their hearers, and the struggle for the possession of
which led to the diefseaceful riots that have occurred
the last two Sunday,. The-police have ascertained
that the supporters of the Pope iiitena to muster in
the park in strong force on Sunday next to renew the-
disturbances, and accordingly additional precautions
of a very stringent nature will be taken to prevent
any further breach of the peace. On Wednesday
evening another riot took place in Tothill-street,
Westminster, originating in &drinking saloon, where a
number of, Irish attacked the rest of the company with
the cry of 'Up with the Pope, down with Garibaldi.'
, Several of the guards took part in the affray, and four
. of " the Coldstreams, named Edward Barnes, John
Jones, John Elliott, and John Hibberd, were so
seriously cut and injured that they had to be taken to
Westminster Hospital for surgical assistance.

EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE. SHIELDS, Monday.—A
good deal of excitement has been caused by the extra-
ordinary suicide of a young man named Thomas Reed,
a chemist, belonging to South Shields, which took
place recently. The unfortunate man took a boat at
the lew,part of the town, and, after giving the man to
whom the boat belonged a shilling, he pulled out into
the middle of the stream, and then shouted—' Good-
by.p.'. He took the boat over the bar out to sea, and,
while in twelve fathoms water, he was observed by
Some men in the steamboat Goliah to pull off his clothes
and tie them up into a bundle. He then placed the
oars in an orderly manner, and stuck up the boathOok,
With his hankerchief, half-mast high, as if for mourn-
ing. Be shouted to the steamboat men, whose suspi-
cions that there was something wrong with him had
been aroused, and they were making towards him with
their boat. But, before they could reach him, he
leaped from the boat's gunwale into the sea, having a
large stone fastened about his neck with a rope, and
sunk instantly, of course, and was drowned. Upon
getting hold of the boat, the steamboat men found it
ea written over with chalk, the deceased blaming his
partner, a Mr. Taylor, for being the cause of his death;
but there is little doubt but that the poor creature was
lightheaded at the time he destroyed his life. The
boat is in charge of the river police. There will be
some difficulty in rernering the body,..-Manchester
Xxaminer,

PONTOON FOR THE VICEROY OF
EGYPT.

An interesting experiment was made on Saturday
afternoon by the let Middlesex Engineer Volunteers.
A pontoon bridge, of very beautiful construction, has
recently been made from the designs of aptain Fo.ke,
R.E., on- an . improved principle, for his Highness the
Viceroy of Egypt; and-it PM for the purpose of testing
the bridge previous to sending it out that the experi-
ments carried out with success on Saturday afternoon
were made. The bridge consists of 18 pontoons, with I
the necessary adjuncts; and though somewhat smaller
in diameter than those used in the army. possesses all
their qualities, in addition to being more portable, and is
wide and strong enough to admit of a troop of soldiers
to trot or march across, four abreast, with ease. The
Ist Middlesex Engineers mustered at their drill ground,
South Kensington, at three o'clock, and marched, under
the command of Captain Thompson, to the spot
selected for throwing' the bridge, which was situated
about sixty yards from the end of the Serpentine,
where a number of spectators had assembled, including
many military officers. Arrived at the river, about
forty members were selected from the corps to keep the
ground, and the pontoniers, thirty-two in number, were
reinforced by a small party of the Royal Engineers,
under Captain Fowke. The experiments commenced at
four o'clock, when the working party, having taken
their assignekpositions, some at the pontoons and others
at their supports, working gear, grapnels, planks, floats,
&c., they set to work to make the bridge, on the com-
pletion of which the actu-11 trial took place. The pon-
toniers-' fell in,' and having executed a few preliminary
movements, were marched and trotted across it 'four
deep,' subjecting it to the greatest possible strain, which
it bore without wetting a plank. At the close of the
movements a number of the spectators and several mili-
tary officers inspected the bridge, after which it was
taken to pieu,n3, and placed un the, hank with. th.a Atamie
precision which,attended its construction.

CONTINENTAL FRES C 0243.

In the principal railway station at Munich, Mr.
Echter, a well-known pupil of Koulbach, has just
executed two fresco subjects of more than usually
ambitious character. The two subjects were selected as
being appropriate to the railway system. They are
'Steam' and the Electric Telegraph.' The power of
steam, in the form of a huge Titan, has been yoked to a
magnificent car, in which a female figure of command-
ing aspect, representing intellect, holds the reins and
goad. The harnessed Titan, his impatient breath gush-
ing from mouth and nostril like jets of hissing steam,
plunges madly forward; and at his approach crowds of
old-world prejudices, habits, and customs are scattered
in every direction. Prim sentinels at frontiers,
and dogmatic officers of custom dues, scamper out
of the way of the careering monster, Steam; while
a whole cloud of stamped and signed and counter-
signed official papers are carried off in a whirlwind
of vapour. Notifications, permits, passports, are also
vanishing into space as the chariot of Intellect is carried
impetuously forward by the subdued powers of the huge
Titan, Steam. The allegory which represents the
Electric Telegraph is more complicated still, and would
require some good training in a school of German
philosophy to enable an ordinary spectator to make it all
out. The interpretation of the main features, however,
which are strikingly depicted, is easy enough after a
little consideration; though they might puzzle the usual
company of an English railway station pretty con-
siderably. The genius of the Telegraph is represented
by a majestic female figure rising from the earth, whose
golden hair spreads into wide radiations like electric
wires, which might be carrying forth Thought from its
seat in the train, the outstretched arms pointing to the
far-distant horizon. This figure is merely a symbolical
personification of the electric power of the telegraph; the
working principlebeing much more elaborately expressed
in another feature of the allegory. A kneeling nymph
is seen whispering into the ear of a child floating in the
air. The child is simultaneously whispering the message
into the ear of another floating child holdinc, the hand
of the first; a third receives it from the second; and so
on through a long line of gracefully floating children, in
a thousand playful attitudes linked hand to hand, each
transmitting the message to the other at the same
moment; while, at the end of the line—faint and
slender in the far distance another nymph receives the
message from the last child, and inscribes it on a scroll
which has been prepared for its reception. It must be
admitted that all this is ingenious, though rather com-
plicated. The execution is, however, so good that even
those. who will not accept the composition as a clear alle-
gory will admire it as a good picture.

We understand that the Osborne is-about to proceed
to the Mediterranean. Her exact destination is not
known, but it is believed she will be placed at the dis-
posal of the Princess of Prussia during her sojourn in
the South.

A pamphlet has just been published at Turin, entitled
'The Policy of the Ministry—We will have Rome It
is written by Count Bargnani, a Lombard, and as it ex-
presses the sentiments of the public, its sale has been very
extensive.

A letter from Dresden of the 29th ult. states that on
the previous day the Prince of Wales attended Divine
service in the protestant church in that city, and, after
having visited, in company with the King, the Here-
ditary Prince, and Prince George, the fortress of Kcenig-
stein, dined with the royal family at Pilnitz. On the
following day there was to be a grand hunt and a
state dinner at Moritaburg.
RICE IN SpAnl.—+The profits of the rice crop are in-
ducing its cultivation in the extensive swamps near the
mouth of the Ebro in Spain, a proceeding which raises
considerable opposition in other quarters on account of
the fevers which it is alleged to generate. This cultiva-
tion, however, does not generate those fevers, for they
formerly existed in those marshy grounds; on the con-
trary, if properly conducted, it establishes a kind of
draining. It has been known near Valencia to reduce
the intensity and prevalence of the disease; but there is
no denying that the first pioneers in those waters must
be great sufferers.—The Grocer.
A CONFEDERATE STEAMER RUN DOWN IN THE
CLYDE.—The lona, which had been sold to the Confe-
derate government about three weeks ago, was run down
and sunk on Thursday night off Gourock. On her
return trial trip, the Chanticleer met the lona, which had
been getting her compasses adjusted that day, steaming
towards her anchorage ground in Goitre& Bay, when a
collision ensued, the Chanticleer running right into the
starboard quarter of the other vessel, cutting her nearly
in two aft the mainmast. The Chanticleer backed out,
and the lona sank six minutes afterwards. The crew,
numbering 21, escaped into the boats of both vessels,
and were taken on board the Chanticleer without delay.
The lona was built in 1855 for Messrs. David Hutche-
son and Co. and. since that time has been the favourite
passenger steamboat on the Clyde. She was 220 horse-
power, and her tonnage was 325 tons.. She had on
board a full cargo of coals and general stores, which
together with the vessel were insured.
ENCOUNTER WITH A Woes.—A farmer, named
Poublan, whose residence is situated on the road from
Pau to Vic, was informed a few days ago by his young
sheep-boy, with an air of terror, that two large wild
dogs had penetrated into the shed and killed a number
of sheep; that one had fled on his opening the door, but
that the other was still in the midst of the flock. The
farmer hastened to the shed, and from a hole in the door
perceived a huge wolf lying in the midst of more than a
dozen sheep which it had killed. Being tired of tiie
carnage, the wolf had gone to sleep without having-com-
pleted the destruction of the entire flock. Poublan armed
himself with a pitchfork, and not being able to persuade
any of his men to accompany him, entered the shed alone,
and closed the door behind him. Going straight to the
animal, he struck it vigorously with the points, but the
wolf being only wounded sprang at him fiercely. The
man, however, defended himself with great coolness, and
after a ;contest of two or three minutes succeeded in
pinning the animal in a corner. The labourets, who
had witnessed the fight from without, then seethe' that
there was no further danger, came in and despatched it.

SCHOOL FOR THE BLIND.

On the 6th an examination and musical
of the blind pupils of the -London Society for Teaching
the Blind to Read and for - training them in industrial 1
occnp .thins took place:at the-institution, Upper Avenue- !
road, Regent's-park, in the presence of a large number
of ladies and gentlemen. The concert was under the !
direction of Mr. Edwin R-trnes, professor of music at !
the society's school, and the programme comprised
selections of sacred and secular music from-the works of:
Haniel, Mozart, Beethoven; Mendelssohn,-J. S: Bach,
Zingarelli, and other eminent composers. In the first
part the choruses- Thus rolling surges rise' and '
'Glorious is Thy name' were much applauded, and two
organ sales, played by William Allen and M try Ann
Condon, and an adagio, Symphony in 0, played- by W.
De Vere Bell, three of the • advanced 'pupils, w ere per-
formed in a manner which showed the careful training
they had undergone, and elicited the marked approba-
tion of the viskors. In the second part three part-songs.
entitled Red Leaves," Summer is flying,' and "rhe--
Peppies ' were-well rendered., as were also three piano-
forte solos, perfermeerespectively-lq IL .I:Ush, W. De
Vere Bell, and Allen. Between - the first and second
parts of the musical performance the-pupils read 'with
much fluency portions of Scripture-from trie.• embossed

as- to the meaning of what they had -read by the Rev.
0. R- Brigstocke, answering the questions propounded

articles.text:
linlIAN SACRIFICES.

OAe of the moit-diffitnlt tasks of Vie Misr Gtvern=
ment.4 India is that of winning._ such.. wild tribea_aa
the a., fiondl to civilisationa In thb annual ` statement
showing the progress and Conditidn'-of India,' recently
issued by the Government, there is a report by Captain
A. C. 11.'Neill, from which it is plain that the practice
of female infanticide has not ceased in the hill tracts of
Orissa; legal evidence, however, is seldom procurable,
and the only check is considered to be an annual visit
at which the agent insists upon seeing all the children
of both sexes, and it is suggested that the head men of
those villages in which the relative number of the sexes
is preportion al should receive some mark of favour
from Government. Although many more female
children are now reared than formerly it is clear
that infanticide must still obtain to a great extent.
Large districts here are inhabited by sacrificing
Khonds. Captain M'Neill was plainly told in the hill
tracts of Bundhasir of Karoonde that compulsion alone
causes them to refrain from human sacrifice. Among
the Khonds of Jeypoor he found an uneasy feeling pre-
vailing under the relinquishment of sacrifice. In the
last three seasons, he writes, the rains had been scanty
in the Karoonde and Jeypoor Khond tracts, and the
crops of cattle suffered much in consequenee. The
Khonds were anxious to revert to their long-cherished
rite, and applied to the pant rajah of Tooamool for per-
mission to sacrifice, and asked him for a meriah, or vic-
tim. This he declined to give stating that human sacri-
fices had been prohibited, but offered them buffaloes and
sheep. The offer was rejected by the Khonds, and they
resolved that, be the consequences what they might, a
public sacrifice should take place at the full moon of
Poosoo last year. The question was then raised where
a victim could be procured, and was solved by a Khond
stating that he would hand over for sacrifice a toorie,'
who, though not purchased as a meriah, was an agrarian
slave, bought for five rupees. The offer having
been accepted, the intended victim, an elderly
woman, was removed to the village of Puckre-
goodah, 'and there he-tvily ironed, and, on an un-
successful attempt on the part of the paut rajah to
rescue her, was taken off and secreted on the hills. The
pant rajah then sent an express to the agent, and within
anhour a guard of 58 sebundies started under a trustworthy
sirdar, marched 52 miles in 38 hours over a very hilly
and rugged country, and reached the scene of sacrifice as the
victim was - being removed to the post erected for her
immolation. The assembled Khonds, at least 5,000 in
number, found themselves at the last moment deprived
of what they fancied no power could dispossess them.
A most determined attempt at rescue was made; but the
sirdar, making a judicious disposition of his small party,
and of fifty matchlockmen sent by the pant rajah, was
able to defeat the attempt, though he 'a as obliged, in
self-defence, to fire when attacked by the Khonds. Too-
amool, the scene of this determined attempt at sacrifice,
is an elevated plateau, rising abruptly from the plains of
Karoonde to a height of 4,000 feet. The plateau is about
50 miles in length, and its extreme breadth from 15 to 20.
miles. It is an undulating country, well watered; the
lower ranges of hills are covered with dense bamboo and
other jungle, the upper ranges are overgrown with a very
rink coarse grass, which in many places attains a height
of 12ft. or loft. No less than 53 intended victims for
sacrifice were rescued in the hill tracts of Orissa in this
one season. In Chinna Kimedy the Khonds, when in-
terrogated regarding the renouncement of the meriah,
endeavoured to avoid the question by evasive replies,
such as—' How can we sacrifice meriahs when the sircar
has taken them away Yet 30 persons dedicated to the
Meriah Goddess, and intended for sacrifice, were rescued
there in the season 1860-61. The Khond chiefs were
invariably carefully exhorted to remain true to their
pledges and not to be led away by the evil counsels of
badly disposed men; the yearly visits of the agency alone
prevent a return to the old state of affairs.

Tilt CARTIER_ OF DUKE PASQUIER.

M. St. Marc Gitardin is now publishing in the Debats
a series of articles on the career of Duke Pasquier. In
the last he relates the following anecdote
What constituted Napoleon's strength in negotiation
and in war was his army, ever formidable to the enemy.
M. Pasquier mentions a curious -testimony of the fear
with which that chief and its force inspired their
enemies. On the evening of the Ist of April,' he
says, I was summoned to a council of war at the
Prince de Schwartzenberg's, and my opinion was
asked as to the necessity of leaving troops in Paris
for the purpose of maintaining order while the
army marched towards Fontainebleau against Napo-
leon. I hesitated to answer, and remarked that I was
not a conipetent judge in such a- matter. However,
being pressed to reply, I said that in my opinion at
least 30,000 men oughtto be ordered to remain. All the
generals present protested agtinst this, and maintained
that only 12,000 or 15,000 could possibly be left in
Paris. I then called attention to the immense popula-
tion of the capital, its vast extent, and the necessity of
occupying the.villages north of the city, where the battle
of the 30th of March had been fought; that a French
'corps d'armee was said to be advancing on that side;
that if they attacked Paris on that side, while the allied
armies •advanced along the Essones • road; it was greatly
to be feared that the faubourgs would rise and
juin the said corps d'areaeo. Notwithstanding my re-
marks, Prince Schwartzenberg declared that it was im-
possible to leave 30,000 men in Paris; the number was
too great. Yet,' I replied, if I may rely on the
muster-rolls, and the rations demanded, the allied troops
can toned in Paris and the environs amount to 160;000
or 170,000 men; so that if 30,000 remain in Paris; you
will still have 130,000 men in the field.' 'Yes, but
how many do you think Napoleon has with him ? '
Not above 40,000, I should say.' 'You are right.'
Well, with 130,000 •ag dust •40;000,- you Will be more
than three to one. Whathave you to fear ?"Oh ! it
is plain enough that you are not a soldier, and that you
di riot -know what that man can do on the field of battle.'
'What a homage,' said M. Pasquier, was this to our
aiany and to Napoleon! I have never forgotten it, and
Lam proud to relate it.'

Tim Dm runs IN WIGAN.—An assistant overseer in
Wigan has been the first to-set at nought the opinion ex-
pressed by Sir George Grey, in the House of Commons,
as well as the views of the public, by striking a large
number of voters off the list because they were in the re-
ceipt of relief. The revising assessors expressed regret
at the course adopted, and the mayor thought the assist-
ant overseer to be a little too officious. The distress in
the town seems to have reached its utmost extent. Out
of nine thousand operatives employed in the cotton trade
only three hundred have any employment at all, and
even that is only partial and precarious.
CONFESSION OF THE KIRKHAM MURDERER.—Patrick
Cain, in custody on the charge of murdering Mr.
Henry Rawcliffe, at Kirkham, has confessed his crime.
On Friday night he called Police-constable Fletcher to
him, and said he must tell the truth—he threw the
poker at the deceased, but he did not intend to kill him.
He expressed regret for the occurrence, and added, 'li
they only spare my life, and don't hang me, I shan't
care.' He said he got the poker out of Jemmy Cain's
house; that he had seen it there three years. Mrs.
Cain, wife of Jemmy (who is in custody for resisting
the police) denies that the poker is hers, and protests
that she has no knowledge of it. The prisoner was
brought up on Monday, and committed on the capital
charge. Michael Kilburn, who was in custody as an
accessory, has been released, there being no evidence
against him.

the 6th the wife of a- labouring man, named Ann

Chelsea. The unfortunate creature was promptly
removed to St: George's Hospital, where, although she
received prompt medical attendance, she gradually sank
and died between two and three hours afterwards.

The interest felt in ballooning just now, gives valne-

Lest any incorrect account of the accident which oc-

fitted for the object desired. Numerous spectators were
expected from Portsmouth, Salisbury, and. Southampton;

only jnst ascertained that, in consequence of the defec-

manager)', the balloon could not be filled in barracks
without a fresh arrangement, which there was not then
time to make; so that the only remaining chance of not
disappointizg the public w;as to fill the balloon at the
gasometer, a distance of' 900 yaills fr,in the barracks;
Strict secrecy was kept to avoid any, crowd, and the -
filling was most saccessfully and vigorously performed
on Monday night by a detachment of soldiers; who
received orders, given with much forethought b3r,Colonel
who.energetically directed everything. Such
were the cheerfniness and :intelligence -of .themen that
Mr. Coxwell remarked of one that he thought he must,
,beforerentistingi-have-had experiencein• balloon filling.
• The weather caused nitteli anxiety., bit the frequent
,chowore yro had during the night had 11111 M the wind, and
!at sunrise there was adeaclfealm,,theugh ithkevety.4li-
-4c.ttion:of a stiffigale corning on, and this we felt in violent
gusts just as the balloon was ready for moving, at seven
a.m. on Tuesday. Then, during a favourable lull, 65-
soldiers, obeyine, Mr. Cox well's signal's under their own
officers with such accuracy as only dis:ipline can insure,
started with their capricious and bulky infant, guiding
it on its way to the barracks by three ropes, Mr. Cox-
well and some others riding aloft in the car at some '
thirty feet from the ground. Our success, however,
met with a check before we had travelled 150 yards,
from the balloon touching a tree; three tears -was the
result. Mr. Coxwell, with his characteristic patience,
took it to a neighbouring field and repaired the damage
done. He proposed, however, to leave the balloon
