way to the bottom, without allowing an instant for the
valve being opened; everything consequently came to
the ground, and our hopes of an ascent on this day were
at an end.

articles.title: AN AffERICAN COLONEL.
articles.text:
AN AffERICAN COLONEL.

The following letter has been addressed to the Times:
Sir,-1 have the honour to request you will give
publicity in your valuable journal to the following stato-
ment of facts, which I am sure you will agree with me
deserve publicity, in order to show the state of affairs
rind feeling in North America. I was travelling on the
Baltimore and Washington Railway this morning, and.
had occasion to stop at Relay House to wait two hours
for a train. While there a train containing rebel pri-
soners arrived. I remarked to an officer of the United
States' army, who happened to be standing near me, that
they were fine-looking men; to which he replied that
they were so if lice and dirt could make them so. I
stated that that had nothing to do with it, and that they
were in my opinion fine men. He then asked me who
was? I replied, An Englishman.' He said, Yes, a d—d
infernal Englishman.' 1 replied that I supposed he must
be a Yankee of that description. He then seized my
arms, which were folded, pushed me off the railway
platform nearly on to an engine first, and then back,
and kicked me as I fell. Meanwhile I naturally
resisted, and aimed a blow with my right fist at his
face, which only took partial effect, fortunately for
him. He then fetched a guard to take Me prisoner,
which I quietly assented to. He brougllt me to Balti-
more, and took me before the Provost Marshal. I sent
for Mr. Bernal, the English Consul, who came at Once,
and I appearedlface to face with my accuse; Lieutenant-
Colonel Massy, 2nd Marvlands. General Wool read
his charge, to which I replied that it was in the main
correct, but that I felt deeply insulted at the lieu-
tenant-colonel forcibly pushing me back, to which
General Wool said I was wrong to express my opinion
so freely, and that the lieutenant-colonel was also wrong
ia using three to me. The General advised me to leave this
town forNewYork at oxce, and that he could not give me
leave to visit the Federal army, as I had expressed
Southern Secession ' opinions. I replied that I was
willing to do SO, but wished to have s mite satisfaction
from him for the brutal treatment I had experienced
from a United States' officer. Lie said Lieutenant-
Colonel Massy would afford me personal satisfaction,
but as to any other I must apply to the civil power. 1
told him I did not require personal satisfaction, but
military. He declined having anything more to say. I
then retired with the consul, and am now en route for
New York. Such facts speak for themselves. I only
wish them to be known in England, that travellers may
know what to expect in the North United States.
General Wool also advised me to leave the town as
speedily as possible, as it was not safe for me to remain.
I am, Sir' your obedient servant,
Baltimore, Sept 20. G. LONGLEY, Major, R.E.

articles.title: HARVEST HOME.
articles.text:
HARVEST HOME.

Among:the harvest-home celebrations one held at
Abrewas, on the estate of the Earl of Lichfield, is much
talked of. There was Divine 'service at the parish
church in the rdorning,, which was much decorated for
the occasion, and the congregation generally wore floral
or cereal decorations on their dress. After the service
there was a dinner, presided over by the Earl of Lich-
field, at which 220 persons sat down, a few speeches fol-
lowed:and the noble earl's, health having been drunk,
he, in responding, said there was nothing that a person
in his position, with the control. of A large estate, 'could
feel so much interested in as the good feeling which vt as
evinced on all occasions when he met them. He had
been present on many interesting occasions in that
locality, but he did not know that he had ever been
more pleased than he had been on that day. That plea-
sure arose from two principal causes. One was the assem•
bling together of landlords, tenants, and labourers, which,
he hoped, • now would become a permanent institu-
tion, as it was evidence of an improved .moral and
religious feeling in the country. The other principal
cause of pleasure - Was that it brought together all
classes, in whatever condition they might be, and
created a consequent sympathy and interest which was
of the deepest value and would be attended with the
happiest results. After referring to the distress exist-
ing in Lancashire and other parts of the kingdom, the
noble earl alluded to the advantages which the labouring
classes enjoyed in that neighbourhood, and the improve-
ment which had taken place' in their general comfort,
observing that, notwithstanding all those advantages,
there was still greater happiness in store for those who
brought up their children aright, and who lived virtuous
and happy lives themselves. As long as the world re-
mains (continued his Lordship) there will be a great
difference between the highest and the lowest, and it is
only natural to conclude that 'he who has lived re-
spected by his neighbours will in times of misfortune or
distress meet with that sympathy from those around
him which Will afford happiness unenjoyed by others.
Tea was afterwards served to 200 women. - -

THE EASTERN FISHERIES.—The herring fishery is
progressing favourably. The deliveries of fish at Great
Yarmouth have been good, and prices have been well
supported at Lowestoft as well as Yarmouth. Active
preparations are being made for the autumnal voyage,-
and arrivals of fish continue to take place from the North
Sea.

A correspondent of the Freeman reports the following
attempt at abduction A desperate attempt was made
on -the night of the 30th ult. to -carry off by force from
her father's house,. near Sligo, a respectable young
woman named Eliza Davy. A man named Michael
O'Connor (a rejected suitor), accompanied by three other
men, armed, having obtained admittance, O'Connor
seized the girl and forced her outside the door, and
placed her in a car which he had in waiting, while two
of the men who accompanied him held her sister and a
servant girl and prevented them from giving any alarm.
However, the sere .ms of the young woman so frightened
the horse that he commenced kicking, broke the shafts
of the car, and ran off, as did also O'Connor and his
companions on he,tring persons approaching to the
rescue. The girl immedittely returned to her father's
house. She was dreadfully frightened, but received no
other injury. Her father could render no aid at the
time of the abduction, he being ill in bed. O'Connor
has been arrested and committed to gaol. None of the
other three men ' can be identified by any of Davy'..2
family.'

A correspondent states that a dispute took place on
Friday morning between two men, named James
Ormonde- and James Sheeran, who were drawing turf
from the bog ,of Coolraine, near Mountrath, when the
'latter struck the former a blow on the head with his
closed fist, which knocked him down, and ho almost in-
stantly expired. Sheeran was immediately arrested and
committed to gaol, pending an inquest. The prisoner
appelis to feel very much the unfortunate occurrence,
as ()monde and he were a:ways good friends.

EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE.

Mr. John jermings, director; secretary, an share-
hblder of the North Carrock Mining Company, has been
summoned before Aldermin Gabriel, at Gurldha.ll, for
unlawfully, and by means of false pretences, obtaining
two dividend warrants, for the respective sums of
£ll5 9s. 11d. and £l9 55., and four banker's cheques,
for the respective sums of £l2 10s., £l7 Bs. 3d., £l3 its,
and £2l 48. 9d., irom Messrs. Newton, Keates, and Co.,
of Liverpool; and the summon; further alleged that
the defend4nt had not accounted for any portion of the
value of the said securities.

Mr. Metcalfe, for the prosecution, said he was in-
structed on the part of the directors of the North Carrock
Mining Company to place this case before the court.
The company was originally formed for the purpose
of working a particular mine, and the defendant was,
some ten months ago appointed secretary. He also
held some shares, and lied been a director. His salary
as secretary was £5 per month. In August last it was
proposed to purchase some property in connexion with
the mine a!ready the property of the company; but as the
funds would not admit of it the speculation was aban-
doned, to the great annoyance of the defendant, who
had suggested it. He therefore refused to produce the
books he had in his care; and other circumstances tran-
spired which led to his dismissal from the secretaryship.
He acquiesced in that dismissal until the 11th .of Sep-
tember, when he obtained access to the office and pos-
session of the books and a letter containing the securities
mentioned in the information upon which the summons
nas granted. The amount of those securities was £199,
and although they had fai ed in tracing some of them,
they had ascertained that others had been actually
cashed, and no account rendered of the money. Under
these circumstances the present charge was preferred.
Mr. Jesse John Tustin said the defendant was ap-
pointed secretary pro tern, on the 6th of February last.
There was no subsequent appointment with regard to
the,secretitryship; and, nothing was mentioned in the
resolution of the directors about salary, but an arrange-
ment was afterwards made by which the defendant re-
ceived a per month. I acted as chairman of the com-
pany. The defendant acted as secretary before he was
appointed, and the last payment made to him as salary
was on the 11th of August last. On the 13th of the
same month there was a board meeting, which was ad-
journed to the 14th. The defendant was present on
both days, and ultimately, after refusing to produce his
books left the meeting in consequence of the directors
declining a proposal of his in connection with an addi-
tional parch Ise which he wanted the board to
make. I did not feel inclined to find the money
for that purchase, and the company had no funds. I
have not seen him since but I have been informed by
a clerk that on the 11th of September the defendant
called at the office at No. 7, Tokenhouse-yard, ab-
stracted from a box certain books, and also took away
with him a letter from Messrs. Newton, Keates, and
Co. On the 21st of August, in consequence of defen-
dant's absence a letter was addressed to him requiring
him to place al the company's books, papers, and docu-
ments then in his possession under the control of the
directors; and upon his not complying with that requi-
sition they, on the 25th August, took possession of the
box, and then ascertained that EOM of the books had
been abstracted. The books, &c., missing were the
banker's pass-book and cheque-book, the petty cash-
book, the articles of association, and the key of the
common seal of the company. On the 28th of August
a resolution was passed dismissing defendant from the
secretaryship, but no notice of such resolution or dis-
missal was forwarded to the defendant. I knew the
defendant was about, and also knew where to find him.
The defendant sent a reply to the letter of the 21st of
August, requiring him to give up the company's books,
&c., in which he explained the reason of his continued
absence to be that the offices were to undergo repairs
and to be repainted, and as soon as the work was done
he would return to his duties. On the 14th of August
a firm of the name of Newton, Keates, and Co., of Liver-
pool, were indebted to the company in the amount of
£199 Bs. 11d, for lead supplied, and the letter acknow-
ledging the receipt of the securities to that amount and
the receipt are in the handwriting of and signed by the
defendant. The endorsement on the cheque which has
been cashed is also in the defendant's handwriting. It
has passed through the London and Westminster Bank.
Mr. Lewis: I am quite willing to admit the receipt
of the cheques, and cashing them also. My client
claims a certain sum, and has only secured himself by
what he has done, so as to enable him to litigate the
question if necessary.
Mr. Tustin (cross-examined) :—On the 28th his dis-
missal was entered on the minutes, but no notice sent to
him, and on the same day he was removed from his
office as director.

Mr. Lewis :" Was that at the meeting of "directors or
shareholders-?

Witness: It was an extraordinary meeting.
Mr. Lewis: So it seems. (Laughter.) But it was a
meeting of the board, was it not?
Witness : No, Sir; it was a meeting of the share-
holders. He was dismissed from the secretaryship at a
meeting of the board of directors, and from the direc-
tory by a meeting of shareholders.
Mr. Lewis: Now, at the meeting of the 14th of
August, did not thedefendant say he would not sit at
the board to permit such a deception to be practised on
the shareholders as to take away the best mine?
Witness: No, sir, not in those words.
Mr. Lewis: Did he not say that he would withdraw
his attendance from the board rather than see the share-
holders plundered?
Witness: No, sin
Mr. Lewis: Did he not say, he would not attend if
such a matter were allowed to go on?
Witness? He did, sir. Ido not admit that he said he
would not attend. I only recollect there' was some
noise, and a good deal of bluster.
Mr. Lewis: Who were the directors left after you
removed defendant and Mr. Hodgson?
Witness: Myself, my son, and my intimate friend
Mr. W. Bayley Bray.
Mr. Lewis: And after removing the defendant and the
other gentleman you got the whole matter into your own
hands?

Witness: Yes, sir; but I did not get rid of Mr. Hodg-
son, for I have his letter, which will show the reason of
his leaving.
Mr. Lewis: Are you not aware that defendant has a
large claim against the company for secretary's salary
and director's fees?

Witness: No; his salary was paid regularly—Xl ss.
per week—but there was no money to pay any of the di-
rectors their fees.

Alderman Gabriel; How much money has been paid
upon these shares?
Witness: The banker's book will tell you.
Alderman Gabriel: Have you allotted the shares upon
which you,have received deposits? -
Witness: No, sir. _

Aldermen Gal rid: : That is a very extraordinary pro-
ceeding. Your prospectus states your capital to be
£20,000 in 4,000 shares of £5 each, deposit ss. per
'share, and 15s. on allotment. As there has been no
allotment of shares upon whicdi deposits have been paid,
who were the shareholders who dismissed the defendant
from the board of directors?

Mr. Lewis: How many shareholders were present at
this extraordinary meeting?
Witness: Three, sir. (Great laughter.)
Alderman Gabriel: Who were those?
Witness: Myself, my son, and Mr. Bray. (Renewed
laughter and cheering.)
Mr. Lewis: That is what you call an extraordinary
meeting? (Laughter.)
Alderman Gabriel: Or perhaps you would call it'an
influential meeting of shareholders (Laughter.)
Mr. Lewis; Those were persons who had received
transfers of shares from you to qualify them as directors.
Was any one present at that meeting who had paid one
shilling on his shares?
Witness: Yes. There was a party there who hgd,
paid thousands of pounds.
Mr. Lewis: Who was that?
Witness: Myself. (Roars of laughter.)
Alderman Gabriel: I see by the articles of association
that there are a number of gentlemen's names. put for-
ward as directors in 1860. What became of those
names? _ _ _ . _ _

Witness: They resigned in February, 1862.
Alderman Gabriel: Had they held any shares?
Witness: No, sir.
Alderman Gabriel: Then putting their names in this
prospectus was all a sham?
Witness: No, sir, for they were to have taken shares.
Alderman Gabriel: But you sent out a prospectus to
the public announcing these persons as properly qualified
directors. Would not the public be justified in coming
to the conclusion that all those gentlemen held shares in
the undertaking?

- Witness: Ceitainly, they would.
Alderman Gabriel: Then do you not think it is a
sham and a fraud upon the public to put forth such an
announcement? Ido not hesitate to say that it is a
sham and a fraud on your part towards the public to send
out a book like this, with a list of directors totally un-
qualified according to the articles of your association.
Mr. Lewis: My client was not connected with the
company at that time.
Alderman Gabriel: My observations do not apply to
your client, Mr. Lewis. The whole thing upon the face
of it is a fraud upon the public, and I should advise
you, Mr. Tustin, to have a little more thought in future
before you place yourself again in such an equivocal
position. Really, the public ought to be obliged to you
—(tremendous cheering and laughter)—for bringing this
matter forward as a flagrant instance of the manner in
which companies are got up by persons for the' purpose
of putting money into their own pockets. You have
placed yourself in a most disgraceful position, and I do
not think it necessary to go any further into the case,
I therefore dismiss the summons.

ettrittus.

A letter from Coburg states that ice was found- on the,
surfoce of the water two mornings back, and that a thick
white frost covered the g.trdents.

The bands of all the regiments at Vienna meet daily,
and exercise together for a time, in order to get a uni«
formity in taking the time of music.
A newspaper is spoken of as on the tapis which isle be
issued twice a-week, and be illustrated with photographs of
passing events, vice the word cut superseded.
Two good•looking girls were taken am mg the Gari-
baldians. They were clad as soldiers, and their sex did not
seem so be known to their companions in arms.
The number of visitors at Baden-Baden this season hav-
been over 50,000.
A New York paper says it is understood i at Washington
that from six hundred to eight hundred white persons have,'
been murdered in Minnesota by the Indians, and' that,
two-thirds of the State has been deserted by the white,
settlers.

It appears that there has not been a single act of violerim
Committed in the International Exhibition building since.
the opening, and that the bad money taken has been under
£4O, including only one bad half-sovereign.
_ _

• Alarmed at the increase of drunkenness in the-army, the,
Federal G-,,vernment have stopped the sale of spirits in,
camp, and abolished 'grog' in the navy, the sailors receiv..
ing five cents a-day as compensation. It is said the change'
has produced great dissatisfaction.
. . . _

At the ball- lately given in Seville by the King and -
Queen of Spain, it is stated the ladies who, were invited'
wore diamonds worth at least fifty millions of francs.
At the city registration, on Tuesday, it was stated that'.
one of the old city companies, the combmakers, is on the.
point of extinction, as there is now only one member of the'
venerable body.
It is stated that the wine harvest on the Rhine, and in‘
the surrounding districts promises now to be excellent,
both in quality and quantity. This circumstance tends
considerably to increase the confidence inspired through-
out Germany by the abundant character of the wheat
harvest.
A Varignano telegram informs us that the apparattzs.
got from England on the order of Dr. Partridge has been,
applied to Garibaldi's foot. The suppuration of the
wound has diminished.

A gentleman, while passing through the streets of the
city on Friday, was robbed of his pocket-book, containing
Peruvian Scrip and Certificates and other valuable pro—
perty representing more than £25,000. Fortunately the
numbers of the scrip are known, and its payment has been
stopped.
A. boat race took place a few days since in Toulon
Roads between the flag-ship's hunch and the gig of the
Sylphide yacht, belonging to the Marquis of Downsbire..
Though the latter was steered by a lady, she won by half
a boat's length'
Mr. George Robert Stephenson has this week taken the
whole of the crew of his yacht, the St. Lawrence, to see
the International Exhibition. They were quartered at his
town house, treated to the Exhibition and the theatres,
and had every expense paid for them to London and back.
The French Jockey Club have declined to alter the-
running of the Grand Prize at Paris next year from Sun--
day to a week-day, at the suggestion of the English autho—
rities; and many noblemen and gentlemen, it is feared,
will decline to start their horses in consequence.

The number of vessels brought into Queenstown by the
southerly winds is increasing, and now constitutes one of
the largest fleets that has ever occupied that capacious
harbour—numbering, as they do, at least 300 sail. The
vast m tjority of these are grain laden, fr,,m ports in the
Mediterranean and Black seas and New York. Already
the market has manifested the effect of so I,,rge an influx,
of grain, and there appears every probability of a further
reduction in prices.

An amusing tygographical error occurred the other
day among the list of subscribers to the Garibaldi Surgical
Fund. 'A poor bookbinder' gave 55., and the next sub-
scriber in order was an Italian lady, married to an English
gentleman named Fletcher. This lady's name is A. Legit
Fletcher, but her subscription was acknowledged as from
'a ledger stitcher.'
The French sloop Bossuet, of Nantes, 210 tons, bound
from the Island of Sardinia to Dunkirk, with a cargo of
lead ore, went on shore on the 4th inst. at 1 a.m. at Am-
bleteuse, three miles from Boulogne.
It is rumoured (says the United Service Gazelle) that
the Rongership of Greenwich Park, vacant by the death
of Earl Canning, is to be conferred on his Royal Highness
the Duke of Cambridge. The ranger's Louse is being-
fitted up firr the residence of his Royal Highness Prince
Arthur.

His Excellency Count Bernstorff, it is definitively-
arranged, will resume his post as Minister Plenipotentiary
and Envoy Extraordinary at the Court of St. James's, A
telegram from Berlin conveys instructions to prepare the-
Prussian Legation for the count and countess's arrival in
about a fortnight.
In. the war in Spain the French General Ilarispe
issued a proclamition forbidding the peasantry to supply
the English with provisions or forage on pain of death; it-
stated that we were savages, and, as a proof of this, our
horses were born with short tails. This absurd proclama-
tion, was published in French and the Basque languages,
and distributed all over the country.
. . _ _

At Gainsborough, the other day, at a dinner of the
Rifle Corps, Major Hutton said he had bad the pleasure
some little time ego of visiting Garibaldi at Caprera. The
first thing spoken of on reaching his house was the
Volunteer movement. I consider it,' Garibaldi said, to
be the finest thing England ever did.' For a full hour he
continued to put questions about the movement, and in
bringing the conversation to a close he said, So long as
this movement lasts, England never need fear an enemy.'
We hear that Liverpool is busy in preparing to send out
all sorts of stores and materiel for the Confederate party
in America, and that, amongst other things, a large iron
steam ram is being openly built at a yard in the Mersey
for their behoof.

The -deat h of Major- G eneral Sir John Inglis, K C.B. ,
will cause no army promotions, inasmuch as the gallant
officer was on the supernumerary list of general officers
promoted fax distinguished service. The Colonelcy cf the
32nd Light Infantry and th lonian Islastds command are
however, rendered vacant.----

-On Sunday last a Methodist minister in the west of
Cornwall, having bo preach to a crowded audience, and
the heat being very oppressive, said before ho gave out his
text, I have seen men strip ta curse, and sweqr, and fight,
and run a race; and now I will take off my coat to preach
the Gospel, and lam not ashamed to do it.' He then took
off his coat and preached in his shirt sleeves.

A correspondent os the Express says :—There is an
article now in the market called rice meal, which is nothing
more than fine sawdust. Put a certain quantity in a
saucepan, and boil it for, say, a quarter or half hour, the
water will be only just stained, and the sawdust then will
show itself in a perfect state. The sawdust is made from
beech timber. Never was there a more wicked fraud ;.
cattle fed with a mixture of this stuff would almost
certainly die.
. _ _

It appears that the exportation of arms and ammu-
nition from this country is rapidly increasing in propor-
tion to the prolongation of the American war, and that the.
shipments during the first eight months of this year have
amounted in value to £1,303,000, or at the rate of about
£1,750,000 per annum. During the month of August the
quantity was especially large, amounting to £286,110.
Captain D. Robertson, R.N., has been appointed by
the Royal National Lifeboat Institution its assistant in.
spector of lifeboats. The fleet of lifeboats of the institu-
tion having so largely increased, the appointment of an
additional inspector had become indispensable. Captain
Robertson had prev;ously filled the office of honorary
secretary of two branches of the Lifeboat Society; he has
therefore had considerable experience of the important
duties that will devolve on him.

A gentleman well acquainted with the property of
Colonel Hare and with the tenants who signed the address
to him, expressive of indignation on account of the atro-
cious mutder of Mr. Braddell, has informed us that some
of those very tenants whose signatures were affixed to
that address were, with their families, englged in the
daily repeating of the Rosary' for the preservation of
Hayes and for a successful escape from the constabulary.
This was their practice at the very time that the address
was in preparation and in course of signature. What is
the value of such an address? Can we wonder that the
murderer still evades justice?
Part of the jewellery intended for the marrive of the
Princess Pia with the King of Portugal is exhibited by
Mr. Hancock. It includes complete suite of diamonds
of novel pattern, and some very beautiful ornaments com-
posed of diamonds' rubies, and pearls. Mr. Hancock has
just dispatched a bracelet, presented to the Princess by
Lady Dinorben, the centre being a horshoe of diamonds,
inclosing the device A. E. I. in emeralds, rubies, and
diamonds, which represent the colours of Italy, red,
white, and green.
The large tract of land so long devastated by the Middle
Level floods has been at length got clear of the water.
The soil generally turns up very mellow-looking, but grave
doubts are expressed as to the probability of crossing the
land next year. The extensive breach which was the
immediate cause of the inundation has been nearly filled
up. On the site of the coffer dam a most stupendous work
is in progress—the fixing of the syphons for permament
draining of the 140,000 acres of Middle Level district. It
is computed that each syphon will discharge 3,000 gals.
per minutel which for the sixteen syphons will give an
aggregate discharge of 2,880,000 gals. per hour. It is said,
however, that even this will be insufficient to carry off the
waters from the extensive district drained by the cut.
Several hundred men are still at work.
The Pacific Telegraph Company have erected their
wires between the Missouri and the Sierra Nevada, and
thus completed the telegraphic communication between
the Atlantic and Pacific in four months and seventeen
days. The companY have entered into an arrangement
willw t h
construct
t conjointly, they
Erunactpearcoornotfinirousssialinebythwrohuieghll British and Rus-
sian America, across Behring's Straits, and through Asia-
tic and European Russia, so as to connect Petersburg and
Washington. This line will be 14,000 miles in length.
Russia has already completed' 3500 miles, and collected
materials for extending the wires fromsiberia:to the mouth
of the Amoor, the Mississippi of Asiatic Russia.
A singular atmospheric phenoraenon was observed near
Yvetot (Seine-Inferieure) three evenings since, about six
o'clock, by several persons ‘7llO were walking along the
Havre road. The sky was covered with dark clouds, and
gusts of wind with occasional flashes of lightning in the
west seemed to portend 0, storm. All at once a strange
appearance presented itself in the south-west horizon. Tee
clouds seemed to forta an inclined plane sloping down to
the shores of a lake, the blue waters of which were rippled
by a gentle breeze. The lake seemed to be surrounded
by trees of unequal height, and the whole back ground of
the picture presented the aspect of a vast amphitheatre.
This mirage remained visible till lost in the darkness of
night.

articles.title: EZIESID ENT LINCOLN' P.ROCLAHATION:
articles.text:
EZIESID ENT LINCOLN'
P.ROCLAHATION:

President Lincoln has issued a proclamation, stating;
that the war would be continued to re,tore the Con-
stitational relation.s between the States, and that he
shall again recommend the next Congress to adopt a
practical measure, tendering pecuniary aid for the free
acceptance or rejection of those States now in retellion
which may adopt immediate or gradual abolition of
slavery within their limits. Efforts to cot nise ne_re3s
with their consent will be continued. The President
' further proclaims that on January 1, 1863, all slaves
within any State or part of a State, the people wheleof
shall then be in rebellion against the Federal Govern-
ment, shall be then, thenceforward, and for e%er t es.
The Federal Executive an naval and military autho-
rities will recognise and maintain the freedom of such
persons, and will do no acts to repress them in any
-efforts they may make for their actual freedom.
The Federal Government will designate on the let
January the States and parts of States which will then
be in rebellion; and the fact that any State or the
people thereof shall on January Ist be in good faith
represented in the United States Congress, by members
chosen at elections wherein the mak), ity of the qualified
'voters of such States shall have participated, shall in the
-absence of strong countervailing testimony, be deemed
conclusive evidence that such State and the people
thereof have not been in rebellion against the United
States. The President orders the military and naval
zauthorities specially to observe the acts of Congress
prohibiting the return of fugitive slaves, and calls atten-
tion to that portion of the Confiscation Act referring
apecially to slaves. The proclamation states that the
Federal Government will in time recommend that all
citizens who have remained loyal throughout the rebel-
lion shall, upon the restoration of Constitutional rela-
tions, be compensated for all losses, including hos of
slaves, by acts of the United States. •

articles.title: AFRICAN SETTLEMENTS.
articles.text:
AFRICAN SETTLEMENTS.

The colonial blue book' recently issued comprises
reports from our settlements on the West Coast of
Africa. From Sierra Leone we learn that the census
taken in 1860 found a population of 41,624, with 11,418
dwellings. 15,782 of the population were liberated
Africans, and 22,593 had been born within the limits of
the colony. Of the whole population only 3,351 re-
mained Pagans, and only 1,734 were Mahomedans.
15,180 were Methodists, and 12,954 Episcopalians.
11,016 children were taught in the schools in
the year. The Governor reports that the Customs
receipts have increased to £20,000, and that the
internal trade of the colony is steadily growing, owing
partly to the number of small native traders who
have started in business of late years, and partly to
facilities afforded by credit being given for import duties.
British protection supplies a stimulug to native improve-
ment and enterprise, and the population are rapidly
learning
i the generous customs of civilised society, en-
gaging n commercial transactions with surprising dili-
-gence and avidity, submitting on the one hand to the
various necessary imposts, and on the other gladly reap-
the benefits of enlarged communication, and in many
instances amassing wealth enabling them to vie with
European enterprise. Sierra Leone is thus proving not
only a refuge for those who are rescued from slavery, but
-a nucleus of civilisation and school of Christian teaching.
A general subscription had been made for erecting a
permanent arch to replace the temporary one binder
which Prince Alfred passed on his visit to Sierra Leone.
From Gambia the Governor reports a great
• want of labour. ' Cotton, he says, is grown extensively
in the interior, but only because there are no means of
transporting ground-nuts and other produce to the coast.
to be bartered for the cotton manufactures of Great
Britain, and therefore the people grow the material and
.manufacture country cloths for themselves. These cloths
form a ready currency throughout the Gambia and
adjacent rivers, and for all trade purposes are as potent as
the 'mighty dollar.' The growth of cotton, however, is
only for home use and for barter with neighbouring tribes
for rice, and not for export; the native prefers light labour
.and quick returns of thenut farm. But the Governor con-
--eiders that with cleaning gins supplied to them, and the
transport lightened, the natives might be convinced that
the-cultivation of cotton for export is to their advantage.
From the Gold Coast the Governor writes that the na-
tives can live with little labour, and the mass appear to
have no ambition to do more than live. In the erection
of a church in the town of Cape Coast it has been ne-
-cessary to bring labourers front Sierra Leone for the
Gold Coast men were found so intolerably indolent, as
well as independent, that the -building made very- slow
progress in their hands. The population is sparse;
you may travel for hours in-the-interior and not meet
With a human being. The superstitions of the
people would prevent a census being taken, but the
number within the protectorate is estimated at about
-450,000, of whom 00,000 live on the seaboard, or
within a day's journey from the coast. The exports of
1860 amounted to £110,475. The presence of British
government exercises. says the Governor, an im-
mense moral influence on the seaboard of the pro •
tectorate, and to some considerable distance into
the interior, and the external slave trade is extin-
guished here; but, if the object be to raise the people
in the scale of c:vilization he considers that funds
must be found foe extending the judicial system,
so essential in a semi-barbarous country, where
reverence for the law should be made the primary
step in the attempt to govern. The local Govern-
ment does not possess the means to carry out the ad-
ministration of justice beyond a limited distance from
the forts on the coast, and consequently, many. barbarous
Fetish rites and extortionate acts are practised in the far
interior. At the same time, the Governor is of opinion
that there is no possible way of increasing the revenue
to any extent, owing to the peculiar position of these
settlements with reference to those of the Netherlands
Government; so that, in his view, with the British
public alone rests the further progress of the settlements
on the Gold Coast.' He remains, however, that the
chiefs living far from the coast are glad of British pro-
. tection, and so anxious not to be left to the mercy of
the King of Ashantee and his chiefs that the dread of
them aids our rule in quarters where otherwise we
should have the least control.

CURIOUS CRINOLINE MISHA.P.-011 the evening of
Sunday a congregation in the neighbourhood of Whitby
were suddenly, and as if by magic, plunged into total
dartness. The cause was that crinoline had just
entered; a lady's dress caught in the key of- the gas
meter, the lady dragged the crinoline, the crinoline
_dragged the key, and the light was locked Out.
SLEEPING OUT or Towx.—We will assume that you
ere living at Richmond, which is barely to he reckoned
as country. You happento be late for breakfast, swallow
it hastily, lest the train be missed, and either take an
imperfect meal, or take it with a rapidity which taxes
digestion. Munching a bit of toast as you hurry along,
you are thrown into a flurry by hearing the whistle of
the approaching engine; you set off running at full
speed, and dash into the station blown and heated. *Dr.
C. B. Williams-alludes to this anxiety 'about catching
the train al peculiarly dangerous to persons with any
disease of the heart. I have known sudden deaths and
several aggravations of valvular lesions to be caused in
this way.' But you.are happily at ease on that score;
there is nothing wrong about your heart. Still you
have reached the carriage greatly heated, and are whirled
to London at a rapid pace, the cold air blowing upon
Your heated body from the. open window or windows.
The risk of a sore throat, bronchitis, low fever, or at
least a cold, is considerable. Perhaps after all you have
missed the train. You have then to cool down,' much
exasperated, on a windy platform, or in a waiting-room
dreadful with draughts. Three quarters of an hour or
more are !Vent in vexatious weariness, and by the time
you get into the carriage -you are thoroughly chilled.
The cold air, which was dangerous when you were heated,
is not less dangerous now you are chilled; but yourfellow-
passengers cannot think of having the window closed.
You get to town, go about your business, and in the
evening have to repeat the experience of the morning.
How many days in the course of the season are these risks
incurred? and what amount of benefit derivable from
sleeping in the country can fairly counterbalance them?
—Cornhill Magazine.

articles.title: CIRCASSIAN- CHIEFS AT lIACCLESFIALD,
articles.text:
CIRCASSIAN- CHIEFS AT
lIACCLESFIALD,

On the 3rd October the two Circassian chiefsewhe have
visited this country for the purpose of presenting an
address to the Qaeen, attended a meeting held at
Macclesfield Town Hall. The object of the address,
which was presented during the month of September,
was to obtain protection from the Queen of -England
against the Russians. The Circassian chiels. came
over to this country in the capacity of delegates, pre-
sented the address and received a formal reply from
the Foreign-office, intimating that England could not
interfere in the matter. Tee Circassian chiefs have
accordingly visited the north, apparently with a view
of enlisting sympathy in their behalf. On Thursday
they attended a meeting at Preston; and within a day
or two they will visit Manchester. The meeting on
Friday was called by large placards of a somewhat sensa-
tional character, which quoted the opinions of Mr.
Urquhart and Lord Ponsonby as to the treatment of the
Circassian people. The announcement that the chiefs
would appear m their native costumes attracted a 'large
audience, the hall .being well filled. About half-past
seven Mr. S. E. Rolland, the two Circassian chiefs,
Colonel Lapinski, commander of the Polish legion in
Circassia, and a few working men, ascended the plat-
form. The chiefs were attired in long, loose, blue
coats, with red facings, and on their heads they wore
hats combining the characteristics of the bearskin and
the artilleryman's bat. They carried long swords, and
daggers were also stuck in their girdles. They are
tall, goodlooking men, and one of them especially would
pass for an Englishman. A look of deep seriousnees
adds to the somewhat strikieg characterS of their
appearance. They remained covered during the pro-
ceedings. Mr. Thomas Norbury, a working-man, was
voted to the chair, and the proceedings were opened
with the usual formalities of plaettrd reading.
Mr. S. E. Rolland said it was no light matter that
he had to introduce to the meeting. He was using no
rhetorical flourish nor oratorical trick when he told
them that there never was an event of greater import-
ance than that which was now taking place. Whom
had they before then? The placard had furnished the
answer—apparently simple in itself, but still full of
serious meaning. Was not Poland a dead nation, and
was not Circassia a nation, all but dying with the
sword and dagger in its grasp? Grevious as might
be the distress from which our operatives were suffer-
ing, and black as might be our future what was all
that as compared with the feelings of Colonel Lapinski,
who belonged to a nation without a foot of soil to call
their own, whose very language was proscribed, whose
sons were forbidden to read their own tongue, whose
daily food was stripes, whose daily drink was tears.
Such was a Pole, and such was one of the gentlemen
now present. At his side were two men of whom he could
not trust himself to speak; no words of his could con-
vey the simple and child-like, yet heroic words in
which they had, in his hearing, recited the story of
their lives, and their anticipations as to the future.
One of those Circassian chiefs for 45 years had been
engaged in struggling sword in hand against the
Russians, and he had seen the blood of his compatriots
quenching the blazing rafters of the village where they
lived. He had told chiefs that at the present
time the people of England themselves wanted help,
but that notwithstanding that, they would help the
Circassion people. That day, their words to him -were:
We are men devoted to death, and all we hope is
that the Muscovite plough may not be driven over our
sepulchres.' At a meeting at Preston, on Thursday
evening, at which he (Mr. Rolland) was present, the
chiefs expressed themselves thus
'We are as near despair as brave men can be; we
are in the fire night and day. We have heard of the
English nation, and we have been told that it protects
the distressed; and our wives, our children, our old
men, and our little ones said, with tears in their eyes,
"You must yo to that nation and get us help." They
said that we must go to the English nation and tell
them that, if they would not help us, we must be
destroyed by Russia. For forty years, every hour of
the day and night, our houses and our villages have
been in flames, our sons' throats have been cut, and
our old men have been killed. Unless the English
nation help us we must die, for there is no one to whom
we look for help but to the people of England.' Mr.
Rolland then proceeded to read the address recently
presented to the Queen, and the reply of the Foreign-
office thereto. Respecting the latter he said that they
needed no comment of his upon this most infamous,
most vile, and most atrocious answer, which was but
the logical consequences of the betrayal on the part,
not of the people of England, but of its government, of
these gallant mountaineers. After further pressing the
claims of the Circassian-people, and giving much in-
teresting information respecting the country itself and
its inhabitants. Mr. Rolland introduced Colonel
Lapinski and the Circassian chief to the meeting.
Each made a short speech, which w as interpreted to
the audience.

A PROVIDENT HUSBAND.-A few days ago, Catherine,
the wife of John Clarke, residing in South-street, Mil-
burn-place, North Shields, died, and was interred in a
coffin whichlad been provided for her by her husband
about twenty years prior to her death. John Clarke,
the husband of the deceased, is well known for his
eccentric notions. He formerly resided at Coble-dene,
and in one room of his house were placed the coffins of
himself and family, which he had made re2dy in case of
death. The coffins, which were made of mahogany,' and
French polished, bore the names of the members of the
family for whom they were intended. Some of the
family have died, and have been interred in their respec-
tive coffins.

THE CONDEMNED MURDERESS. - Catherine Wilson,
who is ordered for execution on Monday, the 20th, still
continues, in Newgate' the same . callous indifference
which has characterised her ever since she has been in
custody. She has only been visited once by a person, a
female, who described herself as a friend. She appears
to have no relations, as no one has visited her in that
capacity. She still professes not to have heard a single
word of what the 'gentleman' (as she calls the judge)
said to her in passing sentence, and appears to have no
alarm at the prospect of death which awaits her. Mr.
Neale, the solicitor who defended her, has sent anaemo-
iial on her behalf to the Home Secretary, but beyond
that no section of the public has made a movement, by
petition or otherwise, to obtain a commutation of the
sentence.—Observer.

Major Myles O'Reilly, the 'heroic' member for
Longford, has addressed a letter to the Dublin Morning
News from Brussels, in which he states that a number
of leading Roman catholics have resolved to call a meet-
ing of their co-religionists in Louvain during the present
month. This meeting, which will be similar in its
object to the German and Swiss Pius Verein,' will
take council on catholic interests throughout the
world.' Its first effort, as regards Belgium, will be the
establishment thereof of a Pius Verein ' Association;
but, as it is hoped that the meeting will be attended by
representative Roman catholics from all countries, its
deliberations and its sympathies are •to extend to all
catholic interests.' Mr. O'Reilly promises to keep his
Roman catholic countrymen informed of every step taken
by this congress which has 'originated with the well-
known M. Dupeliaux, and men whose names will com-
mand the confidence of Catholic Europe.'
Curox.A. SillPS.—Althoagh very little progress is
being made in the building of the Royal Sovereiga.
cupola ship, the fact must not be looked upon as being
altogether unsatisfactory. According to present in-
tentions, the armament of the Royal Sovereign has
been fixed upon to consist of eight guns, protected by
cupolas. The two centre ones are to be of the heaviest
now known, and the remaining six to be of Sir William
Armstrong's or Mr. Whitworth's 110-pounders. The
Royal Sovereign is in a state to enable the dockyard
people to strengthen her in such a manner as would
enable her to carry even one of the monster Horsfall
guns' weighing 24 tons. It is quite a mistake to sup-
pose that because our seamen have hitherto looked
upon the old service 68-pounder as the heaviest piece
ordnance to be managed on board ship, guns of great
weight and calibre should not be introduced
into the navy. Many of our naval officers can bear
testimony to the fact that some of our bloodiest en-
gagements were fought with guns of very light weight,
and that when eighteens, twenty-fours, and. thil ty-
twos were introduced into the service it was supposed
that we had reached a pitch of destructive power not
to be easily surpassed. We now talk as coolly of 70-
pounders, 110-pounders, aud 150 pounders as in olden
times we conversed upon the 'pop-guns,' which under
Falkner, Pellew, Seymour, Phillimore, and other dashf
ing capturers of enemy's frigates, did such excellent
execution, and with the introduction of steam und:per-
fe4ion of machinery we cannot- be reconciled to the
absence of the largest known manufactured guns from
our floating batteries. The Americans have shown us
that where there is a will there is a way. Our Ad-
miralty coach is heavily dragged, and if its passengers
were not well able to pay for the horsing, there would
inevitably be a terrible upset. The Royal Sovereign
should be hastened on to completion, and the question
of her guns should remain, under existing circum-
stances, an open one.

articles.title: COLLISION &IV THE NORTS-BAST_EEN
articles.text:
COLLISION &IV THE NORTS-BAST_EEN

JZAILWAY.

A very serious accident occurred near Milford Junc—
tion, a few miles from York, on the 3rd Oct., which re-
sulted fatally, and Wit& attended with much destruction
of property. It appears-that a heavy goods train from
Darlington, consisting of about forty carriages, laden
with pig iron, arrived at the Sherburn-branch end of
the Old Junction (which runs and joins to the Bull
main line) about 11.15 p.m. At the same moment a
Hull goods train, laden with grain, was passing along
this loop line, which joins the main line in an oblique
direction, near to the Sherburn station. Both trains
were proceeding with some degree of velocity; conse—
quently when, through some misunderstanding or
negligence in the signalling, the two trains unfor—
tunately met, the shock must have been terrific. The
left butter of the Hull engine struck the right front of
the approaching one from Darlington, and shattered a
large portion of the latter to pieces. The sudden inert—
ness of the front acting against the mornemum of the
latter portion of the Darlington train caused the wag-
gons to burst asunder in the middle and take a side-
ways direction. Some of them struck the engine-tender
and crumpled' it to pieces like a piece of tissue paper.
Some 20 to 30 yards of the main line was torn up, and
the debris caused by this and other means had the effect
of stopping the traffic for some time. The driver of
the northern train was jeiked off his engine a long dis-
tance on to some waggons, and was taken up very much
shaken and bruised, but fortunately no bones were
broken, and after a few hours he was enabled to depart
home to Darlington. His companion, the stoker, un-
fortunately met with a more melancholy fate. He
seems to have been oiling the fore part of the engine,
when he probably noticed the converging train, and
jumped into the six foot-way to save himself. Here he
must have been knocked down by the loose waggons,
for his mutilated remains were found under one of them,
crushed to the most minute atoms. He was killed in-
stantaneously. His name is Markham, and be has left
a destitute wife and three children, who at present re-
side at Darlington. The driver and fireman of. the
Hull train were also seriously shaken and bruised, but
they sufficiently recovered to proceed to Hull by the
next train. As to the cause of this unfortunate affair,
nothing probably will be known until the inquest takes
place on the body of the deceased, but a knowledgo of
the locality, which may be described as particularly
flat and unobscured. If blame attaches to any one, it
will probably rest between the signal man and the
driver of the Hull goods train. It cannot be believed
that the affair is purely accidental, and consequently a
searching investigation will no doubt result.

articles.title: ANOTIIEB .MARSIIZAND SLUICE DESTBUY.ED.
articles.text:
ANOTIIEB .MARSIIZAND SLUICE
DESTBUY.ED.

KING'S LYNN, Oct. 4.—The series of misfortunes in
the train of the Middle Level catastrophe seem almost
endless. At about six o'clock on Saturday evening
the outfall sluice of the Marshland Sineeth and Fen
drain—an important arterial drain, running into the
Ouse about 200 or 300 yards northward of the ruined
Middle Level sluice—became the subject of an acci-
dent precisely similar to that which destroyed the last-
named work on the 4th of May last. The result has
been again to flood a portion of the fen country, and
the extent of the inundation will very probably be, in
a day or two, as great as that of the celebrated 'Middle
Level deluge.' It may be recollected that in conse-
quence of that 'deluge,' a great quantity of water bad
to be discharged off the drowned lands through the
Marshland Smeeth and Fen drain, and the adjoining
Marshland sewer, both of which run parallel for a
considerable distance to their (Artisan sluices, the one
draining the Fens, and the other the higher lands of
Marshland proper. This unusual test of the two
sluices calmed some apprehension as to their safety;
and in consequence, shortly after the Middle Level in-
undation, both sluices were strengthened by an 'apron'
,of clunch, held up by piles being laid against the
outer face, and the adjoining banks faggoted and
further secured by walls of sheet piling. In the case
of the Smeetb. and Fen drain, these precautions have
proved unavailing.- Nothing peculiar was noticed
about the work until about ten minutes before the in-
jury was fully developed. At that time the sluice-
keeper Smith casually observed what he thought was
a log of 'wood' across the roadway over the sluice-
bridge, and, going to the spot, found it was a deep and
extensive fissure. He had scarcely time to examine it,
when the bank against the southern side of the , sluice
fell in with a crash—leaving a gap of 401 t. width in
the roadway. The cause of this evidently was that
the water rushing down the drain had undermined
and scoured away the earth behind the southern flank
walls of the sluice, exactly as in the case of the Middle
Level sluice, but with this difference, that the sluice
itself (which consists of one arch only) is at present
left standing. It is; however, very much injured; the
bank on the north side is cracking and crumbling in;
and in a tide or two the sluice must inevitably fall into
ruins. In the meantime the water • runs through the
gap it has made for itself, and such is the force of the
stream out, and the tide inward, that the bed of the
drain is partly filled for a hundred yards upward, with
bricks, stone, 'earth, and other debris washed away.
from the sluice. The occurrence took place about an
hour and a half after high water, and of course on
the return of the tide the sea water flowed up the
drain, and though the springs have only just begun to
'put in,' the top of the tido was sufficiently high for
the water to pour over the banks, for a space of some
300 yards above the sluice, into the adjoining Marsh-
land drain, running up into the Marshland internal
drains, and causing great apprehension. It also, at a
distance of a mile or two up the drain, overflowed the
opposite bank, and again flooded some of the identical
lands, in the occupation of Mr. Little, Mr. Robert Coe,
and others, in Marshland Fen, which were drowned
by the bursting of the Middle Level banks, and had
only within the last few weeks been • reclaimed and
brought into cultivation. The flood has also run
through the culverts under the Middle Level drain,
and again drowned some of the land in Broad and
Short Fensi and threatens Bardolph and Stow Fens.
Steps have been taken, by damming, &e., to remedy
the disaster, but the result is yet doubtful.

Four convicts avllo recently escaped from the French
penal settlement Les Hattes, arrived on the 16th ultimo,
under the guidance of a fisherman, at Paramaribo, and were
handed over to the custody of the police. These people
were exposed to all sorts of privations in travelling along
the coast; when they reached Port Oranje after a distressing
journey, they were in a starving condition. Undrr the
subsisting regulations they will, we understand, be returned
to the French government, which would probably rather
have their room than their company.—Demerara Paper.

CENTRALISATION.—Lord 'Stanley, in his speech at
Stockport, made one singularly inaccurate remark. 'I
do not,' he said, hesitate to say that the habit of acting
individually and collectively, without reference to any
central authority, constitutes one of the main distinc-
tions between an energetic and a feeble- community.'
The sentence is intended, we suppose, to deprecate over
centralisation ;but though well meant, it is not histori-
cally true. The most- energetic community which ever
existed was that of Rome, whose patricians habitually
referred everything to a central authority, the Senate.
The people of Franco, whose centralisation is perfect,
whatever their defects, are certainly not a feeble com-
munity ; While the people of Germany, who have no
centre, whatever their merits, certainly are. The de-
feat of the Northerners is at this moment owing to the
absence of that self-restraint which the habit of refer-
ence to a central power always produces; and in Eng-
land the general ,government is far better and stronger
than the parochial administration. The best illustra-
tion of all is, however, the Roman Catholic Church,
whose enormous strength is secured almost entirely by
the practice-which Lord Stanley ,holds to he ,always. a
source of feeblenes. Centralisation may pushed too far,
but so may individualism. We do not want to see all
the trees in'the forest chopped to a pattern, but neither
do we want to see the stars :all wandering on the self-
government principle.—Speetator.,

articles.text:
A VISIT TO Aff 411-1311 CAN

BOSPITAL

(From a Correspondent of the Times.)
WASHINGTON. , 13.8, e3ept. 19.—People my liav
read fall accounts of this- war, from. the firing on tort
Sumter to the invasion of Msryland; accounts of death
on the long march, on the fetid, morass, in the sickly
camp, and on the red field of battles but it is neither the
inspired pen nor the eloquent, voice that can make them
realize in full the horrors of this bloody struggle. It is
to the hospitals, teeming and choking e ith their many
occupants, that they must eas before they can say War
la hellish ; war is diabolicalt'.' There is a shed, dignified
with the name of hospital, in Georgetown, the interior
of which reminds you more of the cattle pens in Copen-
hagen-fields than a sanitary building in .a civilized
country. Here, in one room, are upwards of 60 beds,
so•close to one another that the nurses- can scarce move
about without striking the couch of some poor sufferer
to.whoin the slightest touch is agony,san€l even the vi-
bration. of the floor is pain. Badly.litrbadly ventilated,
the atmosphere humid, stagnant, and reeking with dis-
ease, is this a place in which a man with only a slight
wound can speedily recover, or in which. one bAlly hurt,
though not fatally, will not die?. The doctors do their
best;. the insufficient staff of nurses do their best; bat
it is next to impossible to battle successfully against
sickness in such an overcrowded dismal den.
This place is, I am bound to say, not a type of the
hospitals in Washington and Georgetown. The Douglas,
the Judiciary, the Seminary, and several others I could
name, are well conducted. The one I allude to is only
lately opened, and perhaps the local authorities intend,
in the course of their serene leisure, to improve upon its
present arrangements. I visited it last Saturday evening,
and they in whose minds the horrors of Scutari are still
vivid, can follow me with sympathetic interest as I pass
along the double file of white faces and helpless forms.
Here,. on the first bed, with a coverlet over him which
might have been clean 14 days ago, is a young man
desperately wounded. A piece of his skull the size of
half-a-crown lies on the battle-field of Manassas. There
is a ball in his right thigh, and his left leg was ampu-
tated in the morning. Does he groan? No ; the brave
heart saps the pain, and the utterance knows it not.
Have we whipped them out of Maryland yet?' he asks
with a feeble smile. Opposite to me I see a broken-
hearted mother weeping silently over the yet warm
corpse of her son. For days past he had been yearning
to see her, momentarily expected her, and she has but
just arrived, and he died 10 minutes since. There,
under -the influence of an opiate, sleeps a youth on whose
pallid countenance lurks no suspicion of a beard. On
the next bed a boy, still in his teens, moves in an uneasy
sleep. `The prairie! the wide prairie!' he utters. Poor
fellow. Doubtless he dreams of his far Western home,
his youthful sports, his parents, and the pleasant days of
the long ago. I pass on. Groaning piteously, a short
distance up, lies the skeleton ot a once robust frame.
He is dying by inches. Ten days, he tells me he lay
on the field, almost glued to the earth by his own blood.
He got grains of food and draughts of fluid, but what
they were and who gave them to him he does not know.
Sight left him on the sixth day. 'Take off my host,' he
moans, 'it burns me so.' Delusion. There is no
covering on his foot. But it is fiery red, and on the
heel there is a round black spot. Half an hour later,
when I passed his bed, the toil-worn body lay stiff and
stark, and the immortal soul, released, had fled to
futurity.
In the midst of so much misery, happy are they
whose mercurial temperament enables them to make
light of their present troubles and salute you with a
joke instead of a groan. I stand at the foot of a bed in
which reclines a Maine man. My coat almost touches
the ropes that suspend. the splinters in Which rests his.
shattered leg. Get away, or I'll kick you,' he laughs.
The invalid next him has a pot of honeybroughtlim
by sonic visitor to which he is paying his respects. I'd
advise you to hide tat bees'-juice, or I'm bound to get
up in the night and steal it.' 'What's out at "Grover's"
to-night; I want to go.' This from a man with a ball
through his right lung, another in his hip, - and in
'hourly expectation of having his leg amputated!
Here is a poor fellow who had a hemorrhage this
morning, lying weak and exhausted. Give him some
strong beef tea at once' orders the: doctor. But the
cook has no beef, and refers the nurse to the stew aid.
The ste ward has none either, and it is two hours before
the , patient obtains the nutriment, which, if admi-
nistered sooner, might have saved his life.
At the further end of the dimly-lighted room a hero
from Sumner's division liesla-dying. Lower and lower
ebbs the vital spark. Fainter and fainter comes the fast
departinglreatli. Mutely, with fixed and earnest eyes,
he appeals to Heaven, strives with painful effort to catch
a stronger breath, with which he may articulate some
word yearning to be borne, fails in the endeavour, and
expires.
And as I pass out into the cool refreshing air of a
September night, and look down at the dead-house by
the water side, the moon, penetrating into obscure
corners, shows again his ghastly face. Oh, pomp and
circumstance of glorious war ! This poor man had been
sighing after glory. To earn it he lefthis home, his wife,
his child, to battle against insidious disease and an im-
placable foe; and after 18 months of hard service in
Virginia swamps a leadembullet sends him to a reeking
pest-house, and there he dies, unknown to his friends,
his name scarce noted in the physician's book, and, en-
closed in four deal boards he occupies a piece of free-
hold six feet by two. And this.is war's reward! This
is glory!

WILLS AND BI.QUESTS.

The will of Jacob Ricardo, Esq., M.P., of Lowndes-
square, and of Exbury House, Fawley, Hant' s Wa3
proved in London .by his relict, the Right Hon. Lady
Catherine Ricardo, sister of the Earl of F.fe. The
personalty was sworn under £50,000. Mr. Ricardo
died at the age of 50, having executed his will in 1860,
which is very brief, appointing his wife, Lady Cathe-
rine, sole executrix and also residuary legatee of his
property, both real and personal, and bequeathing to
his son his shares in the Norwegian Trunk Railway,
or in lieu thereof a sum of £13,000. Legacies axe left
to all his servants, who have been with. him for a
lengthened period.— The will of Thomas Wakley,
Esq., 81.R.C.5., late M.P. for Finsbury; and coroner
for Middlesex, of Bedford-street, Strand, and of Mat-
lock, Bath, near Buxton, -Derbyshire, who died at the
island of Madeira in May last, was proved in London
on the 18th of September. The personalty was sworn
under £12,000, the executors nominated being his
son, Thomas If. Wakley, Esq., of Arlington street,
Piccadilly, and Thomas Spalding, Esq., of Hendon;
the BOA alone is noting executor. The will, which ,is
of moderate length, was executed in 1861, and is
strictly of a family nature, directing his estate at Mat-
lock, consisting of messuages and land, and all other
real estate, to be sold; the net proceeds arising there-
from, together with his personal property, to be equally
divided between his three sons. Mr. Wakley was in
his 68th year.

The press/we-of public; opinion, in the shape of nume-
rous meetings,, petitions, and-memorials, and. not least
the strongly marked comments of the press, brought to
hear upon the Home Office in the case of Jessie
MtLachlan, have-at length tad the intended effect. A
respite of the sentence passed upon the unhappy woman
was received by the Lord Provost of Glasgow on Friday
I;.at, from the Secretary of State, staying the execution
until Saturday, the Ist of November. At the same time
the conviit has been officially .apprised by the
atithorities that the respite has been granted
only for the purpose of instituting further inves-
tigation into 'the facts and circumstances connected
with- the perpetration of the crime;, and that should
the result of such inquiry not tend to confirm the
truth, of the statement made by her as to her
share- in the transaction, no hope of a commu-
tation can be held out to hen In the meantime the in-
vestigation referred to, involving the examination of
every person who, it is supposed, can throw any fresh
light upon the facts contained in the extraordinary state-
ment made by Jessie M‘Lachlan, is being very actively
carried on by the authorities of Glasgow, under the
direction of the Lord Advocate, and not by any person
sent specially by the Secretary forthe Home Department,
as hal been previously stated.,, The Scottish law under
which, it is asserted, a person once admitted as witness
for the Crown cannot be indicted for the same crime, is
the subject of much discussion, inasmuch as if the prin-
ciple is adhered to, it is clear that old Mr. Fleming can-
not be tried for the murder, but for perjury only, what-
ever the discoveries or disclosures that may be made,
implicating him in this cold-blooded and atrocious
act. Trio gre Aest anxiety is felt by all classes as
to the result of the inquiries in progress, the ten-
dency of popular opinion being sufficiently indicated by
the numerous petitions that have been transmitted,
praying for a fuller investigation, and a respite of the
sentence. On Friday 'afternoon at Edinburgh, a depu-
tation, appointed at a meeting held on Monday last,
waited, by appointment, on the Lord Advocate, to urge
on his lordship-the necessity for a full investigation 'by
the authorities into the whole c•ase, and the propriety of
a respite being extended. The Lord Advocate having
received their representations, gave them to understand
that the fullest investigation would be officially made
into the whole circumstances of the case.

stands, and that she has an' idea she will at least escape

at the prison for her every day, which, after passing
through the hands of the governor of! the prison, and

LIIPEBIAL EXCU.i2SIOY.

The Emperor, the Empress -of • the French,- and
thirty persons of their suiie left the Villa Eugenie
three days ago to make an excursion to the mountain
of La Rbune. M. Dihursubehere, who resides in the
neighbourhood, had been requested to organise every-
thing that was necessary( to facilitate the ascent, and
he accordingly met the imperial party at Sare at 3
o'clock. Their Majesties found in readiness for them
12 well-caparisoned mules the use of the Empress
and the ladies of her suite, and 24 saddle horses for
the Emperor and the gentlemen who accompanied him.
Amongst the persons.present were MM. de Toulongeon,
de La Grange, do la Pagerie, Marshal Niel, Count and
the Countess .Sclafanie,le. de Ravneval, M. and
Mme. de la Poeze, and M. 'lamella. *Before leaving
for the ascent their Majesties partook of- refreshments
offered to them by the four daughters of M. Dihursu-
behere. Nothing could be more picturesque than this
numerous party proceeding along the sides of the
mountain, with thirty.fine young men acting as guides.
The travellers were delighted with the fine views
which constantly present themselves. The summit of
the mountain was reached at five, and after a short
halt the descent took place their Majesties and those
who accompanied them hafting on the plateau of the
Petite-Rhune, after whibh the remainder of the excur-
sion was got over by torchlight. Two bonfires were
lighted on the heights, and the party arrived at the
village of Sare about seven. The houses were all illu-
minated, and their Majesties were greeted with loud
acclamations. While • the Emperor was addressing
questions to the authorities about the wants of the
country, the Empress and the ladies of her suite rested
for a short time at the house of M. Goyetche, the
deputy-mayor, 'where refreshments were offered them.
Their Majesties afterwards entered their carriages at
half-past eight, and reached the villa about eleven.-
--
Galignani.

The monument to George Stephenson, erected by
public subscription in Neville-street, opposite to the
central station in Newcastle-on-Tyne, was inaugurated
on the 2nd instant, With every demonetration of popular
respect. It consists of a statue of the great engineer
by his townsman, Mr. Lough, one of the.most eminent
-sculptois of the day, together with emblematical figures,
representing a blacksmith, a plate-layer, a pitman, and
an engine-Liver. The whole is extremely effective,
and the likeness is considered •to be very good. The
day was set apart as a holiday in all the principal fac-
tories and places of business in the town and district,
and. the proceedings commenced at noon by the work-
men employed in Messrs. R. Stephenson and Co.'s fac-
tory; in those of Messrs. Hawks, Crawshay, and Sons;
Messrs. Thompson and Co.; Messrs. Hawthorn, Els-
wick Engine and Ordnance *Works • Messrs. J. Abbott
and Co., Messrs. Crowley, Millington. and Co., and
the members of the Ancient Order of Foresters and
Odd Fellows, with the members of other friendly so-
cieties; marching in -an immense procession through
the principal streets to the Town Hall; where they
joined the executive committee, the members of the
Institution of Civil Engi eers, of Mechanical Engi-
neers, and of Mining Enei.,eers, the president and com-
mittees-- of educational sou' .tics in the town and dis-
trict, the members of Parliament for the district, and
foreign consuls, the mayors of all the towns in the
neighbourhood, with the chairmen and members of
other corporate bodies, the chairmen and directors of
the North-Eastern and other railways, the members of
the Coal Trade Association, and proceeded to the in-
auguration. Lord Ravensworth delivered the inaugural
address.

tECOVEILY FROM APPAIIENT DEATIL—My -authority
for the following anecdote is a lady who heard it related
some years ago by the gentleman initialised R.' in my
text The late Baron Platt, when a young man, ,had
a severe illness, of which he apparently died. ,Two or
three days after the fatal event, some gentlemen, friends
of the deceased, went ,together to the house where the
body was laid out, and obtained leaVe.to take a farewell
look of their old assoeiate. While standing beside the
corpse, one of them . said, "Ah I we shall :never again
- drink .a glass of wine with poor Platt ;" whenpoer Platt
immediately exclaimed, "But you will, and a good
many, too, I hope." All fled in terror from the room
except Mr. R., and he remained until his friend's resus-
citation was assured.'—Notes and Queries.

TIM lIAILVEST IN Aynsinne.—Although the last
week has been unsettled; the month of September as a
whole has been a period of delightful harvest weather.
After the middle of the month the temperature was
high enough for fine midsummer days, and the evenings
were balmy and pleasant. The late crops have been im-
proved beyond all reasonable expectations, and will be
gathered, we may again hope, in most eases before the
approach of winter. About one-half of the grain has
. been carried in the earlier districts of Ayrshire. On
Tuesday afternoon and Wednesday forenoon wheat was
stacked-in- fine condition, and thus far there is almost a
complete absence of Sprouted grain. On highly culti-
vated and friable lands the crops looked well in stocks;
and as far as can he judged-at present, oats will give a
good produce in proportion to the amount of straw.
The remnant of , the early potato crop has suffered
greatly from disease wherever, it has been grown upon
land that is even slightly tenacious. The late crop is
becoming affected, but aftersnch a favourable September
farmers are indulging in the expectation that it will not
suffer severely. It is certain that a very small supply for
winter use and seed remains in this county.
-WHAT is a. LUCKY' Rom 1)--A shepherd who was tend-
ing'his . flock last -week on the 'eastern slope of the
mountain of Super-Bagneres, near Bagneres-de-Luchon,

already been dead some hours, was recognised, as that
of M. D—, an advocate residing at Pau. This
desperate act is attributed to temporary- derangement,
caused by embarrassed circumstances and losses at play.
Great excitement was produced at tuchon by this sui-
cide, and many persons were . very anxious to know
what had become of the fatal rope, probably thinking
of the vulgar belief that the cord which serves to hang discussing the
brings good luck. One of the groups,
point, seemed to bc greatly disappointed when informed
by a lawyer of the environs that, if found, it would be
of no value, as the only rope possessing any virtue was
lone which, having been employed to hang a condemned
criminal, should bhalc under his weight, and thus awe
his life.. _ .
