articles.title: FOREIGN SUMMARY.
articles.text:
FOREIGN SUMMARY.

• The younger Princess of Savoy arrived at
Lisbon on Monday, and on that day was mar-
ried_to the young King df Portugal, in person,

by the Patriarch.. He had been
.previously
married, by his proxy, or representative, at
Turin. On the same day the King of Turin
published an amnesty for Garibaldi .and his
followus, excepting deserters from *he army
or the navy, who will be probably tried in
accordance with military and naval laws, and
be pardoned, after their •condemnation, by the
King.
Disturbances in Sicily have gone so far, and
daggers are so common there, that the govern-
ment has issued an order for the delivery of,
all arms to the authorities. Some French,
papers hint that Britain .should occupy Sicily,
and the measure would excuse France in the
retention of Rome. •
Rumours of a settlement of the Roman'

question are again current, and find people
who believe them, as we shall readily do when
we hear that the French soldiers have all left
Civita Vecchia; but France is now converting
that place into a first class fortress at a great
outlay.
The Russian Government have banished
Count Zamoyski out of their dominions. This
act is considered more severe than the old
punishment of a trip to Siberia. Differences
of taste are unaccountable, but we should pre-
fer the new to the old way.
Circassia continues to be the obstacle of
Russia on an advance to the South. Very few
persons have ever seen a bog in motion. It
may be easily imagined, although it is a ter-
rible spectacle. 'the monster comes on with a
scarcely perceptible, slow and stately motion,
absorbing and covering up au green fields in
its way. The advance of Russia among the
small nationalities has been of that nature. It
had overborne and sunk all beneath its own
system, until it met,-tle Auvafr--zunt- ruck laud
of Circassia. Against this rampart it has
spent power and strength. Still the contest
proceeds, and severe losses are said to have
been sustained by the Russians during this
summer's war.

The political crisis in Prussia remains.
Politics among the Germans take time. Even
the King amid the dispute has been able to
visit "Baden Baden " and his relations there,
and the Prince and Princess of Prussia pro-
pose to pass the autumn in Italy; and we
may infer that nothing very serious is expected
at Berlin.

Austria and Hungary are expected to arrange
their difficulties in a peaceable manner, and
the Hungarians seem again disposed to take
their place in the consultations of the Austrian
empire.

M. Fould, the French Financial Minister,
reports favourably on his department, not-
withstanding the great addition to the pay-
ments caused by the proceedings in Mexico
The floating deficiency had, he says, at the
commencement of 1862 reached 41 millions
sterling. By the conversion of the 41 per
cent. stock, it had been reduced to a, little over
34 millions sterling.
Intelligence from China comprises the re-
sumption of hostilities, and the interruption of
the silk exports by the Taeping-Wangites.
Some combats had occurred with the Im-
perialists under Colonel Ward and the Revolu-
tionists. At Pekin the authorities had struck
off -the heads of several defeated Generals.
Cholera prevailed in several parts of China,
and many deaths both among Europeans and
natives had occurred.

Mosquera., the President of New Granada, has
suppressed the monasteries and nunneries, and
ordered the priests and nuns to leave the
republic, as they were found to be connected
with all the reactionary proceedings. Jaurez
and his Government have decided on offering
a determined resistance to the invasion of
Mexico by the French; and have strongly
fortified their capital and Pueblo.
The Confederates claim a victory in the last
great fight of September at Antietam. They
defended their position, and repelled the as--
sailants. After the day was, done their stores
obtained in Maryland had passed over to Vir-
ginia, and they had no further use for the posi
tion. Two of their general officers were
slain and five wounded. Fifteen of the Federal
Generals were, it may be remembered killed or
wounded. The Confederate's train, which passed
through Harper's Ferry, was said to to be
ten to twelve" miles long.

..
MR GLADSTONE ON THE STATES.

THE entertainment to Mr. GLAI)STONE at
Newcastle on Tyne, upon Tuesday- afternoon,
was a splendid gathering. Newcastle prospers
by the policy of Mr. GLA.DSTONE. He helped
to raise the price of coals, and Newcastle at
present is burning itself out rapidly without a
thought on the possibilities to future dwellers on
the Tyne. Even the existing difficulties in other
centres of trade are scarcely felt on the Tyne.
Its population are well employed, and its 'pro-
ductions sell. Newcastle has long aspired to
a lead in politics, and the energy of its people
entitle them to the place. Their invitation to
Mr. GLADSTONE emanated perhaps from that
old design of theirs, along with gratitude for
favours obtained. It was accepted for several
reasons, and among others, because Mr. GLAD-
STONE says these meetings afford, to the re-
sponsible advisers of the Crown, an opportunity
of making known their opinions during the
recess. This is one reason given by him, and
to be noticed by the public in relation to some
of his statements respecting passing events,
and their nature and probable results.
Mr. GraDsToNE's reference to the condition
of parties in the Northern and Southern States
caused " sensation" at the dinner party, and
a "sensation" in the press. He declared that
"Jefferson Davis and his friends had formed
an army, were forming a navy, and, what was
of more importance, had formed a nation."
The statement is regarded as an intimation,
that the independence of the South will be
recognised at an early date by our Government,
acting doubtless in conjunction with other
European powers. The Emperor of France
had, it was said some time ago, proposed an
arrangement for the extinction of slavery, as a
condition of the acknowledgement of nation-
ality desired by the South. If this statement
be correct, NAPOLEON was probably acting in
conjunction with the British Government;
but as we at present acknowledge other slave
powers, such as the Brazils, Holland, until the
present date, Spain and the old union, or the
Federal union of States, we doubt whether
any condition could be attached to an ordinary
recognition of sovereignty, and, therefore,
NAPOLEON'S scheme may have included an
offer to mediate.

Mr. GLADsTorrE entreated his hearers, and
the public here, not to say hard things of our
brethren in the Federal union, anything to
cause "additional shame, sorrow, or pain, to
"those who had already suffered much, and
"who would probably have to suffer much
"more." These are sharp words. We have
not supported the claims or conduct of the
North from the commencement of this con-
test. Their constitution had an apparent flaw,
and made provision for disunion. Individual
states, north and south, had asserted the right
to decompose the union or disunite themselves
from Washington. Zealots here and there

overlooked these facts, were -:ignotant of the.
constitution on which they qpcike .and wrote,
or card nothing for accuracy. on 'the subject.
Any assertions made by thetengineer or stoker
wilt not, however, prevent an eexplosion of a
boiler witha crack in the plates when itis -worked
at 'very high pressure. The 'Union :exploded
and all parties should have endeavoured to re-
pair the damage, and do allintheir power with
the fragments. ,
The conduct of the Northern statesmen has
been obnoxious in many instances. They have
neither conciliated their .enemies nor their
friends. They hurled 'confiscation against
their late partners of the South, and their
former partners of Great Britain. Charles
ton was to be sown with salt; and
Canada annexed to the State of Maine
perhaps. 'All these assertions found' a ready
response in the Nortliernteities. Vanity seems
to be the ruling passion of the people, fed at
their schools, on their platthrm, in the press,
and really we fear occasionally in the pulpit;
but -very possibly the people never dreamed
of doing all the wickedness -summed up in
their leader's, and in their politician's words.
We hope and trust at least that they did not
contemplate seriously to raise hostilites against
our nation for instance, since we only suffered
by their war. Still these hopes are liable to
he shaken by the favour shown to such men as
Coco, and MEAGHER, and CASSIUS CLAY
—no relative of the late member for the Tower
Hamlets—and other men, and the many jour-
nals, engaged in denouncing this country, and
stirring up a bitter feeling against Britain and
British interests ; _ Canada, and ,Canadian in-

terests. Soft words cannot always be chosen
and picked by persons who suffer from attacks
so v.Knouus,iza thy o roferrod f3O pOrOlOtOrlt
and unjust, yet it might be prudent and cor-
rect not to speak of" shame" in this struggle,
except as respects " outrages " incidental, but
not necessary in the war.

Carnage cannot continue for ever, yet the war
seems one of extermination, unless powerful
nations interfere so far at least as to urge
peace upon the combatants. In this country
a amall party seems still to enjoy the brief
narratives of days in which ten thousadd were
killed, and twenty thousand wounded; but all
humane men, and all friends of fhe Anglo-
Saxon race, must desire to have an end of them.
The North cannot conquer the South without
the loss of life and property fin- more valuable
than any connexion that will ever exist be-
tween them. The South cannot expect to
conquer the North and appropriate New York.
No "shame," therefore, in a military sense,
will attach to either of the two parties if they
will bury their dead and their feud together,
and see to the support of the helpless men,
the orphans, and the widows, made in this war,
and, by a future of industry in half a century,
repair the losses Of two fatal years.
Their separation will not convert a re-
public into a monarchy, or a monarchy into a
republic; it wi;l not make "an aristocracy the
-more, or a democracy the less." In politics
north and south will stand nearly as they were,
and either section will have sufficient territory
to secure a prosperous future to populations,
far greater than the thirty millions scattered
over the States before the commencement of
this quarrel.
We do not know that Mr. GLADSTONE'S
speech foreshadows any change in our policy.
It is.probable from the tenure of his words
that mediation may be offered, and that a re-
cognition of the South would follow its refusal
by the North; but the recognition of any
nation does not suppose an intervention in its
wars. Some commercial, some monetary, and
some moral advantages, might be gained by
recognition to the South, but the act would
not by and in itself imply intervention or any
other active proceeding of that nature. It
would not aid the North in its,assault or the
South in its defence; unless it may be that a
nation blockading its own coasts, is allowed to
take more liberty with itself, than it would be
permitted when blockading coasts and ports,
recognised to be the property" of another and
an independent nation.

articles.title: CAB DRIVERS' CLAIMS.
articles.text:
THE CAB DRIVERS' CLAIMS.

THE Cabdrivers who stand in Farringdon
Street, looking towards Blackfriars, may read
on one public building before their horses'
heads, that "diligence leads to honour." The
; statement requires to be qualified by con-
fining it to diligence in a good purpose. Per-
sons have passed, and no doubt will pass, on
that street, whose diligence must lead them
in some other direction than that of honour.
The explanation is scarcely necessary, for all
parties who can read can also understand from
the scroll that diligence in a good object leads
to honour.

The Cabmen must have read the engraving,
and decided to act upon the statement, as they
have been diligent for some time past in the
vindication of their claims, and, we believe,
with considerable success. Their diligence has
brought them more honour and respect than
was formerly, and even lately, shown to them.
Their trade had fallen into disrepute in the
police courts and in the press. An idea was
prevalent that a cabman could not possibly be
in the right of a dispute with his customers.
Unhappily, from the nature of his trade, the
latter phrase is scarcely applicable: the cab-
driver has not many regular customers, but
drives strangers for half his rounds and time,
and meets all descriptions of persons. That
peculiarity in the business might make one
man more exacting, and another more suspi-
cious, than either of them would be in ordinary
circumstances, but the drivers are no more
likely to err than the hirers. One class, and
a numerous class, of persons consider them-
selves detectives when they enter a cab; and
they appear to make the discovery of errors
their business for the time. They- employ
considerable freedom, bordering on licenti-
ousness of speech, and yet they never expect
in reply more than the mildest words. Men
who do business with this determination in any
line, invite, and are likely to meet occasional
rudeness. If they were to treat their shoe-
maker, or their tailor, in the same manner, it
is probable thit they would also exhaust the
patience of these respectable tradesmen. Cab-
men alone are expected to meet insult or mis-
representation with equanimity and patience.
Certainly if they can always act on that princi-
ple, it is the best possible principle to pass
through the world with. We have met with
cabmen who endeavoured to cheat, and were
far from civil, but they were exceptions to our
experience. As a rule, the men seem quite as
just and obliging as the average of society, and
they are placed under more than ordinary
temptation, and meet with worse than ordinary
treatment. We are not astonished, therefore,
that they have made a combined effort to set
themselves right before the public. The alter-
ations proposed by them in the law regarding
cabs, are reasonable; and the regulations sug-
gested by them are calculated to render fares
and other matters clear and plain to the public.
The city authorities, or some of them, object
to the cabs loitering in the streets for casual
hire, and insist that they should be driven to the

Tlestnated stands without any:loss,of time, but
akvabman, if he sets down .a fare, must drive
in -some direction, and humanity to his horse
uiight induce him to drive •slovvly. If the city
.authorities would always go to the nearest
•etand to hire a cab, and never on any account
-step into a passing vehicle, their object would
be secured.

Differences arise occasionally from cabmen
declining to take fares .in some directions or for
long distances. We heard a gentleman, ap-
parently a gentleman, arguing for some time
with a cabman who declined to take him a long
distance in a direction away from the drivers
home, and the horses stable. The hirer could
have easily obtained another cab, but he wanted
to vindicate the law; although the driver alleged
that he had been eleven hours on the street.
Some limit must be placed to these exactions
on man and horse, or they may be made the
Wandering Jew and his horse; and never be
allowed to stop anywhere, until the officers of
the Society for the suppression of cruelty to
animals bring the man before a magistrate,
and his horse to a rest.

A Company with a. capital of £200,000 is
proposed for the purpose of supplying a supe-
rior class of cabs to those now in use, and
working them on a plan differing from the
present sy,stem. The company instead of
; letting out their cabs and horses to the drivers
would engage the latter at fixed wages. One
evil would be removed, for;the men find the pre-
sent practice injurious, it leaves them little
profit; and all the risk of employers. It must
be occasionally attended by profit, but is over
the season probably less advantageous to drivers
than stated wages. A wide distinction exists
between men driving their own cabs and horses,
and other drivers paying by the day or night for
the use of a masters horse and vehicle, for the
principal profit is extracted by the capitalist,
and the driver who deals with him must be
.contented with the crumbs the odds and ends
of the business, and endeavour to increase
them.

A large new company after the manner of
the General Omnibus Company, is not the
best means of remedying these evils. The
managers would endeavour to buy up or over and swamp all the drivers who employ
their own horse and vehicle. In order to
secure dividends they would follow the example
of the Omnibus Company and establish a
monopoly. If therfbre the cabdrivers have
profited in any respect by the legend " diligence
leads to honour," in their agitation to amend
the law, they should also apply it to the agita-
tion for the improvement of cabs. Some time
ago a Co-operative Cab Company was pro-
posed.

- It was a healthy scheme, and the originator
suggested either that the men should buy out
their cab and horse by stated payments, or act
as partners in the company, Eifher plan, or a
combination of both plans, would be popular
and useful; and "diligence "just now in its
promotion might lead the men to riches, and
bring the public into harmony with them.

articles.title: CRIMINAL LUNATICS.
articles.text:
CRIMINAL LUNATICS.

TEM Financial Reform Association of Liver-
pool is an excrescence from the Manchester
school, which has survived the parent stump.
Cheap goods,property,work are the crop sought
by those persons who labour at its root. They
are all rich men who believe in the right of
money to rule the world. All reductions in
the price of labour or of property, are actual
additions to their money, or to its power.
A monthly periodical called the Financial
Reformer, expounds the opinions of the Asso-
ciation and promulgates them. Many of these
purposes are commendable, but the great
" drift " of the society is a different thing, and
is sought by three classes who may be compre-
hended under the different terms "criminal,"
"lunatic," or "stupid." The Reformer in its
number for October, referring to one series of
its articles entitled " Words for Workers and
Employers," admits the " verbal " accuracy
of our statement, while unfolding a pitiful and
sad story. The author of these articles is and
has been for a long period, confined in
Bethlehem hospital as a "criminal lunatic."
He was insane at one time and killed his
wife, to whom he is said to have been greatly
attached, in a fit of this disease, when he
believed that a great calamity was immedi-
ately impending. He committed the crime
to rescue her from deep sorrow and suffer-
ing as he supposed. He was tried and ac-
quitted, on the plea of insanity, and committed
to the hospital. Reason was restored to the
prisoner in the opinion of Dr. HOOD, the medi-
cal superintendent, but he is still kept in the
hospital under restraint.

fermission was afforded by the board, in the
circumstances, for the "criminal lunatic "to
recommence literary writing, subject to the
approval of his manuscripts by Dr. lioon or
Dr. HELPS, and the interdiction of all subjecte
such as relate "in any manner to the govern-
ment of the country, the administration of the
law, and the treatment of the insane."

The condition of censorship, and the excep-
tion of subjects are alike ludicrous and un-
worthy. At some period, after the censorship
had existed for a time, the prisoner thought
that it had not been conducted, with justice,
and he sent some manuscripts out of the house
by the assistance of one of the attendants, who
promised to forward his writings. The " crime "
against the laws of the asylum was discovered
and the "criminal lunatic," officially pro-
nounced to be altogether recovered and per-
fectly sane, is deprived of pen, ink, paper, even
books or access to the library;' and these pri-
vations are calculated, we think, to restore his
formerly diseased state of mind, and for ever
terminate his " words for workers and their
employers."
This is the tale told in the Financial Refor-
mer, a tale of grief and manifold suffering.
The restoration of sanity seems to a man in
these circumstances, with the darkness and
depth of that immoveable shadow on his mind,
a torture, which this miserable tyranny will
not permit him to alleviate by work. The
authorities may have an excuse for the exercise
of great caution, before restoring liberty to a
person in whom lunacy had once been deve-
loped, to the destruction of life; but they can
have no excuse for exercising an absurd cen-
sorship over the manuscript of this man, or for
inflicting the severest intellectual punishment
for a breach of regulations, not by any means
prudent in themselves. They may be assured
that editors will exercise all the necessary
supervision over contributions from Bethlehem
Hospital, without the assistance of its medical
gentlemen; while, in ouropinion, nothingmore
obviously tinged with lunacy can ever appear
in manuscript, from any hospital, than may be
found in the writings of reputedly sane people,
engaged in trying to pull down the price of
labour under false pretences, and to shift
the peas in the matter of taxation.
The exposure of the particulars in this case
may not only 'remove the wicked restrictions
put on this writer, but lead to some improve-
ment on the cpndition of other persons, who,
if they must continue in confinement, should

have all the 'alleviation of their fate that can
be supplied by a generous and prudent sym-
pathy.

WHAT ONE MAN CAN DO.

A REMARKABLE application connected with
the Lancashire distress was made a few days
ago at the . Mansion House here, by a young
man, who came up from Lancashire, bringing
abundant evidence that his errand was genuine,
and that his application for a few thousand
pounds deserved a favourable response. He
had a few leisure hours, and commenced a great
business; not, without capital, for a nobleman,
who preferred that his name should not be
known, gave him one thousand pounds and
paid him a Subsidy of forty pounds weekly
after the expenditure of the first donation.
With this money, the yQung man who
ap-
plied to the Lord Mayor for aid in his schemes,:
supports schools in Manchester, and the
neighbourhood in which from eighteen hundred
to nineteen hundred female operatives are
employed, who, except for this interference'
would have been idle, and exposed to all the
temptations of idle people in want.
The benefits conferred by the nobleman's
money,and the labours of the applicant show
how much may be done by one person with great
energy and perseverance in a good cause. The
payments on aviunt of these sewing schools
amounted to £250 weekly, and only £lOO re-
mained to meet the draft for the current week,
.when the Lord Mayor pupplied the £l5O de-
ficient, and urged their promoter to form a
special committee in Manchester to assist him
in this benevolent work. The Manchester
Committee have a considerable sum of money
on hand, and it will not be creditable to that
great town if an enterprise so hopeful as these
sewing schools be allowed to rest either
financially or in any other sense on the leisure
hours of one man ; or on the money largely
and generously given by another man, who as
a landowner and Peer in the neighbourhood,
has no doubt publicly subscribed to an object
which he aids liberally in private, for assist-
ance commenced by a gift of £l,OOO, and pro-
ceeding at the rate of £2,000 annually, re,
quires some sacrifice, even from a man of
great possessions and wealth.

PRESIDENT LINCOLN'S PROCLA-
MATION.

ON the 13th of September President Lin-
coln wrote to Chicago that he was opposed to
emancipation. Within a week he issued a
document which has caused some excitement.
It is a warning that on the Ist of January,
1863, he will declare all slaves in "rebel
states" to be free; but if any states now out
of the union repent, and return before that
period, he will not emancipate their slaves.
President Lincoln gives the slaves an interest
in perpetuating the rebellion until new years
day of 1863, for if the masters give in before
then, the slaves will be hopeless. Next he
offers freedom to the negroes over whom he
has no control, and keeps in slavery those
other negroes within his power. Thus he as-
sociates his Government with slavery by mak-
ing slaveholding the reward to the planters of
rejoining that old union.

THIRD EDITION, SATURDAY EVENING.

FRANCE

PARIS, Oct. 10

The Honiteur of to-day announces that the Courrier
du Dimancke has received a. second warning, for- an
article signed by Mr. Prevost Parade], as the said
article excites to hatred and contempt of the Govern-

articles.title: ITALY.
articles.text:
ITALY.

TuniN, Oct. 9.
Intelligence received here to-day from Fort Varig
nano, states that Garibaldi passed a very quiet night.
The wound had ceased to be painful, but- was still
swollen. The General has been attacked with rheu-
matism in the right shoulder.
Information haring reached the Government that
Mazzinian intrigues are being carried on in Switzer-
land, the greatest precaution is being taken against
their success.

The Discussione of this evening says that a visit of
Signor Ratazzi to Paris could only take place after ne-
gotiations which would ensure a success beneficial to
the national cause.

TURIN, Oct. 10

The Nationalites of this evening publishes a letter
from Dr. Ripari, 'stating that Garibaldi's wound pro-
gresses favourably. The physician expresses a hope
that the cure will be more complete than was appre-
hended.

A proclamation, signed by two Hungarians, formerly
belonging to the Hungarian Legion, was sent from
Verona to Alexandria, with a view to induce their
comrades to return home, Austria guaranteeing them
a free pardon. General Turr invited those who wished
to accept this proposition to declare themselves and
leave the Italian service. The Hungarians have, how-
ever, rejected it with scorn.

articles.title: PRUSSIA.
articles.text:
PRUSSIA.

BERLIN, OCT. 10.

In the Upper House to-day, Herr von Arnim-
Boytzenburg introduced an amendment supported by
fifty-eight of the members. The amendment propos,es
that the House should reject the budget of the Cham-
ber of Deputies, and adopt that of the Government.
It is expected the amendment will be carried, and the
two Chambers will thus be in collision.

THE GARIBALDI CITY MEETING.—The sub-committce
appointed to arrange the details of this meeting assem-
bled last night. It was resolved that the meeting
should be held at that place on Friday next, the 17th
inst., Mr. Weston Wood, M.P., has consented to take
the chair, and that Baron Rothschild, Sir J. Duke and
Mr. R. W. Crawford, the other City members will be
invited to take part in the proceedings. members,
an
amendment will be allawed to be moved, any syste-
matic disturbances will be met by the offenders being
given into the custody of the police.
THE HYDE PARK MEETlNGS.—Yesterday, Sir R.
Mayne, the Commissioner, issued a police notice' ex-
tensively placarded in London, to the effect that in
future no meetings or assemblages of persons will be
allowed in any of the parks in future. Should any
meetings be called, they will be put down by the
authorities. The guards have been ordered not to
enter the Park to-morrow. This is one of the effects
of the miserable conduct and management of tne
Working Mena' Garibaldi Committee. Save us from
our friends!

TRIPLE MURDER IN FRANCE.--A frightful triple
murder has just thrown the neighbourhood of Fos
(Bouches-du•Rhone) into a state of consternation.
Two Spanish workmen arrived a few days ago in the
above.mentioned village, and took up their residence
at an inn kept by a man named Leautaud. A neigh-
bour, temporarily driven from his own house, by
repairs going on there, also -slept at the inn on that
' night, in addition to the wife and child of Leautaud.
' About three o'clock in the morning the two men got
up and called the landlord, and on his appearing
stabbed him several times in the breast, and, to make
sure of their object, cut his throat from ear to ear.
The wife of Leautaud, hearing the noise, hastened to
the assistance of her husband, and immediately shared
his fate. Lastly, the child, who had followed its
mother in its night-dregs, was seized at the foot of the
staircase, and its head cut off. The neighbour, who
had become aware of the horrible carnage which was
going on, and knowing that his death was certain if
he appeared, leaped from the first-floor window and
hastened to give the alarm. Some courageous men
repaired to the scene of the crime, and arrived while
the murderers were occupied in plundering the house.
One was arrested after a short struggle, but the other
made his escape by a back door.

articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

PUBLIC MEETINGS.
MR. GLADSTONE AT SUNDERLARD.—Mr. Gladstone
arrived at S underland yesterday morning, and, under
the escort of the Mayor and Sir H. Williamson, visited
the town and docks. Ile afterwards proceeded ta the
Athenmum, and received an address. In replying, he,
eulogised the principles and personal conduct of the
late Sir Robert Peel; spoke of the desire of the Cabinet
to see Italy free and United; deeply lamented the
struggle going on on the other side of the Atlantic;.
vindicated the conduct of the Government in the San
Jacinto case, and praised the part taken by France in
that affair. He left for Middlesbro' at about one o'clock.
THE ATTORNEY-GENERAL AND HIS CONSTITUENTS:—
On Wednesday night the Attorney-General (Sir Wm.
Atherton) addressed a numerous meeting of his con-
stituents in the City Hall, Durham. The topics dwelt
upon included the distress in Lancashire, and its con-
nection with the war in. America; and the Poaching
Act came. in for some remarks, in which Sir William
designated it as highly impolitic, ill-considereJ, and
ill-expressed.
SIR JOHN PAKINGTON ON AMERICAN AFS'AIRS.—At
a dinner of the Worcestershire Agricultural Society,
on Wednesday, Sir John Pakington said he thought
the time was come when not England alone, but Eng-
land in conjunction with France, and possibly with
Russia, ought to offer mediation in America, of course
on the basis of separation, and on the clear understand-
ing that, if mediation was not accepted, recognition
must follow.
THE RIGHT HON. SIR E. B. LYTTON, M.P., AT
HERTFORD.—The annual meeting of the Hertfordshire
Agricultural Association was held on Thursday. Sir
Bulwer Lytton addressed the meeting at great length,
in which he reviewed foreign politics, expressing his
pleasure at the progressin Italy, and his belief that.the
American Union could not be restored.
THE SOUTHERN CONFEDERACY. The 'Southern
Association' in Liverpool, at a meeting on Thursday,
agreed to a proposition which had for its object the
memorialising of Government for the recognition of
the Confederate States of America. This movement on
the part of the Southern Association has been chiefly
caused by the opinions enunciated at Newcastle. on
Tuesday last by Mr. Gladstone. It is said that the
members of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce have
or are about to petition -Government as to the neees-
bity of recognising the South as a separate nation.
NORTH WALSHAM AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—The
annual meeting of this society was held last evening
in this pleasant little Norfolk town, Lord Suffield pre-
siding: Mr. G. Howes, M.P., the county member, in
the course of his address, spoke in favour of the Night
Poaching Bill. His remarks were received with much
disapprobation by the tenant farmers and replied to
with much spirit by one of their number, a Mr. Read.
CITY or LONDON COLLEGE.—A meeting for the annual
distribution of prizes and certificates, gained by stu-
dents at the recent examination, took place last night
at the City of London College, Leadenhall-street, Mr.
Alderman Rose in the chair.

GARIBALDIAN* DEMONSTRATION IN THE TOWER
HAMLETS.—A public meeting to express sympathy
with Garibaldi, and to protest against the French
occupation of Rome, was held yesterday evening in
the Beaumont Institution, Tower Hamlets. Mr.
Walker occupied the chair, and a goodly number of
gentlemen of local influence were on the platform.
The room was crowded. The meeting passed off with
great spirit and without opposition.
THE DISTRESSED OPERATIVES AND THE LABOUR TEST.
—The operatives of Manchester, out of employ, held
an open-air meeting yesterday, at which a deputation
to the guardians was appointed to request them to,
discontinue the application of the degrading test at
once, and to give all relief in money instead of a part
in kind.

ITALY AND LORD RUSSELL.
Some Italians have got up a subscription, and have
presented Earl Russell with a statue and an address
in testimony of their gratefulness for what the noble
Foreign Secretary has done for Italy. Earl Russell
I said in his reply :—Gentlemen,—lt is with feelings of
deep gratitude that I accept your gift of a statue, the
work of the excellent sculptor, C:trlo Romano, and
representing 'La Convinzione dell'Unita d'ltalia.' It
has always been my persuasion that Italy herself was
the fittest judge of the mode best adapted to secure her
freedom, her happiness, and her independence. Her
own fortitude, her own moderation, and her own
patience have been conducive to her further progress;
and her constancy will, I trust, complete the edifice of
which the genius of her people laid the broad founda-
tions.

LATEST POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

articles.title: GUILDHALL.
articles.text:
GUILDHALL.

THE CLERGYMAN AND THE CAEMAN.—The Rev.
Frederick K. Harford was summoned before Alderman
Gabriel for refusing to pay a cabman his legal fare.
John Murphy, the complainant, said defendant hired
him on the day named in the summons in Charles
-
street, Grosvenor-square, and he (complainant) waited
for him outside a public house for about three-quarters
of an hour, at the expiration of which he came out
smoking a cigar, and directed him to drive to Myddle-
ton-street, Islington. He waited there for him for
about twenty-five minutes, and then drove him to the
General Post-office, when the defendant offered him
as. 61 He demanded 48., but the defendant refused
to pay it, and at the same time took back the
38. 61. he had already given- him, and then de-
clined to pay anything unless summoned. He
then drove defendant to the police-station, and
obtained his name and address. Alderman Gabriel
said he thought the distance and time entitled
the cabman to demand more than he had asked.—The
cabman said he had been so often deceived by persons
hiring him and not giving correct addresses that he
took defendant to the police-station. He knew it was
a 48. 6d. fare; but, as it was a very close one, he pre-
ferred taking 61. less to having the trouble and losing
the time in summoning the gentleman for it. Alder-
man Gabriel said 48. 6d. was justly the cabman's due,
and he did not see why he should forego any portion
of it. He confessed that it certainly did appear to him
that the cabman had been very unfairly dealt with.
It was quite clear that he had asked less than was due
to him, and it was a great injustice to bring him to
this court to enforce his claim. He therefore ordered
defendant to pay 4s. 6d., the amount of the full fare,
88. for the summons, and 4s. for the cabman's loss of
time.

11OW STREET.

THREATENING SIR RICHARD MAYNE.—An elderly
man, named John Paget Tremlett, was brought up in
custody of Inspector Beare, charged with writing a
threatening letter to Sir Richard Mayne. The prisoner,
who seemed labouring under much excitement, was
remanded fur the purpose of obtaining medical evidence
as to the state of his mind.

The prisoner was brought up again yesterday, when
Mr. Henry said that the language contained in the
prisoner's letter, which had been read in evidence, was
certainly calculated to produce alarm; and as the pri-
soner's medical attendant thought him capable of dis-
tinguishing right from wrong, he must be held to bail,
in two sureties of £5O each, and his own recognisances
for £lOO, to keep the peace for twelve months. The
prisoner and his bail were then bound over, and he
was discharged.

WESTMINSTER..
THE CHARGE OP FELONY AT THE MILITARY 'STORES.
—John Morelli, an Italian master tailor, of the Grena-
dier Guards, appeared for final examination, charged
with stealing a quantity of cloth belonging to the
Secretary of War. The prisoner was committed for
trial, but admitted to bail, Colonel Burnaby kindly
being one of his sureties.

WORSHIP STREET.
COMMITTAL Pon 3ilAwsLAuonraa.--.lVilliam Barr, in
an extensive way of business as a cabinetmaker, at 115
and 116, Curtain-road, Shoreditch, appeared upon his
bail to answer the separate charges of drunkenness,
furiously driving, and thereby causing the death of his
wife. He was committed for manslaughter, but ad-
mitted to bail.

ACCIDENTS AND OFFENCES.
ACCIDENT TO A WORIEMAN.—A fatal accident oc-
curred yesterday afternoon to Charles Clemente, a
workman employed at the new military church now
being erected on WOOIWiCh COllllllOl3. it appears that
deceased by some means slipped, and fell from a height
of 50 feet, receiving such injuries to his skull that
death was immediate.
THE DISPUTED VERDICT.—The decision in respect
to the special verdict in the case of Stephen J. Meany,
at the Middlesex Sessions, has been postponed to
Wednesday next.
DROWNED IN WINE.--Yesterday morning the body
of George Elliott, late carman in the employment of
Messrs. Bannister and Co., British wine distillers,
Finsbury, was found by his fellow- workmen floating
in the wine contained in one of the steep vats on the
premises.
SUICIDE IN lIIINCLNG-LANE.—Mr. A. S. Griffith,
trading under the firm of A. S. Griffith and Co., fruit
brokers,
9, Mincing-lane, committed suicide by taking
poison,
between the hours of ten and eleven o'elock
yesterday morning.
FIRE IN THE EUSTON-ROAD.--Yesterday morning a
fire broke out on the premises occupied by Mr. Carter,
-r
zinc manufacturer, Eastonoad. The result was that
the back workshop upon the basement was burned out,
the back rooms on the ground floor and contents de-
stroyed, and the remainder of the premises with their
contents seriously damaged by fire and breakage. The
adjoining premises of Messrs. S whiny have also sus-
tained some damage.

articles.title: TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE 'BRITISH IfINER' ON WAGES

AND STRIKES.

When a new journal starts out, professing to advo-
cate the interests of 300,000 men, so important to the
progression of the country in their labour as are the
miners, and so injuriously affected by their'labour as a
class it may not be out of place to compare the means
by Which improvement is sought, with the end to be
attained, in order to judge whether the means are
likely to achieve the object.
A. celebrated political writer has said, 'lt is the
credence of the world that determines its condition ; '
and I am sorry to point out that the sympathies and
credence of the editor of the British Miner are entirely
on the side of that unjust capitalists philosophy that
originates in practice all the evils of which he com-
plains; which has made the miner a slave to toil, and
leaves him a serf to capital.
This will appear at once on perusal of the first
article on 'Labour and Wages,' and especially so in
that on the Wigan strike. In tlxe first he makes the
payment of labour dependent on the amount of the
wage fund, or capital; whereas it is notorious there is
no necessary connection. Capital has increased
within the last fifty years at the rate of 500 per cent.;
but labour has not received more than 25 per cent. in-
crease. It is quite true that labour cannot receive
where there is nothing to divide; but it is quite clear
also that while there is abundance of capital to divide,
labour has not received proportionately. The disparity
in division of the resu:ts of labour betwixt labour and
napitsa has naturally led to dissatisfaction, and to con•
tention on the part.of labour; and though all the
political economists, and the British Miner 'to boot,'
were to tell the working collier that while coal has
risen 60 to 100 per cent. during the last ten years, and
while his wages have not increased more than 20 per
cent., that this arises by an inevitable and natural law,
and -with which he ought not to struggle, but there-
'With to be content; his natural sense would rise up
against the doctrine • and declEtie if this be law it is an
'unjust law, and ought not to prevail, even if it does.
-Yet such is virtually the teaching of the British Miner,
and when the said miners do rebel against the unjust
practice of doctrines so unjust, he lectures them ac-
cordingly.
The relation, the equity, and the disparity of the
sharing of capital, is said to depend upon the competi-
tion of the labourers for wage, and of the capitalists
for labour. Unions of both are admitted to exist, to
serve the especial interests of each, in opposition to
each other; and both are stated in the long run to be
in vain to effect tho results. But if the law of relation
or competition did operate as stated, how is it that
labour and capital have not shared equally in the
modern increase of wealth? Either there is no law by
which results do equalise themselves, or the unions
of the capitalists are efficient in maintaining their
interests supreme. Now to obtain a just balance of '
rewards,—or, in other words, a fair day's wage for a
fair day's work,' labour can but do two things: it
must either restrict itself in numbers or time; or it
must strike, which is another mode of doing the same
thing. The apparent counsel of the British Miner
Is that which has for some time obtained in capitalist
circles :—viz., by the preventive check, to the
development of the labourers, by not marrying, &T., in
order to reduce their number relative to capital. Now,
for the present, looking over the immorality of the course
advised ire result (the unsexing of the sexes, &c.,)
it will be apparent, on the slightest consideration, that
the cure can only succeed by killing. 'Wealth is the
result of labour, and to restrict the labourers is to
restrict 'wealth. Profit, and trade itself, depend
upon demand; and to diminish population, is to
diminish demand, exactly as the population are
restricted. Yet such is the teaching of this friend of
the British Miner!

Men will strike against injustice ;—the occasion
made or the time may be right or wrong, but to ignore
the right to strike, or to teach its incompatibility with
possible success, is to ignore human natute itself, and
the results of all past and all present history. in the
face of the results of the Wigan strike (that notice of
reduction was withdrawn by the strike) the Editor of
the British. Miner asserts' ' We maintain that a strike
for wages is never in the long run attended with
success.' Than we beg to ask of the said -Editor how
are the colliers to succeed .? They succeeded in resist-
ing a second redaction at Wigan ;—they succeeded
after a 'lock-out' in Scotland a few weeks ago, in
adding a shilling a day to their wages, and in 1859-60,
the miners of West Yorkshire obtained a rise instead
of a proposed reduction of 30 per cent.; and after a
severe eight months strike have still retained it? If
the advances that labour has obtained by strikes had
been half as much paraded as its failures have been, it
would not admit such fallacies as the above being pub-
lished by Editors, for the interests of even capital
itself. _ _

It would seem that one of the chief objections of the
British Miner is, because in strikes the management
generally falls into the hands of some illiterate dema-
gogue of a stump, who ends by fleecing the
poor dupes, either by stealing their funds, or in
living upon them at an exorbitant expense. Apart
from the fact that the charge is not true 'generally'
—the objection says nothing against principle. It
would, however, not be out of place to ask for proof
of the assertion. Two scamps, one who fled with 25
and one with £l6O of the men's money are instanced.
But was there never a Judas among the twelve before?
A pill maker is said 'modestly.' to ask for £2OO a year
for his services. And what then? A pill maker may
be a good leader, and if he can make more by pills for
himself, or make more for the people as a leader, then
£2OO a year may be a very small salary, indeed, for
his services. It is said a certain educated gentleman,
an unpaid agent, spent rather more than that, in hotel
and cab fares, in less than three months, on behalf of
the British miners! And we believe that gentleman
has a very close connection with the editor of the British
Miner, who himself will scarcely exist long without a
salary, also. To rail against leaders is fashionable; it
is easy, and looks disinterested; but so long as leaders
that arise from the people are marked men, and are
discharged from work, as some of the most honest and
worthy operatives still are; and who, themselves ob-
jecting to strikes sincerely, still become the instrument
of them, by will of their peers,—so long as such men
are, therefore, kept from work, they must of necessity
be maintained by those for whom they labour and for
whom they suffer. In the long run it will be found far
better and more economic to keep and pay a fit man
well, to look after the colliers' interests, than it is
to trust to capitalists for justice. No doubt strikes
are bad, in both principle and effect, but that they are
matters of necessity to obtain justice, and of ultimate
benefit also, is a fact so well known, that we believe
the editor of the British Miner would clo well to
look over his articles carefully before he blames
strikes admitted to be successful. We would, how-
over, that he should sit down, and, divesting himself
-of the old prejudices and platitudes of a worn-out,
.effete, and false philosophy, he should reconsider the
gdations of labour and wages,' setting to himself the
motto of the greatest good to the greatest number'
as a guide and test of any scheme of operation, to be
judged of or pro-pounded. In-that case we believe the
2ntemBts a the British miners will then be likely to
receiffe assistance and not injury from the editor. A
journal really serving the objects this professes to be,
is much needed; but if we are to judge of the future,
by the tendency of No. 1, the collier may well
pray to be 'delivered from his friends (?). J. H.

BRISTOL OPERATIVE STONE-MASONS'
SOCIETY.

PRESENTATION OF £lOO TO A DISABLED

MEMBER.

On Monday evening a meeting of the members of the
operative Stone-masons' Society, which was very
largely attended. was held at the lodge-room, St. John's
Porter-house, Stone-bridge, Bristol, for the purpose of
presenting the sum of £lOO to Brother James Weir,
who has been incapacitated from following his occupa-
tion by an attack of paralysis.
Mr. Samuel Cowlin, who was in the chair, stated
that they were met upon that occasion for the purpose
of presenting a member of their society the sum of
£lOO under the provisions of the laws of their society,
Which enacted that any member who should be
Prevented from following his employment by any
aceillent during work, by the rupture of a blood
vessel, or by an attack of paralysis, was entitled to
the sum of £lOO. Whilst it was a painful duty, it
was a pleasure to know that by his prudence and
forethought, Brother Weirhad placed himself in a posi-
tion which would keep him from going to 'the Bastille.'
He stated that, according to the reports of the society,
during the last six years £10,391 16e. 40. had been
disbursed in sick..pay, £5,045 7s. 9d. for funerals,
£2,900 for accidenta, and £12,325 15s. paid to members
whilst travelling in search of work. The chairman
proceeded to detail the
many benefits which the so-
ciety offered, remarking that if a member was killed
by accident his widow received a sum of £5O, as well
as £lO for funeral expenses, and by the widow con-
tinuing to pay is. 6d. per quart, her relatives were
entitled to the expenses of her funeral, just the same
as if her husband was living. The Chairman said
there were very few societies that could boast of hav-
ing conferred so great an amount of benefit in return
for the small weekly amount paid by the members,
and remarked that not only did they provide for their
members in time of sickness, but they also contributed
largely to the various hospitals of the country, a sum
of £456 15e. having been thus expended during the
last six years.

Mr. E. C. Howell, the secretary, then i proceeded to
make the presentation. He observed that it was with a
feeling of pride that he then, in the name of the so-
ciety, presented Brother Weir with an address, which
was accompanied by the sum of £lOO, which was
awarded him on account of hts being afflicted with
paralysis, and which sum, if properly applied and in-
vested in some lucrative business, would enable him to
maintain himself for the remainder of his days. On
the other band, he was sorry to see him in that posi-
tion for it was a hard thing for a fellow-creature to
be deprived of the use of a limb. He was happy to
think, however, that Brother Weir was thus rendered
independent of parochial relief. The speaker then
presented the address, which was printed, and framed
and glazed. The address bore testimony to the con-
sistent character of the recipient during the 26 years
that he had, been a member of the society, and stated
that the privilege which he was about to receive at
their hands that evening was not to be looked upon as
a charitable gift, but as the honestly earned reward of
his integrity and forethought.
Mr. Wm. Wedlock, the treasurer of the society, then
presented Brother Weir with £lOO in hard cash, re-
marking that he had been a strict and consistent mem-
ber of the society, and had always acted in accordance
with the rules.
Mr. James Weir, in returning thanks, said he hoped
that with perseverance and industry the sum which
they had presented him would provide for him as long
as he should live ; and it gave him great comfort to
know that he could remain a member of their noble
institution by contributing so small a sum as a half-
penny per week to provide the sum of £lO to defray
the expenses of his interment when it should please
God to separate his soul from his body.
Mr. William Sheen spoke at some length upon the
advantages of the society, contending that the large
amounts disbursed by it in times of sickness and death
were a great relief to the ratepayers generally.
Mr. George Earle also addressed the meeting, in
which he congratulated them upon the close of the
recent prolonged strike, hoping that, through the
advantages which they had gained by it, they would
be enabled to make their homes comfortable, and
educate and bring up their children in a respectable
manner, after which the meeting separated.
[ls not the above another direct proof that Trades
Unionists are not that selfish, intolerant, and un-
principled class, which even some so-called religionists
endeavour to lead the public to believe? To all we
would say, "Copy the above as an example, and go
and do likewise."—ED.]

LONDON ROPEAUKERS' STRIKE.—The following sub.
scriptions have been received by the committee since
our last :—Belgrave Society of Painters, two weeks'
subscription, £l. London Amalgamated Association of
Painters, No. 1 Lodge, 75.; No. 3 Lodge, 4s. 9L; No.
7 Lodge, 12s. London Shipwrights' Provident Union
£5. Carpenter' (Adam and Eve) £2. Cigar Makers'
Mutual Association Giff , £5. Loan £l9.
THE HOUR SYSTEM.—A carpenter, F. Percival, em-
ployed in the firm of Messrs. G. Myers, of Lambeth,
noted for 'enforcing the hour system, and employing
the ' Black Brigade,' when Saturday arrived, instead
of receiving payment at the rate of 7d. per hour, as he
anticipated, was only paid a fraction over 6d. per hour;
consequently Mr. Myers was served with a County
Court summons for the remainder of the money, at
the rate of 7d. per hour. But not wishing to appear
in court before a judge and a respectable solicitor, Mr.
Myers preferred paying the money into court. Mr.
Percival is a member of the Old Lambeth Society meet.
ing at the Bell, York-street.
THE MANCHESTER STONEMASONS.—This strike, Or
lock-out, is still in progress. About 500 men left
work, the great majority of whom have left the town,
and obtained employment elsewhere, mason's work
being tolerably plentiful at the present time.
THE LONDON Mesorrs.—Business is brisk, and the
society men are all in employ. The, negroes' have
almost entirely disappeared. The have carried their
'black' looks, and still blacker hearts, into more con-
genial localities, where steadiness, industry, skill, and
principle are at a discount.
MINERS' PERMANENT RELIEF FUND.—The committee
of the above society met on Saturday, in the school
room of St. James's Chapel, Manchester, Mr. John
Howie in the chair. The report of the actuary (Mr.
Spens, of Glasgow) was received, and the discussion
upon it was adjourned till next meeting.
SCOTCH Ml.Nnus.—The miners out on strike in the
district around Coatbridge, have received promise of
the advance demanded, viz., 6d. a day.
GLASGOW.— STRIKE OF HANDLOOM WEAVERS.—On
Tuesday, the men employed in Messrs. Fyfe's weaving
factory, Main-street, Bridgeton, numbering nearly
200, struck work in consequence, it is said, of a reduc-
tion made in their wages. _ _

THE CAMPBELL TEsrimomAL.—The miners of Scot-

land have their intention to present Mr.
Alex. Campbell, of Glasgow, with a testimonial worthy
of his valuable services on their behalf, is well as for
promoting the cause of the working classes generally.

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE liNTELLI-
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE liNTELLI-

GENCE.

Sr. JAMES'S.—A considerable number of the members
of this society met on Monday evening at the
Newcastle on-Tyne, Broad-street, Golden-square, for
the purpose of giving a farewell entertainment to Mr.
Davies, the father and originater of their society, ere
leaving London for his native place, Swansea,_to spend
the remainder of his days, and to rest his bones with
his fathers,' after the fashion of his prototype, the late
illustrious Robert Owen. Mr. Lloyd occupied tits
chair. Several speeches were delivered, and songs
given, appropriate to the occasion, by Messrs. Lunn,
Harris, Vizan, Edgar, and others, each and all expressive
of regret at losing BO valuable a member, whose honest,
straightforward, and impartial conduct, coupled with
the highest order of intelligence and civility, had, by
consistent perseverance, won him the respect of all.—
Mr. Davies replied in a neat speech, thanking his
brother co-operators for the honour they had paid
him, and assured them that in whatever part of the
world he might find himself he should always feel
himself a man prepared to do battle for justice and
right. The meeting was an enthusiastic one, and did
not separate until a late hour. The society is doing
business over £6O per week.
BEDLINGTON EQUITABLE INDUSTRIAL CO-OPERATIVE
SOOIETY.—The fifth
..quarterly report of this society
was laid before the members on Saturday evening.
Twenty members have been enrolled during the quar-
ter, making a lota of 124 members, while two have
withdrawn. The society's capital is £332 163. Goods
were sold during the quarter to the amount of
£943 ss. 8d„ being an increase over last quarter of
£lO2. Dividends were declared on members' pur-
chases at 2s. 2d. in the pound, and 5 per cent. on paid-.
up shares, while the fixed stock has been depreciated
to the extent of £6 2s. The steady progress that has
been made here is very gratifying to the friends of co-
operation.
GREAT Horrox, NEAR BRADFORD. Dr. John
Watts, of Manchester, laid he corner stone of a block
of new buildings, which are to be appropriated to the
purposes of co-operative stores at Great Horton, in
the borough of Bradford. The building will include
a provision shop, a draper's shop, and a butcher's shop
on the ground floor; a show-room and warehousing on
the second storey; and a large lecture ball and rooms
above. The outlay, exclusive of the cost of the ground,
will be £2,000. Aco -operative store was established, with
37 members, about, three years ago' at Great Horton,
and the number at present is 600, and the receipts
amount to about £3OO a week. The original store is
now so scanty that larger premises have become ab-
solutely necessary. The laying of the corner stone
was made the occasion for a great demonstration in
favour of the pringiples of co-operation. Dr. Watts
addressed the large assembly at great length; and
in the district, also addressed the gathering in terms
expressive of sympathy and good-will. A public
meeting was subsequently held at the Primitive
Methodist Chapel.

ON A RUIN.

Thou hast had thy day of glory and pride,
Grey mass of crumbling walls,
And hast seen bright knights thro' thy portals ride,
Dames in thy stately halls ;
But they are all gone,
And left thee alone,
To moulder away, stone by stone.
Thou hast heard the tripping of merry feet,
Thy corridors along,
And hast echoed the sound of music sweet,
The soul inspiring song;
But none now for thee
Trill a monody,
Save the low murmur of the sea.
The sun, as he rose from the rubied East,
All Nature to adorn,
Then saw no gratitude in thy proud heart,
But age was met with scorn;
He's now in the sky,
And, as he rides by,
He laughs at thee with mocking eye.
Thy turrets once menaced each pearly cloud,
With dark and haughty crest,
They foster the grass which weaves thee a shroud;
In which the reptiles rest;
And the hollow howl
Of the horned owl
Is echoed by the wild dog's growl.
W. J.
