articles.title: REGISTRARS REPORT.
articles.text:
REGISTRARS REPORT.

The report for the year 1861 of the Registrar of
Friendly Societies has just been published. Daring
the year the registrar examined and certified the rules
of 1,288 new societies, besides revising and certifying
alterations in the rules of 1,182 societies already in
existence. Notices of dissolution had been received
from 112 societies, the cause of the dissolution most
frequently being the excessive superannuation allow-
ances provided for by the rules, which, with a
diminished membership, had completely impoverished
the societies, and rendered necessary a dissolution, and
the distribution of the funds among the members. In
one instance that of the Friendly Institution at Wor-
cester, the solvency of the society had been impaired
by its being composed of women and men, while
the rates of subscription were framed on calculations
made for men only; whereas it was well known that
'in female clubs the sickness experienced was
considerably greater than in male clubs, and the
annual payments towards deferred annuities for
females were much greater than for males.' In addition,
the contributions for all the benefits were kept in one
account, and not divided with respect to the benefits
subscribed for. A good deal of correspondence had
taken place between the registrar and friendly socie-
ties in the cotton districts, its to whether their sick and
funeral funds could be applied to the relief of distressed
cases, and whether the society, with consent of its
members, could suspend its monthly subscriptions.
To these questions the registrar had invariably an-
swered in the negative; but it appeared that in some
cases the latter course, though illegal, had been
followed out of sheer necessity, scarcely any of
the members being able to continue their subscrip-
tions ; and the registrar had framed a rule, by
adopting which societies would obtain the neces-
saty authority legally to suspend its subscriptions.
The report also contains a variety of correspondence
which the registrar has had in his official capa-
city, embracing such matters as the expenses of
managing the societies, which in some cases were 25
and 82 per cent. of the funds subscribed, and the pro-
cedure in holding annual dinners, and incurring _ex-
penses of that kind, which the majority of the members
of some societies illegally agree to, in spite of the pro-
tests of one or two of the members. The most extra-
ordinary matter, however, about which the registrar
has been consulted is a rule, proposed for a women's
club, providing that any member having a child
within such a time after her marriage as would prove
her to have been guilty of immoral conduct before
marriage, and all unmarried members found in the
family way,' should be expelled. A clergyman who said
he had been mainly instrumental in founding the so-
ciety' had indignantly protested against the rule. The
.rev, gentleman wrote, 'By far the greater number of
females are pregnant in this part of the country before
marriage, and it would be a serious impediment to
the man's proceeding to marriage if his wife was liable
to be brought up and tried by a jury of old maids (the
greater part of the directors being so) as to the parti-
culars of what occurred before marriage, and the issue
quasi bastardised, in opposition to the law, which de-
clares the child born in matrimony under all circum-
stances legitimate. Indeed, a more indecent inquiry,
and less consonant with the laws of the land, I can
scarcely conceive.' The registrar does not state
whether he certified the alteration or not. The report
concludes by giving the abstract of an act, introduced
by Lord Shelburne last session, to establish parochial
friendly societies, under proper superintendence, in
order to obviate the worst evils of such societies, viz.,
the distribution of two or three in a small district, so

that a proper average of sickness cannot be obtained,
and the meeting of the members in public houses, by
which they are induced to spend money for the good of
the house, either out of the society's box or their own
private means and they miss almost altogether the
nroper object of the society.

articles.title: ODDFELLOWS (rANCEIESTER UNITY).- LONDON.
articles.text:
ODDFELLOWS (rANCEIESTER UNITY).-
LONDON.

The anniversary of the Volunteer Lodge was cele-
brated on Tuesday evening at host Saunders's, the
Law and Equity, Carey-street,—P.P.GAl Harris pre-
siding, and P.G. Foster occupying the vice-chair.
After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts, the Chair-
man proposed Prosperity to the Volunteer Lodge,'
the members of which, though young, were full of '
hope and promise that it would become one of the
most useful branches of the Order. The Manchester
Unity, G.M., and Board of Directors' followed, and
was responded to by P.G. Pardon, who dwelt upon the
great good effected by this large society, and its re-
markable progress as shown by the fact that in 1836 it
had only 40,000 members, and in 1862 was increased
to 350,000, with a capital commensurate with the
benefits promised to members. P.G. Foster gave The
North London District and its Officers,' which was re-
sponded to by P.P.G.141. Rough, who stated the dis-
trict was making excellent progress, and must do so
with lodges like the Volunteer, active in the work.
The chairman asked them to honour the toast, Success
to the Widow and Orphan Fund,' and P.O. Bellerby
returned thanks, stating that nearly £27,000 hid been
paid out for benefits, and there was now about £lO,OOO
in hand, and 6,500 members regularly subscribing.
P.G. Banks, sen., next asked attention to the Metro-
politan Benefit Societies Asylum, Ball's-pond, as
especially deserving of all the Orders and their mem-
bers. It had now available cash amounting to £9,000,
and an endowment fund was expected to be estab-
lished, out of which to aid the inmates in supporting
themselves, in addition to present advantages of free
residence, &e. P.G. Chileott proposed 'Kindred
Societies and the Visitors Present,' which was duly
acknowledged, and, after several toasts, enlivened by
some excellent music, the meeting dispersed.
BRISTOL.—At the quarterly committee meeting of
the Bristol District of Manchester Unity Odd Fellows,
held on Monday last, and amount equal to about £5O
was voted by the delegates from the various lodges
present to the fund for the relief of the distressed
operatives in the cotton working districts.
INDEPENDENT ODD FELLOWS AND THE LANCASHIRE
DISTRESS.—A quarterly meeting of the members of the
Independent Order of Odd Fellows, Halifax district
(M.T.T.), was held at their hall in this town, on. Monday
evening Mr. J. A. Riley in the chair. One of the
subjects of discussion was the present distress in Lan-
cashire, and the sum of £lO was granted towards its
relief, with permission to solicit aid throughout the dis-
trict for the same object.

articles.title: FORESTERS.
articles.text:
FORESTERS.

BRISTOL—A handsome silver medal has been pre-
sented by the officers and members of Court High-
land Chief,' Bristol, to Brother Joseph Fewings, in
recognition of his valuable services as secretary for the
last four years.—Court Marquis of Worcester' held
their anniversary at the Rising Sun, Lower Castle-
street, on Monday evening, Brother Cattle taking the
chair, and about 70 sat down to an excellent dinner,
the evening being 'filled in' by speechmaking, sing-
ing, and toasting.
ANCIENT ORDER OF SHEPHERDS' ABHTON
On Wednesday the members of the Loyal St. Michael's
Lodge, with about 30 brethren from various lodges, sat
down to an excellent supper provided by Host
Pritchard, at his sole expense. Afterwards P. C.:S.
' Thomas was called to the chair, and W. M. Smith to
the vice-chair, and the remainder of the evening was
most agreeably spent.

articles.title: DRUIDS.
articles.text:
DRUIDS.

Hum..—The anniversary dinner of the Welcome
Lodge, of the Ancient Order of Druids, was held at
the Whittington Inn, Castle-row, on Wednesday even-
ing, when eighty members sat down to an excellent
dinner provided by Host Wood. After the cloth had
been drawn, Mr. James Hnnrick, N.G.A., occupied
the chair, and Mr. J. L. Whitfield, the vice-chair. The
usual loyal toasts having been given and duly re-
sponded to, the Chairman gave.-.-' The Order of Druids
and the Board of Management,' to which the Vice-
Chairman responded. Mr. Stather, sea., then proposed
The Druids' Welcome Lodge,' to which Mr. R. Ro-
binson, the secretary of the lodge, responded, and in doing
so he read the financial statement of the Welcome
Lodge, which was as follows :—Funeral money during
the past year, £23 is. 1014. ; money paid to sick mem-
bers £6O 2s. The total income from 1801 to 1862 was
£293 ss. 6d., leaving a balance in hand of £ll7, which
has been deposited in the bank. The total property of
the lodge at the present time amounts to £485 2s. 3d.
In 1855 the lodge only numbered 85 members, but
since that period it had increased both in wealth and
numbers, and at the present time there were no less
than 211 names on the books, being an increase of
129. The lodge had been in existence 23 years, and
he (the secretary) was happy to see that there were
four of the members present that night who were in
the lodge at its formation. The health of the officers
of the lodge was then given, the chairman responding.
The Vice-Chairman gave, The Lodge Surgeon,' to
which Mr. Arden responded, and the rest of the even-
ing was spent in a convivial manner.

articles.title: EXAMINATION OF THE HYDE-PAR) RIOTERS.
articles.text:
EXAMINATION OF THE HYDE-PAR)
RIOTERS.

The prisoners taken into custody on the Sunday
were brought up to Marlborough. street police-court for
examination on Monday. A large number of persons
assembled at an early hour in front of the court, and
much excitement prevailed.
The following were the names of the prisoners, and
the offences with which they were charged :—Dennis
Harrington, Michael Collins, John Kirby, James Con-
don, Francis Sullivan, Edward O'Hara, Patrick Dal-
ton, Thomas Morris, Peter Tacci, John Mahony, James
Fenwick, James Daly, Patrick Maearthy, for creating
a disturbance in Hyde-park, Kirby being also charged
' with an assault; John Smith, Henry Sowdon, Alfred
Watts, James Taylor, throwing stones to the common
danger of passengers in Hyde-park; Thomas Welsh,
for assaulting Mr. Jonathan Potter, chemist, Clifton
road, Maida-vale •' Pietro Ansoni, an Italian, for
attempting to stab John Williams, of Nightingale-
street, Marylebone.
Inspectors Swanson, of the A division, and Draper,
of the C division, attended to watch the case on the
part of the Commissioners of Police. Mr. Edward
Lewis, of Great Marlborough-street, appeared for
Axsoni and the other prisoners.
But few of the persons who had been assaulted and
injured by the prisoners attended, and the witnesses
against them were chicfly police-constables, whose evi-
dence was mainly a repetition of the account given
abole.

The following were the punishments inflicted upon
the prisoners, who were nearly all Irishmen :—Kirby,
two months' imprisonment. Harrington and Collins,
405., or a month each. O'Hara and Sullivan, 205., or
a month. Fenwick, 10s., or a month. Dalton, 205., or
a month. Morris and Tacci, £5, or a month. Ma-
hony remanded for a week. Condon, 10s. Watts
discharged. Sowdon, Smith, and Taylor, 405., or a
month. Walsh, two months' imprisonment. Daly
discharged. Macarthy 405., or a month. Ansoni re-
mandect for attempted stabbing. It is a fact worthy of
notice that only one case of felony arising from the
disturbances in the Park came before the magistrate—
that of a young man stealing a watch.

articles.title: MORE ASSATTT,TS BY IRISHMEN.
articles.text:
MORE ASSATTT,TS BY IRISHMEN.

At the Marylebone Police-court, on Tuesday, three
Irish labourers were charged with assaults of a most
violent nature upon the police, arising out of the Pope
and Garibaldian disturbances. The names of the
prisoners, all of them described as labourers, are James
Hishon, John Brown, and Patrick Kennedy. Brown,
238 D, said: Between six and seven o'clock on the
previous evening, while on duty in Duke-street, Man-
ehester-Equare, I saw the prisoners and, others coming
along, calling out as loudly as peissible, Down with
Garibaldi, and up with the Pope ! ' I desired them to
be quiet, when Brown said, I'll see you first,
and if you interfere with me, I'll knock your brains
out.' He then struck me with a large stick, and his
companions also kicked and inflicted blows upon me.
I feel the effects of the blows now. The prisoners
were all armed with large sticks, and Hishon said that
if I didn't let him go, he'd rip me open with a knife.
Mr. Mansfield said that the cry of Garibaldi and the
Pope seemed to be looked upon by a certain class as an
excuse for fighting. He wished it to be distinctly un-
derstood that in such cases as the present he should
not inflict any fine; and he committed the prisoners to
hard labour in the House of Correction for a month.
On their being removed to the lock-up-room by Ansted
the gaoler, a lot of Irish, male and female, shouted
out, The Pope for ever, and three cheers for him!'
On Wednesday, at the Clerkenwell Police-court,
Matthew Hurley, a powerful fellow, a blacksmith, was
charged with a violent assault on Charles M'Nalty.
The complainant was standing at the bar of the Hope
public-house, Smithfield, when the prisoner came in
and accusing him of being a Garibaldian, struck him a
violent blow in the mouth, and was proceeding to other
acts of violence, when the police were called, and he
was taken into custody. Fined 40s. or one month.
On Tuesday, at the Bow-street Police-court, three
Irishmen, named Brown, Wallis, and Hennessey, were
charged with creating a disturbance in a public-house
in Broad-street, St. Giles's, and assaulting the police.
Hennessey was further charged with stabbing Police-
man Dray, 106 F. The prisoners, who had been at-
tending with a numerous party of their friends at
Marlborough-street to hear the examination of the
Hyde Park rioters, returned to St. Giles's in the
afternoon, and created a disturbance in the public-
house above-mentioned, calling the other persons
present Garibalians,' and challenged all corners to
fight. The landlord having called in the policemen
to quell the disturbance, the prisoners attacked them
in the most savage manner. Hennessey inflicted on
Dray, 10 F, a severe wound with a knife, an inch and
a quarter in length, immediately under the temple.—
Mr. Corrie said he would treat the charge against
Brown and Wallis as a mere drunken row. They got
drinking and talking nonsense about Garibaldi, and
were ready to quarrel with anybody. Nor should he
have taken much notice of the matter, but for the
serious consequence in the stabbing of Dray. Brown
and Wallis must pay 205., or go to prison for 14 days.
Hennessey must be committed for trial,
On Monday evening a serious disturbance took place
in Field-lane and Saffron-hill, Clerkenwell, between
two bodies of Irishmen, partisans of Garibaldi and the
Pope. The police were compelled to interfere, and the
whole neighbourhood was in a state of excitement.
The disturbance was not quelled without much diffi-
culty.
On Tuesday evening, during the performances at the
North Woolwich Gardens, one of the vocalists sang a
song in praise of Garibaldi, which called forth great
cheers from the audience. A party af about a dozen
Irish sailors, however, were present, and commenced
hissing loudly, and shouting The Pope for ever I '
On being remonstrated with they became perfectly
furious, and, one of them drawing out. his knife,
attempted to stab a man standing near him. The
fellow was immediately knocked down, and the whole
party were at once summarily ejected from the gardens
by the people, there being no police present.

RIOT AT BIRZENHEA.D.—On Wednesday evening
Birkenhead was the scene of a disgraceful disturbance,
in which about three or four thousand Irishmen, com-
posed chiefly of dock labourers, took part. Connected
with the township there is a small association, called
the Parliamentary Debating Society, which met last
winter in Brooke-street, in the institute attached to
the Holy Trinity Church, of which the Rev. Dr.
Baylee is the incumbent. During the last week
placards were posted on the walls announcing that the
society would meet last evening for the first time this
season in the institute, the subject to be discussed
being 'Sympathy with Garibaldi and Italy.' This
announcemont seems to have given umbrage to a por-
tion of the Irish Roman Catholic population of the
place, and, following the example of their countrymen
in the metropolis, they determined that the Parlia-
mentary Debating Society should not have an oppor-
tunity of expressing sympathy with the great Italian
patriot. No sooner was the gas lighted in the school-
room than a body of men in slops commenced breaking
the windows. Although the lights in the institute
were extinguished, stones and other missiles were
thrown at the windows, and whenever a smash of
glass took place it was accompanied with Three
cheers for the Pope.' Mr. Superintendent Birnie and
nearly the whole police force of the township were
promptly on the ground, but the efforts of forty or
fifty officers to disperse the crowd were of no avail.
The mob then attacked the church itself, breaking
about 300 panes of glass, and it was not until the
attendance of Fathers Golding and Brunditt, who re-
monstrated with them, that the mob could be induced
to disperse. None of the rioters are in custody.

THE RELIGIOUS SERVICES IN THEATRES.—The winter
campaign of the committee who conduct the religious
services in the metropolitan theatres was opened on
Sunday night. At the Surrey Theatre there was an
overwhelming congregation. Hymns were sung and
prayers offered, after which there was a sermon by the
Rev. R. Robinson, minister of York-road Chapel,
Lambeth. It was announced that the service next
Sunday evening will be conducted by the Rev. Samuel
Minton, M.A., of Worcester College, Oxford. Sadler's
Wells Theatre, the Standard, Shoreditch ; and the
Pavillion, Whitechapel, were also thrown open on
Sunday evening for special services conducted by
clergymen of the church of England, and Protestant
dissenting ministers:'
CHAMPIONSHIP or TUE THAMES.—it is with great
satisfaction we have it in our power to inform our
readers that there is every chance of the rival cham-
pions of England and Australia coming together in a
scullers match on the Thames, over the usual metro-
politan course, from Putney to the Ship at Mortlake.
On Tuesday evening, September 30, a meeting of a
few backers and admirers of the Northern champion
was held at Mr. J. Bagnall's the Scotch Arms Inn,
Newcastle, to consider the Challenge from the two
new candidates for the championship. After. some
discussion, it was agreed that Chambers should accept
both matches, but give Green the preference for
priority, in consequence of his being first in the field,
and having travelled so many miles to try conclusions
with him. In accordance with the resolution formed,
£25 were sent to the stakeholder, to make a match to
row Green, a fair right-away wager, either on the
Thames or Tyne, for £2OO a side or upwards, to take
place in two months. A match will also be made
with Everson, for £2OO a side, to take place a fort-
night after the race with Green, win or lose.—lfotts
Guardfen.

THE ALLEGED MURDER IN THE CITY.

On Tuesday, Samuel Gardiner, a chimney-sweep,
residing in Northumberland-alley, Fenchurch-street,
and Elizabeth Humbler, also residing in the same
place, were again placed at the bar before the Lord
Mayor on remand, charged with having murdered
Elizabeth Gardiner, the wife of the first-named pri-
soner. _ _

Mr. Lewis, of Ely-place, appeared for Gardiner, and
Mr. Sleigh for Humbler.
The facts of this extraordinary case have already
appeared in the evidence taken before the coroner's
jury, who returned a verdict of wilful murder against
both prisoners.
The examination of the numerous witnesses, which
was simply a recapitulation of that taken before the
coroner' occupied the entire morning.
Mr. Sleigh proceeded to address his lordship, and
said he did not see that there was any evidence against
the unfortunate girl Humbler, and his lordship in-
terrupted him, and said it was needless for him to go
on, as he was quite of that opinion—that there was no
evidence to inculpate the female prisoner.
Mr. Lewis, on behalf of Gardiner, said he thought
he would show that there was no evidence against his
client either, and that all his actions were those of an
honest man. In the first place, he was the first to
fetch the officer, which was not the act of a guilty
man. Again, he had called the attention of the police
to the marks of blood, and as regarded the marks of
soot on the arms, the prisoner had slept with his wife,
and there was nothing to show that those marks had
not been there some time, and the prisoner's vocation
easily accounted for such marks as those. As regarded
the scream which was heard by one of the witnesses,
there was no doubt that the act was committed at that

time; and it was clearly proved by another witness
that the prisoner Gardiner was away at the time the
scream was heard, which was six o'clock.
His Lordship said he was of the same opinion as
the witness—viz., that the scream was from one of
the children.

A witness was called, however, James Gardiner, son
of the deceased, who stated that the eldest child was
away, and the only persons who slept in the house on
the Sunday night were the prisoner and his wife, the
prisoner Humbler, and a little child two years and a
half old.

Mr. Lewis suggested that the scream could hardly
have come from the child. The medical gentlemen
gave it as their opinion that deceased could not have
done it herself, but still it was only an opinion. It
was manifestly clear that the act was committed at the
time the scream was heard, and it was equally clear
that the prisoner was absent at that time. There was
no blood found about him, and when he might, if he
had been guilty, escaped, he had remained, and had
given every assistance in his power.
His lordship said. he was of opinion that the evi-
dence was quite sufficient to justify him in committing
the prisoner for trial, and he was bound to send the
case before a jury. He had his duty to perform, and
be considered his duty was to commit him for trial.
As regarded the girl, he had beard nothing to incul-
pate her, and if it were in his power he should dis-
charge her, and as far as he was concerned she was
discharged.
Gardiner then nceived the usual caution, and said
he was not guilty.
The prisoners were then removed from the bar. The
prisoner Humbler will, of course, be detained on the
coroner's warrant, notwithstanding his lordship's deci-
sion.

articles.title: SUICIDE OF A GENTLEMAN IN A PRIVATE LUNATIC ASYLUM.
articles.text:
SUICIDE OF A GENTLEMAN IN A
PRIVATE LUNATIC ASYLUM.

A somewhat lengthened inquiry was held on Wed-
nesday before Mr. Walthew, at Grove Hall Lunatic
Asylum, Bow, touching the death of Mr. B. Ward,
aged forty, a patient of that establishment. John
Hill, an attendant, said the deceased was a private
gentlemen, and had been an inmate of the gentleman's
ward for some time. He had great conversational
powers and spoke quite rationally. On Thursday
evening he watched his opportunity, and contrived to
squeeze himself through a ventilating aperture in the
dining-room window only a few inches in width. He
then dropped down into the flower-beds, and by some
means got over the lofty walls surrounding the
grounds. An alarm was immediately raised, but
he got clear off. No trace could be discovered
until next day, when ho was seen quite accidentally by
the barber of the establishment in Mile-end, walking
into London. The barber, recognising him, came out
of his shop, and to his dismay accosted him, and asked
him to return to the asylum. Though overwhelmed at
the sudden upset of his plans he made no resistance,
but allowed himself to be brought back, and was given
into witness's charge. Witness, to amuse him, took
him into the garden, and he there said that after he
had escaped over the wall he determined to throw his
pursuers out of their reckoning, by walking to
Woodford, which was about seven miles in the
opposite direction to London, and thus avoid the
road they would be almost sure to suppose he had
taken. When he got to Woodford he took lodgings,
where he spent the night. The next morning, how-
ever, he considered that if he could get into London he
should be more likely to escape notice, and he accord-
ingly set out early to enter it unobserved, and he should
have succeeded perfectly only for the accident of Gil-
bert, the barber, spying him from his shop as he was
passing in the morning. He Laid that he had set his
heart on accomplishing his escape. Shortly after this
conversation witness turned his back for a moment,
and directly afterwards missed the deceased. Sup-
posing that he had again tried to escape witness had
the grounds searched, but without avail. Upon the
house being searched, however, he was found hang-
ing to the cornice of his bedstead by a new rope,l
which he must have bought while in Woodford.
The body was warm, but life was extinct. Doctor
Alonzo Stocker, medical superintendent, said that the
deceased when brought back by the barber from the
Mile-end-road seemed extraordinarily agitated. He
said that he was led to make his escape by a vision
which tokl him that his wife was dead. Witness
took from him a small penknife of his wife's and
gave instructions to have him carefully watched,
which the attendants appeared to have done, except
for the instant in which he gave them the slip. The
coroner remarked that it ought to be rendered
impossible for any lunatic to commit suitide in
an asylum. Dr Stocker said that if precautions of an
extreme kind were carried out the place would par-
take of sum a prison-like aspect that the curative.
treatment of the patients would become impossible.
There were 100 or 200 patients in the establishment
who had been admitted as suicidal, but the cheerful
unrestraining system had such an influence on them
that the present was only the second instance of sui-
cide that had been accomplished. The jury regretted
that the attendant should have lost sight of the de-
ceased, and recommended that patients for the future
should be searched. They returned a verdict that the
deceased destroyed himself whilst in an unsound state
of mind.

DISTRIBUTION OF MEDALS BY THE PRINCE OF WALES.
—His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, being
anxious to mark his deep interest in the success of
the International Exhibition—an enterprise which
owed its origin to his beloved father—has, with the
approbation of her Majesty, graciouely undertaken to
distribute the medals and certificates of honourable
mention, at a state ceremonial early in the year 1863,
after the building has been cleared.
A VOLUNTEER COMMITTED FOR STABBING WITH A
BAYONET.-At the Rochdale petty sessions, on Monday,
before James Chadwick, Esq. (chairman), J. P. Pagan,
Esq. (mayor), and other magistrates, John Stead, a
private
in the 24th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers, was
charged with stabbing William Ogden Fletcher, a
fellow-volunteer, with the bayonet. It seems that
on Saturday last the corps of which the prosecutor
and prisoner are members were out on a march to
Whitworth, and on their breaking off for half an hour
there the prisoner took advantage of this to quit the
ranks altogether for the evening, and the corps had
to return without him. About twelve o'clock the
same night the prosecutor Was going down Whitworth-
road, Rochdale, when he met the prisoner, intoxicated,
and having his bayonet at the end of his gun. He
reproved him for the latter circumstance, on which
the prisoner made an attempt to rush at him with
the bayonet, but without success; but a little later on,
the prosecutor having followed him to further remon-
strate, prisoner made a thrust at him again, piercing
him in the arm, and in a minute or so afterwards
repeating the offence. Taken to a medical officer, it
was discovered that the prosecutor was bleeding a
good. deal from the left arm, on the inside of which,
above the elbow, there was an incised wound, and
another on the outer side. The wounds were shallow,
however, and unimportant. The prisoner was com-
mitted for trial.—Leeds _Mercury.

COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.
(Before Mr. Commissioner Holroyd,)

IN RE VEILLARD.-APPLICATION TO EXAMINE WITNESSES.

Mr. Lawrence applied, on behalf Df Messrs. Mappin.
Brothers, creditors of M. Veillard for £1,200, to ap-
point a day for the examination of the debtor, the Hon.
Mr. Cadogan, and other witnesses, in reference to the
terms of an agreement between M Veillard and the
Hon. Mr. Cadogan, which was said to be injurious to
the general body of creditors, and contrary: to public
policy. M. Veillard owed £28,000, and creditors for
upwards of £7,000 had dissented from the deed.—Hie
Honour said it was desirable that notice of the aypli-
cation should be given to the inspectors appointed
under the deed, and the matter stood over for that
purpose.
IN RE THE LONDON BUILDING COMPANY (LIMITED).
This was a petition for winding-up, presented by
Mr. J. C. Arnaud, of Bromley, Kent, the secretary to
the company; and Mr. C. S. Swift, wood-turner, of
Cleveland-street, Fitzroy-square. It appeared that the
company had only been established in February, 1860;
its nominal capital was £20,000, in a like number of
shares, but only £409 had been paid. The petition
alleged that three-fourths of the capital had been lost
or become unavailable, and that the company was
unable to meet its engagements, and on that ground a
winding-up order was prayed. Mr. R. Griffiths ap-
peared in support of the petition. An adjournment
was taken by consent, on account of some proceedings
said to be pending in the Westminster police-court.
The liabilities of the company are stated at £650.

articles.title: MIDDLESEX SESSIONS.
articles.text:
MIDDLESEX SESSIONS.

(Before Assistant-Judge Payne.)
CHARGE OF FRAUD.—EXTRAORDINART SEENE.
Stephen Joseph Meaney, said to be an editor of a pro-
vincial newspaper, was indicted for obtaining by false
pretences from John Martin, a book, value 16s. 6d., the
property of Thomas Edward Whibley, with intent to
defraud. The evidence having been given, the jury,
after deliberating some time, returned the following
verdict That the prisoner made the false pretences,
and that the prosecutors parted with the goods on the
faith of the documents produced, but that the prisoner
ultimately intended to pay for them.' Mr.
Ribton said that this was in fact a verdict
of not guilty. Tho Deputy Judge told Mr.
Ribton that he did not wish to be directed by him.
The learned judge told the jury that he could not take
the verdict they had just returned. If they believed,
the prisoner only used the forged letters with a view'
eventually to pay for them, that was not a verdict he
could receive.—The jury were of opinion that the pri-
soner obtained the books upon the faith of the repre-
sentations contained in the letters.—The Judge: That
is a verdict of guilty.—Mr. Ribton said that the jury
had already said that the prisoner intended to pay for
the books. That certainly does away with the unlaw-
ful detention.—The judge observed that the jury had
returned a verdict which was, in his opinion, one of
guilty, and he should give sentence.—Doctor Bate-
man, one of the Middlesex magistrates, who hap-
pened to be sitting on the bench, said he thought
it was a case in which no sentence ought to be
given. He looked upon it as a verdict of not guilty.—
The prisoner: I demand to have the first verdict re-
corded. I . have been, I maintain, acquitted of an evil
intention.—The Judge: I say the jury have found a
verdict of guilty.—Mr. Ribton: Will you reserve the
case I.—The Judge: Certainly not, it is too simple.—
Mr. Ribton: The prisoner has a right to have the first
verdict recorded against him, and that, I contend, is
one of not guilty.—The Prisoner: Will your lordship
hear what I've got to say ?---The Judge: I refuse to do
so; but, before .I pass sentence, I will consult the
learned Assistant-Judge.—The prisoner: I demand.—
The Judge (to the officer) : Remove the prisoner.—The
officer in the dock obeyed the direction of the judge,
and the prisoner was taken below.

articles.title: PROGRESS OF T_HE EARLY CLOSING
articles.text:
PROGRESS OF T_HE EARLY CLOSING

220VEMENT.

The Saturday half-holiday or early closing move-
ment, as it affects the retail trade of London, having
successfully passed through the somewhat trying ordeal
of the past summer, appears to be increasing in pop-
larity, both with the firms themselves and the public.
In the Edgware-road, Mr. D. B. Johnstone has an-
nounced his intention of forthwith closing at six o'clock
on Saturdays, while in Farringdon-street two em-
ployers (Mr. T. Simpson and Mr. G. Emery) have ar-
ranged to close at 7,8, and 9 o'clock on Saturdays, ac-
cording to the season, instead of keeping open as for-
merly until 12. On the other nights of the week also, the
latter houses have lately made an advance by closing at
8 o'clock instead of 9. Messrs. J. Shoolbred and Co.,
of the Tottenham-court-road, while closing at 4 on
Saturdays, have just commenced closing at 7 on the
other nights of the week. Another large house,
situated in the City, began closing at 8 o'clock in
September instead of October. In Oxford-street, some
of the booksellers and fancy stationers have com-
menced closing at 8 o'clock for the winter, instead of
half-past 8 and 9 o'clock, including Saturdays. As
many as 900 persons participate in the benefit
of these arrangements, and as an evidence that the
assistants are not unconscious of the kindly spirit thus
shown by their employers, it may be mentioned that
the employes of Messrs. Spencer, Turner, and
Boldero, in Lisson-grove, lately presented two members'
of the firm (Mr. Turner and Mr. Boldero) each with
a very handsome silver snuff-box, bearing inscriptions
setting forth that the presentation was made as an
acknowledgment of the spirited and generous manner
in which the firm had promoted the Saturday early
closing movement. It may be hoped that the Edg-
ware-road district will return to that more general
adoption of the Saturday movement which it exhibited
in 1860-61, since which time only two houses in that
thoroughfare (Messrs. Beech and Berrall, and Messrs.
E. and R. G-arrould) have been closing as early as 6
on Saturdays. It may be mentioned that Messrs.
-Spencer, Turner, and Boldero close as early as 4 on
Saturdays in the winter half of the year, the agree-
ment which prevails generally among the larger retail
firms at the West-end and in the City.

articles.text:
THE SMALLPDX IN SHEEP.

SEIZURE OF MEAT IN PADDINGTON.

At a meeting of the Paddington Vestry, held at the
Vestry-hall, Harrow-road, on Wednesday, Mr. Whitler
(churchwarden) in the ehair, the Sanitary and Public
Health Committee appointed by the vestry presented
a report from the medical officer of health, which was
to the effect that the inspector of nuisances had seized
about 1401bs. of meat in a putrescent state from the
premises of Mr. John Oakes, No. 3, Cornwall road-
terrace, which was, on a magistrate's order, destroyed.
Mr. Benson suggested as advisable, considering the
present alarming spread of smallpox in sheep, and the
foregoing report, that a printed circular should be
issued by the order of the vestry, addressed to all the
butchers of the parish, requesting the exercise of due
caution as to what meat they brought into the parish
for human food.
Mr. Prescott (churchwarden) said, as a member of
the Sanitary Committee, it was the opinion of that
body that this was really a vital question concerning
the health of the parishioners, and it was suggested
that the inspector should go round to every butcher
continually armed with a resolution from the vestry.
Mr. Hall looked upon this mutter as deserving their
serious consideration. (Hear, hear.) He could not
quite agree with the churchwarden that the inspector
should be instructed to call upon the butchers and
simply read a resolution respecting due caution, but
that a circular should be issued, and with the exercise
of proper vigilance by the inspector, it would have a
very beneficial effect. (Hear.)
Captain Liveing thought the best course would be
to let the butchers know that the vestry would prose-
cute with the utmost rigour of the law whenever
putrescent meat was found.
Mr. Dickenson contended that by this proceeding
they were unnecessarily alarming the public mind.
It was well known that in all cases of smallpox the
most ignorant person was able to detect it instantly.
He did not think that there was any need for alarm in
the matter.
After some further remarks, the meeting unani-
mously resolved to order the inspector of nuisances to
call on the respective butChers in the parish, directing
their attention to the opiddmic disease amongst sheep,
and to urge upon them the exercise of due vigilance
to prevent the introduction on their premises of meat
affected. thereby.

NEW YORX, September 24. President Lincoln's
proclamation to free the slaves of rebels and the slaves
an all rebel States on the Ist of January, 1863, excites
great di-cussion. It is consider-1 a. blunder by all
except extreme abolitionists. It, aent down the price
of all securities yesterday, and increased the premium
on gold to 181 per cent, and on silver to 15 per cent.
The Democratic /sixty are opposed to it as illegal,
unconstitutional, ill- timed, and unjust, while the Repub-
licans are divided in opinion. The battle at Antietam
Creek becomes less and less of a victory in the public
estimation as the facts are made known. A large Ccn-
federate force is still on the Maryland side of the Poto-
mac, and those which retreated to the Virginia side
retreated leisurely, with all their arms, ammunition,.
artillery, baggage, and sick and wounded. They have
possession of the valley of the Shenandoah, and captured
at Harper's Ferry as many stores, as much artillery, light
and heavy, as recompensed them for all the perils and
losses-of the Maryland campaign. The total loss on
both sides continues to be estimated at 20,000 men.
Commander Treby has been summarily, dismissed from
the naval service of the United States for allowing the
British steamer Ovieto to escape the blockade at Mobile.
His friends deny the right of the Secretary of the
Navy to cashier an officer without a trial, and demand
a court-martial. The public sentiment and naval and
military men support the demand. General Braxton
i Bragg, n command of a Confederate army of 30,000
men in Kentucky, has avoided a battle with General
Buell, and marched upon Louisville. He has de-
manded the surrender of that city. General Nelson,
the Federal commander, has refused, and notified all
the women, children, and non-combatants to depart, as
he intends to defend his post to the last extremity.
It is not believed he can offer effectual resistance.
General Buell is reported to be in pursuit of General
Bragg, while General Kirby Smith is marching after
-Bison, who may thus be placed between two fires and
forced to capitulate. Mr. Morgan, Governor of the
State ef New York, has ordered the draught to com-
mence. on the 15th of October, 40,000 men, the quotas
. due under the two calls of the President. Notwith-
• standing the enormously heavy bounty, £OO money, and
the vigorous efforts made to fill up the numbers, the
• city of New York is 8,000 men in arrear on the second
call, and the State of New York 32,000.
NEW Yonx, Sept. 23, morning. —lt is rumoured
that the Confederateahave crossed Blackwater River, in
force, and are threatening Norfolk and Suffolk. An en-
gagement occurred on the 19th inst., south of Juke,
Mississippi, between General Rosencranz and General
Price. The Confederates retreated South during the
night. The Federals captured 250 prisoners. The
Federals are preparing to attack the forts at the entrance
to Mobile. The Governor of Pennsylvania has re-
called the Stato militia home. The Confederate
Governor of Louisiana has threatened General Butler
with retaliation if the misconduct of the Federal troops
should be oontinued outside the limits of the city of
New Orleans. General Butler replied that if the threat
was carried out he should also retaliate.
SEPT. 23 Evening.—The Federal army is reported
°to be rapidly crossing the Potomac at Williamsport,
lnder the superintendence of General M‘Clellan. It
is rumoured that Generals Ffeintzelman and Sigel are
in Virginia to stop the Confederate retreat. General
Bragg is rapidly marching on Louisville. He has sum-
moned die Federal commander to surrender, but this
the latter has refused to do. Women and children have
been ordered away. General Bragg is close to the city.
An attack is expected immediately, but the Federal com-
mander is confident he will be able to repel it. Gene-
ral Kirby Smith is to hold General Buell in check during
Bragg's attack. The Republican journals approve Presi-
dent Lincoln's proclamation, but say that it will have
no effect. It has caused no public excitement whatever.
SEPT. 24, Morning.—The Federals made unsuc-
cessful efforts on Friday and Saturday last to cross the
Potomac, at Shepherd's-town, into Virginia, but were
each time repulsed. General Stuart's Confederate cavalry
crossed into Maryland on Saturday last, but afterwards
returned to Virginia. None of General M'Clellan!s army
has yet crossed the Potomac. The Confederates do
not show in, force on the Virginia banks of the Potomac,
but are supposed to be lying in ambush a short dis-
tance from the fiver. The Southern journals state
that the Confederates captured 49 pieces of artillery
at Harper's Ferry. The Governor of New :York State
has issued an order for a draught of 40,000 men on
October 10. Mr. Foote has introduced a resolution
in the Confederate Congress, to the effect that the suc-
cess of the Confederate Generals justified the Confe-
derate Government in sending Commissioners to Wash-
ington to propose the terms of a just and honourable
peace. The Journal of Commerce thinks that President
Lincoln's proclamation can only lead to a continuation
of the war.

SEPT. 25, Afternoon.—President Lincoln has sus-
pended the Writ of Habeas Corpus, and declared martial
law throughout the 'United States with respect to all
pegsons arrested for aiding the rebellion or hindering
the draught. The Secretary of the Treasury has inti-
mated that he will receive deposits of
_gold returnable

in gold with four per cent. interest. Tile deposit must
remain thirty days,. with ten days'inotice of withdrawal.
SEPT. 26, Evening.—No Federals have yet crossed
into Virginia. It is supposed that if M'Clellan should
attempt crossing, a battle will ensile._ The Confede-
. .

rates emain on-the line of the Upper Potomac, and are
destroying the Baltimore and Ohio railroad between
Harper's Ferry and Cumberland. A portion of General
Buelrs forces has arrived at Louisville. The city is
considered safe from attack. The Confederates had

seized Salt River Whisky Distillery, thirty miles from
Louisville, and are advancing on the city.

AMNESTY TO GARIBALDI.—An amnesty has at length
been granted to Garibaldi and all other persons encra,ed
with him in the late rising, with the exception of those
who deserted from the Royal army. This latter reserva-
tion still further diminishes the grace of the act, NN hich
had, indeed, well nigh lost all its grace before, from the
length of time which was allowed to elapse before it
was granted, and from the manifest reluctance with
which it has been granted at last._

NnAroLrritx BIaGANDA.GE. —We continue to receive
shocking.news of Neapolitan brigandage. On the 24th
ult. Mare.sta, a priest, a member of the Italian
Parliament, a man universally esteemed and beloved,
was attacked by robbers at his, own house in Sorrento,
and, as he bravely defended himself, the good canon
was shot down dead by the bandits. The public force
ran to the spot in time to seize one of the brigands, who
was found to be a porter on the Castellamare railway.
Brigands are described as being numerous in the vicinity
of Potynza, Foggia, Nola, Avigliano, and even as near
Naples as the village or Camaldoli, on Mount Vesuvius.
This in spite of the state of siege, and of the large force
now under the orders of General La Marmora.

POSSESSION or A RIVER.—When a landed proprietor
possesses the ground on both sides of a non-navigable-
and non-floatable stream, can he, by means of a chain
thrown from one bank to the other' establish a bar to the
water-course? The Civil Tribunal of Poutoise and-the
Imperial Court of Paris have decided in the affirmative.
But is that chain to be respected as an inclosure ? Here
opinions differ; the Civil Tribunal says no, and the
Imperial Court yes. MM. Pauhier and Libert are pro-
prietors and occupants at Gonesse, of land comprising
the two banks of the Cloud, a small stream, which they
have barred by means of a chain fixed from one bank to
the other. The Nonitezir, which publishes the judgment,
adds And we unite lathe opinion of the Imperial Court;
it is in reality their property which those persons barred,
and not the v,atercourse, which can still run as before.
Every one has a right to-tio 'what he likes on his own
property.'—Galignani.
THE EYE OP THE CRAE.—A creature -that depends
upon.. its own exertions to capture the active prey on
which it feeds must necessarily be furnished with power-
ful eyes, which are capable of extending the faculty of
vision over a very large field. These eyes are seen on
the front margin of the crab, placed on footstalks, -and
having a peculiar nacreous lustre on their grey-brown
surfaces. On examination with a good pocket lens the
eyes are seen to be compound, i. e., formed of a great
number of facets, each possessing the power of vision,
and all communicating with their common optic nerve.
The delicate raised lines caused by the serried ranks of
these compound eyes are:the origin of the peculiar lustre
just mentioned. It will be .seen, too, that the visual
portion of these organs passes partially round the foot-
stalks so that when the creature protrudes its eyes it can
see objects on all sides with equal. ease. Now, replace
the crab in the water, and watch it as it exhibits the
instinct which has been implanted in its being by its'
Maler. Advancing with the flowing tide, 'tliftlt ever
remaining within a foot or two of the edge, the crab keeps
its eager watch fot food, and suffers few living things to
pass without capturing them. The whole nature of the
animal seems to be changed while it is seeking its prey.
The timid, fearful demeanour which it assumes when
taken at a disadvantage wholly vanishes, and the appa-
rently ungainly crab becomes full of life and spirit, active
and fierce as the hungry leopard, and no less destructi e
among the smaller beings that frequent the same locality
—Once a Week.

DJ. LIVINGSTONE.

The following letter was read, at the meeting of the
British Association at Cambridge, on the 6th :
Shupanou, River Zambesi, April 29, 186.2.
My dear Sir lioferick Murchison,—With a sore, sore
heart I muFA telt you of the loss of my much loved wife,
whose form was laid .in the grave yesterday morning.
She died in Shu-panga-house on the evening of the
27th, after about seven days' illness. I must confess
that this heavy stroke quite takes the heart out of
me. Everything else that has happened only made
me more determined to overcome, but with this sad
stroke I feel crushed and void of strength. Only
three short months of her society after four years'
separation! I married her from love, and the longer I
lived with her I loved her the more. A good wife and
a good, brave, kind hearted mother was she, and deserved
all the praises you bestowed on. her at our parting
dinner for teaching her own and the native children too
at Kolobeng I try to bow to the blow as from our
Heavenly Father, who orders all things far us. Some
may afford to be stoic l, but I should not be natural if I
did not shed many tears over one who so deserved them.
I never contemplated exposing her in the lowlands. I
proposedAhat the Nyassa steamer should sail out, and
on reaching Kongone cut wood and steam up the river.
This involved but a few days in the lowlands; but
another plan was preferred. She (vie steamer) came in
pieces in a brig. Gladly accepting the kind offer of
Captain Wilson, of her Majesty's ship Gorgon, to
'aelp us up to the Murchison cataracts, we found
by a month's trial that the state in which the
engines were precluded ascending the Shire with the
pieces on board the Pioneer. We were forced to put her
together at Shupanga, and we have been three months
insteed of three or four days down here. Had my plan
been adhered to—but why express useless regrets? All
had been done with the best intentions. But you must
remember how I hastened the first p irty away from the
Delta and,though I saved them, got abused for breaking
the Delta,
Then I provoked Bishop Mackenzie's
party landing at all till these same unhealthy months
were past, and no one perished till the Bishop came down
to .the unhealthy lowlands and died. The Portuguese
have taken advantage of the sanitary knowledge we
have acquired, and send their troops up to Tette at owe.
They lost but two of a detachment, while formerly, by
keeping them at Quiliraane and Lonna, nearly all were
cutoff.

I shall do my duty still, hut it is with a darkene&
horizon I set about it. Mr. Rae put the hull of the new
steamer together in about a fortnight after we brought
up the keel. She-looks beautiful and strong, and I have
no doubt will answer all our expectations when we get
her on the lake.—Ever affectionately yours,
DAVLD LITLNOSTONE.

TEE HON. 1: CADOELY.

It will not surprise the public to hear that the Royal-
Commissioners are about issuing an official reply to the
extraordinary statements contained in the letter of the
Hon. F. Cadogan. When M.. Veillard failed, and his
affairs were examined by the creditors, it was seen at
once that he never had been in. a-position to undertake
a contract of such magnitude and the dissatisfaation
expressed at its being awarded to, him was .so deep and
general that the Commissioners felt compelled to issue
an official statement of their reasons in so doing. This
statement, however, as is not unusually the case with.
such post facto explanations, only made matters worse.
The discovery of the fact that the Hon. F. Cadogan had-
an arrangement by which he was to receive head-money
on M. Viellard's customers has since led to such state—
ments that that gentleman- felt compelled to make a
public- explanation of the nature of his connections with
M. Veillard. In this Mr. Cadogan states that the
existence of this agr, eement (by which he- was to receive--
the head-money) was well known to the-executive,' and
that it was in payment of manyservices.rendered, an 4
above all, in being the intermediary between the exe-
cutive of the Exhibition and M. Veillard in all the
-
endless questions of detail and management,' etc;.
When Mr. Cadogan wrote this- defence of himself he.
must have been aware that he was virtually bringing
very grave charge against the- Royal Commis,ioners..
It is now no longer a question of what was the connec—
tion between M. Veillard and Mr. Cadogan, but what
was the connection between. Mr. Cadogan and the-
Royal Commissioners? On this point we are inforrne
that the Commissioners are about to issue a full expla—
nation. No course is now left to all paaties concerned
but a complete and most explicit statement of all the -
details connected with this unfortunote contract.—
Times.

PROFESSOR SIMONDS ON THE OUTz-
BREAK OF SMALLPDX

On the 6th the introductory address to ~the forthcoming
session of the Royal Veterinary College,. Camden Town,
was delivered by Professor Simonds.
The Professor observed, that although smallpox in
sheep was a disease unknown during the present genera-
tion in this country previous to 1817, it was not un-
common in many of the great sheep . districts on. the
Continent. In the ' case of the human smallpox we
possessed a simple, efficacious, and an. almost altogether
harmless means of prevention in vaccination; but
vaccination afforded no protection to sheep. Where the
separation of the affected. animals from the healthy' ones.
proved insufficient to stay the disease, there reMained
only inoculation, which he recommended as the most
efficacious safeguard. The disease had been introduced
by foreign sheep sold in Smithfield Market;. it had
spread rapidly and committed frightful ravages in
several counties during the years 1847, '4B, and '5O.
Since 1850 the malady had not been heard of among our
flocks until July last,when it broke out in Allington, near
Devizes. Neither the shepherds nor the proprietors
were satisfied as to its real nature until his (the
Professor's) aid had been sought,, and at that time many
animals had been lost. How it was comeaunicated to
Mr. Parry's flock was still a mystery, but it quickly
spread to neighbouring flocks, and subsequently ex-,
tended to neighbouring counties. 'I here was good hope
—thanks to the preventive Pleasures adopted—that the,
malady had been stayed in the vicinity where it had
first showed itself; but as yet it would be premature to
express any decided opinion on the probable further
course of the outbreak. The nature of the disease and
the period of the year alike forbade a hasty conclusion.
He could not conceal from himself the probability—a
probability taught by bitter experience that the disease
might still spread more widely, and, that the visitation
might ultimately prove as calamitous as in 1847 to 1850.
The Profess'or then at some length. discussed the ozone- -
mical and social aspects of the question. Premising that
the value of the flocks of this country amounted to many
millions sterling, he said the loss by death ranged from
one fifth to one half, or even more, of. an infected flock.
This, however, was but part of the loss. The farmer
had to bear the effects of the disease on the breeding
and rearing of lambs, and the fattening of stock. Then
grave as was the sacrifice to. individuals, it was not the
less so to the -whole comninnity, who suffered from a
diminished supply of mutton and its consequent increase
in price. The rising of buteher's meat to the extent of
a penny or a half-penny in the pound would as surely
tell a fatal story in the Registrar-General's returns of
mortality. A large portion of our population at the best
lived but a shade or two above the point of starvation;
a still larger portion were insufficiently fed, and the
outbreak of a malady in sheep might often make the
differential element in the outbreak or not a epidemic
disease amen.- the people. It was from this point of
view that they could obtain the most just ideas of the
true dignity of veterinary science. It was from this
point of view, also, that they obtained tho most accurate
views of the veterinary practitioner's duties, for it was
upon the progress of veterinary science, and the skilful
exercise of she veterinary art, that a community had to
depend for its chief safety from the evils arising. -from
diseases like that which had appeared amongst the
flocks. of Wiltshire.

articles.title: AGRICULTURA hP.ROSPACTS.
articles.text:
AGRICULTURA hP.ROSPACTS.

During the first two days of the week mech rain fell,
with the wind mostly from the south-east. In the
West Riding of Yorkshire it was -stated on Tuesday
that a deal of grain was left in the, fields, which will
want either dry wind or more sun to prepare it for
being carried. From the East Riding on the same day
it was remarked: We have had some rain since last
Tuesday, which, however, though affecting the condi-
tion and further depressing the price of new wheat,
does not seem to have much increased the. demand for
old.' In Suffolk also it was said, The atmosphere has
changed to humid warmth, and, if continued, cannot
fail to injure the condition of all grain, although hither-
to the bula of our supply has been uniformly dry.'
This part of the country was favoured with fine
weather at harvest time, being tolerably forward: and,
being tbeas early, the white wheats had been much
blighted, and the Talaveras very defective and light.
The barleys were later, and a good deal of coarse quality
will be the result.
During the fore part of Tuesday the weather was
favourable, but became showery in the afternoon, with
some heavy rain, and the night dull and unpromising.
'W ednesday was a fine bracing day, the- wind going
from the south-west to the north west—barometer rising,
sunny, and cheerieg. In the late and north districts of
England a good deal is yet to be done before all corn has
been secured; and much has gone up in poor condition.
In Scotland the weather has favoured the progress of
ingathering; halt wheat will prove a poor crop both as
to quantity and quality. The new samples which have
appeared at Edinburgh have weighed from 60 lbs. do an-
wards to 56 lbs. per bushel, and the priaes of such are
proportionably low. There will, consequently, be no
fine Scotch wheat sent south for seed; and the
farmers north of the Tweed cannot be too choice
in selecting from the best English counties the
valuable sorts . now obtainable, whether red or
white. Of the former the run is decidedly on the
handsome samples of 'Nursery,' the sort that has
succeeded best of any this season • and it has
the advantage of being nine e approved of by the milers,
which is not the case with some descriptions of large
berry, though tf)e latter is a favourite with the farmers,
as yielding most per acre. There is now much activity
in procuring prime qualities. Friday proved &splendid
day for sowing, and wherever this could be begun, the
grain went in well. It is, however,, earl e, and there
will be more attention to work the ground well area to
Ow for the present. The fellows are tolerably forward
and are turning up satisfactorily. From Cornwall our
advices say, We have had a very protracted harvest;
it is two rionths since we commenced to reap wheat,
and now there are many acres of barley and oats in the
field in "arish mows." I suppose you .would like to
know whether we have good or bad crops. The whc at
in many places was thin in bulk, but the sample is good,
and saved in excellent condition. I should think in
'this neighbourhood it is very little below an average
crop % Barley about an-average crop, but I think rather
below ;. about one-third saved well, but I fear a great
deal- is in bad condition. Oats no much grown, but
they are heavy in bulk, and the samples fair.'
Saturday proved a thick threatening day, but no rain
fell; wind W. to N.N.W.- There have alaeady been a
good many winter tares planted, and more than usual
will be-sown this seasons .from the moderate price- and
fine sample. The later districts are turning out better
than expected as regards-the yield of wheat. The fens
of Lincolnshire are supposed to have a crop, and that
district is now making larger deliveries than any other.
Prices are very moderate; but the samplea- are not in a
keepable condition, and must go into consumption.
steadily as brought to market, old foreign, being used
for strengthening the manufactured article. Those'
farmers who can keep it. in the 'stack until cold frosts,.
and piercing winds have improved the condition, may
do better than by accepting the present low rates.
Barley has not yet taken favour, the wealherbeing too
warm for-the maltsters commencing work, and only the
choicest qualities can be disposed of at fair prices. We
hear of some people having taken the steam out of thiS
article by warming it on the kiln, and after that process
it germinates fairly.—Oct a 4.

articles.title: VTR DECREE OF AMNESTY.
articles.text:
VTR DECREE OF AMNESTY.

Tunric,Oct. 6,..Evening.•.—The 05eial Gazete, of 'this
evening publishes the Royal Decree of Amnesty, coun-
tersigned, by Signor Ratazzi. The decree is preceded
by a report of the Minister to the King. The-Minister,
in his report, says :
The motives which had compelled your Majesty to
-withstand the generous intentions of your heart no
longer exist. The rule of the law is again conso-
lidated. Confidence in your frank, but at the same
time prudent policy, has moderated the impatience
which had pushed Garibaldi on the path of rebel-
lion. By the catastrophe of Aspromonte we could
perceive that if, while fighting, in your name, he
would still achieve prodigious results, this could not
continue to be the case when, having forgottenlis duty,
he took up arms against your rights, whatever might
have been his ultimate intentions. At present Italy is
reassured, recalls the-services rendered by Garibaldi, and
wishes to forget his errors. This desire of the country
is eohoed by all the friends of liberty and unity of
Italy. When it was 'necessary to combat rebellion the-
Government proposed the most•energetic measures. But.,
all danger has now ceased. The Ministry, therefore..
becomes the interpreter of these generous-wishes, and,
asks clemency from your Majesty. We should have
wished to extend.this aranesty,to all who -have partici-
pated in the insurrection, but. the. necessity of upholding
the sentiment of military duty in the army prevents, us"
from including.soldiers who lave deserted amongst those
to whom pardon is granted. The honour of our flag
forbids our taking extenuating circumstances, into. con-
sideration in. their, favour.' •

FATAL FALL FROM A RAILWAY RILIDGE.—On the 4th
an inquest was held at Driffield upon the body-of Mr.
William Barff, of Beeforth Grange, a well-known agri-
culturist, who met his death in the following singular
manner:—Deceased had. a large number of sheep in a
special North-Eastern train, Which he, along with other
farmers similarly circumstanced, was desirous of. leaving
in the vicinity of Driffield during Tuesday right.
arriving there ie the darkildr. Barff ran along the 'line
towards a friend's house, and had to cross a bridge which
carries, the railway across a stream, and which has only
a .very low parapet. Two persons en previous occasions
have fallen over this bridge, and the deceased alsomissed
his way, and fell some 16 feet among the rough:stones at
the bottom, the,stream itself being intermittent and then
nearly dry.. He was soon discovered, and-was•foind to
have ribs and collarbone fractured, and had also received
some injury to the spinal cord, which resulted in death
on :Thursday night. . The sad affair was purely accidental,
and the place in question, though slightly protected, is
one where the pupil° have no. right to go. Mr. Barff
leaves a family of ten children, and the event has cast a
gloom over the agricultural world,•iu which the deceased
moved as a leading man. -
The tenants of the Castletown Estate, in the county
Limerick; have•sent an address to Colonel Hare, in
.which they. .indignantly deny that his late murdered
agent was harsh or. unfeeling. He was, on the contrary,
as kind and considerate as he could be consistently with
his duty. They have every reason. to deplore his loss,
and to feel most grateful to their landlord. The Cork
Reporter mentions a circumstance connected with this
ease which has not before been made public :—A son of
•Hayes had been tried for the murder of a tenant named
Quinlan, and was acquitted on account of some flaw in
the case,, though evidence left little room for doubt.
When he got out of gaol Mr. Braddell required the father,
Michael 'Hayes, to send him to ,Anierica, on pain, of
eviction, which he readily promised. Mr. Braddell
insisted that it should be done.' It..avas not done, and
proceedings were taken to eject the elder Hayes from his
holding, and were pending when the murder was com-
mitted.

STATE. ,OFT.RADE AND OF CRIME IN

WIGAN.

It is not possible for the cotton trade in this town to
be in a much worse state than it is at present, as out of
9,185 persons usually employed in the mills in Wigan
anctits immediate vicinity, no less than 8,885 are now
out of work. Of the remaining 300 not one is fully
employed, all being on short time, and none having
situations which can be considered permanent. Ru-
mours are afloat to the effect that some of the large
establishments are to be opened shortly in order that
the hands may have a few days' work, but the probabi-
lities are certainly not in favour of such a course being
taken. Of the hand loom weavers, who are abou,
400 in number, two thirds are entirely unemployed,
and of the remaining third only one-talf are on full
time. Fortunately the other trades in the tewn are
in a comparatively prosperous state, though, of cours€
with one-fourth of the population out of employ,
there must be more or less depression in all. The
publieans complain that there is nothing doing,
and many tradesmen say their sales are scarcely
sufficient to keep their ,shops open. The relief
fund is, however, distributed in a manner which
greatly assists this last-mentioned class, the bulk of
wh DI are provision dealers. • Nearly £5OO per week is
paid by the committee, and the whole of this is given ii
food-tickets, which the recipients present at the shops
where they have usually dealt. But for the adoption
of this plan we believe large numbers of small trades-
men would be compelled to close their doors. The
spinners, however, seem to expect the speedy revival of
trade, as soveeal new mills are in course of erection, and
additions are being made to old ones. It is feared the
great difficulty will be to obtain hands for the latter when
they are re=opened, leaving the new buildings out of the
question, as so many of the operatives may be expected
to leave the district,or to apply themselves to other trades
before a plentiful supply of cotton is received. With
the population of the town in the-state above recorded,
it is not surprising that the number of cases of felony
and petty' larceny is largely on the increase. Formerly
one a week was the average number of cases of this
character, but lately, the list, has grown much larger,
and last week the charges were more numerous- than
they have ever been before,. no less than thirteen cases
of felony against sixteen prisoners being determined by
the borough magiArates. The great majority of these
charges are certainly not ag iinst factory operatives, but
occasionally one or two prisoners of this class swell the.
charge sheet. Two et. .he sixteen mentioned above were'
girls, who were proved to have robbed a farmer of
£2 13se immediately after leaving- one of the sewing
schools., There are, we may state, 1,200 girls at these,
and as this is the first charge of serious misconduct
which has been brought against any one of them, it is to
be hoped it will prove the sole exception. In the minor
cases heard by the magistrates, there is a gratifying
decrease, which is to be accounted for by the fact that
these offences are generally committed whilst the
offenders are nieder the influence of drink, and when the
receipts of a family are reduced to the lowest possible
point. Money with which-to get drunk can •rarely be
foaled,

HIGH WAGES 127 THE FREE
STATES.

(From the New Irani: Times.)
• A partilar impression abroad among the ignorant would
be that fire and sword and civil wrath weredesolating
all those rich broad lands of the West whieli once so
attracted the foreigner ;. that neighbour was waylaying
neighbour, burning his crops and carrying off his cattle;
that there was no sure payment of labour, and no safety
for property;. that even in safe districts the poor immi-
grant was still' liable to conscription,and was exposed- to
the heavy taxation of war..
If our words should reach any of those who- control
opinion in foreign countries, we call upon them, as honest
journalists„to correct these popular errors. Let the
, peasants of Germany, and Belgium, end Norway under-
stand that theusual and-the richest agricultural districts
of the west are as undisturbed by.this war as are the
vineyards of the Rhine or the farms of •Holland. Every
man sows and reaps, buys and sells. as he always has
done. Fire and sword, bayonet and shell come not
near his dwelling. Except for the, absence of his
neighbours in. the great struggle he would hardly. know
it was war time. Taxes fall comparatively lightly on
him, being contrived to weigh most on,the manufactur-
ing and commercial community. If a fareign-born citi-
zen—even though he has. declared his intention to be
an American citizen—he cannot be subject to drafting.
His produce is securing high prices, and if a labouring
man, he obtains the highest wages.
There never -was a time,. probably, in the history of
the country when an immigrant had aofair an, opportu-
nity of laying the foundations of his.fortune as now.
The wages paid to agricultural labour in some_ places
have been. incredibly high. We—have hear.l this
summer of- even 2.50 dols, per clay being given a
common farm hand. Probably on many a fine farm in
Illinois a labourer could. earn his own. little freehold, all
broken and cultivated,., by one season's hard work,
which of course is far better than doing a pioneer's work
in the frontier, States. With one million of our most
muscular young men absent in the .war, called, from all
departments of life, there must of necessity be a great
demand everywhere in, all branches-for labour.

This demand will draw after it,. in all branches, high
wages. Now is the time for for.eign labourers to take
advantage of this state of things,. especially before neiv-
machinery has become a substitute for labour. Probably.-
the masses of Europe, who have been labouring and.'
delving so long, with so little fruit, could never find an.
opportunity in which they could so readily and profit.,
ably change their position. Why should. those $O,OOO
industrious and able-bodied people in a single manufac-
turing . town in' England (Rlackburn) be supported by
public charity, vi,hen there is room and. work without
limit for them in. America ? Why should not English.
charity run in the chAnnel of permanent benefit,..and
transport the wen who aro, willing to work to places
which always need works. It is true that many of,
these niannfacturing.labourers are not, fit for field work,,
yet there will be an increasing demand here for
manufacturing hands, as. necessity drives us more and
more to produo within ourselves, and many of our own
industrial workers will turn their attention to agri-
culture.

We believe, as we, said befare, that• Amezioa never
offered eonore profitade field for the poor forigner.

the coroner remarked, that there ,were five men killed,.
but up to this time only one body had been found., He
had no doubt it would, be shown. that, all the men had
• been: killed, by the same cause, and .therefore one inquiry.
would answer for all. After the jury had viewed, the
body, they proceeded
,to the yard below the inn, to view
the iron chains by which the cradle was hku:ig. It will
be remembered that the -cause of the accident was the
breaking of the chain to which the cradle for conveying
the men up and down the pitwas attached.and the con-
sequent precipitation of the cradle and all in it down
the shaft. One .chain was
,pointed out which, it was
said, had stretched 14 inches. A juror remarked that
the chain might be good- in quality
.and workmanship,
but it seemed too small. The master-smith remarked
that it had been made smaller by being stretched out,
and said it •would not have 'stretched that way•if the
quality or • workmanship had been Inferior. After a
lengthened inquiry the jury returned a verdict of Ac,
cidental death.

TEDRIFIC GAS EXPLOSION IN A FACTORY.—On the
6th inst. a violent explosion of gas occurred at the fee.
tory of Messrs. Harris and Sons, Braunston-gate,
Leicester. It appears that on. ,the above evening the
front part of the building was about to be lighted with
gas for the first time this season, and the meter was
turned on about five o'clock by Mr. Broughton, the
timekeeper, who shortly_ after wards discovered a strong
smell of as in his office; he immediately communicated
the fact to a mechanic connected with the establishment
and the meter was immediately turned off. A. person
named E. Shuttlewood then applied, a light towards the
ceiling, when a terrific explosion took place. The
report was heard at a considerable distance, and the
houses on the opposite .side of the street were much
shaken. Mr. D. Shuttlewood, overlooker of the me-
chanics' department, was seriously injured, one side of
his face being ;much burnt and completely disfigured.
Messrs. Broughton,- E. Shuttlewood, and J. English
were also badly shaken, and the latter was burnt
seriously about the neck and hand. In the room where
the explosion occurred the 'plaster was stripped from
the ceiling and a wrapper set on fire, a portion of the
floor above was also _sprung. Had not the precaution
been taken to shut off the gas previous to testing the
pipe' the consequences must have been most disastrous
both to life and property. lathe bar of the Earlflowe's
Arms, about 30 yards from the scene of the explosion,
the reflection of the light resembled a strong flash of
lightning, and many were impressed with that idea until
the facts became known.

Tut TALLOW-TlMM—Among the trees which have
of late been extensively distributed in the North-
Western Provinces of India and Punjab is the tallow-
tree of China—stillinqia sebifera. In China it is largely
cultivated, and it is said that by its proluce alone the
taxes are paid in the district of liongkeng. It grows
equally well on low alluvial plains, on the rich mould
of canal, in sandy soils, and on tile acclivities of mom-
talus. From its seeds tallow and oil are procured,
which are extensively- used in China. Its wood hard
and durable, and its leaves yield a black dye,

There are +tens that light is dawnirrg is' America on
the question ot how to dispose of four millions and-a-
half, not of horses ploughed by the tail, but of human
agricultural labourers, employed by an eqaally losing
process. Fancy that in Ireland, where the difficulty
was first exemplified, the cry had been raised of
Where will you colonise these horses, and what do
you propose to do with them?' What sage or con-
juror will tell us what is to be done with four millions
and-a half of horses that may not be ploughed by the
tail? Ploughing by the tail is an institution, and if you
take it away what will you put into its place? You
want to let the horses loose to eat their masters.
Horses that do not plough by .the tail always eat their
masters. And dream that a Lord-Lieutenant had
been found to hold a meeting with a deputation of the
horses or their representatives, and then and there lay
before them his desire to Make a beginning of horse
expatriation, and the delight with which he would see
the four millions and-a-half of working horses located
in some distant land. Who should have ret•trained the
mirth which would have broken forth? The fraternity
who have since expanded into drivers of hackney
cabriolets, the genuine successors of the shepherds in
Virgil, would have asked with such concentrations of
phrase as they only can accomplish, 0, most fit to be
fed with a spoon!. Unfortunate youth, of whom it may
justly be inquired whether your maternal parent was
aware of your intention to walk abroad! Satisfy our
desire to know whether it never occurred to your lord-
ship that the way to deal vith the horses was to work
them where they were,. only not by the tail. Was the
Lord-Lieutenant ever of woman born that dared stand
the shock? Imagine too that grave commercial men,
respectable householders who might present themselves
for bail at the doors of any bankruptcy court in Lon-
don, had taken up the cry and said they should be
ruined unless the horses were returned to working by
the tail. All they had depended upon working by the
tail. They were certain, they must be starved if any
stop was put to working by the tail.- Surely that ship,
which our ancestoos loaded with the unwise, must
have gone to the bottom with such a freight. No
parallel fcilly has been seen walking in its doublet and
hose; it was reserved for the present age to make this
railroad improvement in the way to Bedlam. If it is
possible to heighten the picture, imagine that a rebel--
lion had broken out on this question of the tails. The'
masters call on God and man to witness that they will
die in defence of their right of tail. And itshall not be
a passive rebellion but an active; they shall land in
Ayrshire and move upon Glasgow. Whereupon our
Lord-Lieutenant is counselled- to mount his cavalry
with the rebels' horses, and ride down the rebellion.
But 'No,' says he, 'I was sent here to preserve the
etatto. quo ante the rebellion. Far be it from me to
ride them down with their own horses till I have killed
a hundred thousand citizens in trying to do without.'
There have been men and actions promoted to a pro-
verb, but this ought to bear away the bell. Ono ques-
tion more. Why is Congress not called together?
The executive is manifestlyplaying fast and loose with
its power from Congress. The combatant in Homer
says, 'Kill us in the light.' If you are to die, die
under the daylight of Congress, and not the hugger-
mugger of a president.
