It were well, in dealing with very ancient floras, in
which equivocal forms occur that might have belonged
to either the land or the sea, tokeep in view those various
plants of the present time the habits- of which are
decidedly marine, but which- are marked by many of
the peculiarities of the seed-bearing plants of the.
land. The superiority, of zostera to the common sea-
weeds of our coasts appears to have struck in the
north of Scotland eyes very little practised in such
matters, and seems to have given rise, in consequence,
to a popular myth. Zostera marina abounds on a
series 01 sand banks, partially uncovered by the larger i
stream tides, which lie directly opposite the 'town of
Cromarty, near the spot pcinted out by tradition as
the site of an earlier town, which was swept away two
or three hundred years ago by the encroachments of
the sea. And these banks, with their thick covering
of green zostera, used to be !pointed out by the fisher-
men. of the place, in my younger days, as the mea-
dows of the old town, still bearing their original
coverings of vegetation, a vegetation altered no aubt
by.the sea change' that had come over it, but still
essentially the- same, it was said, as that which had
sailed around the old burgh, and not at all akin to
the brown kelp or tangle that every storna from the
boisterous north-east heaps along the shore.
It was virtually affirmed that the luxuriant terri-
torial grasses of ancient Cromarty had made a virtue
of necreaity itheir ltorod eiieumetancea-3-na that
settling down into grasses of the sea, they remained
to testify that an ancient Cremarty there had once
been.

Zostera marina,, like most plants of the -land, ripens
its seeds tows.ras,the close of autumn, and .I have seen
a smart niglaVs frost at this season, when coincident
with a stream-tide that laid bare the beds, nip its
seed-bearing sterns by thousands; and have found
them strewed,along the beach, a few days after, with
all their grass-like spikes fully developed, and their,
grain-like seeda charged with a farinaceous substance,
which one would scarce expect to find, developed in
the sea.

In the higher reaches of the Crornarty Frith, the
zostera beds, which are of great extent, are much fre-
quented during the more protracted frosts of a severe
winter, by. wild geese and swans, that dig up and feee
upon the saccharine roots of the plant.
The zostera of the warmer latitudes attain to a
larger size than those of our Scottish seas. A
southern species,' says Loudon, ‘zostera oceanica- has
leaves afoot long and an inch broad. It is used as a
thatch, which is said to last a century ; bleaches.white
with exposure, and furnishes the snow-like material
from. which the envelops of Italian liquor-flasks are
prepared.'--r-From the Testimony, of -the Rocks.

THE METROEOI,ITAN RAILWAY.—The arrangements
for the working of the signals, and, which in a work of
this kind, where so large a portion of the business will be
transacted under ground, requires -very careful conside-
ration, are now nearly completed, and will be thoroughly
tested in the course of a few days by Colonel Yolland,
one of the Government inspectors. In working the
lino the electric telegraph will be extremely useful, and
no train will be allowed to pass a station until the por-
tion of the line between it and the next station is
signalled as clear. The whole of the line is now
ballasted, and the steel rails are fixed. Until the
certificate has been received from the Government in-
spector, no announcement can of course be made as to
the precise day on which the line will be opened to the
public.

THE CAsE or TEE REPORTER GRAY.—We have re-
ceived a sovereign from Father Drowsey towards a
fund to be raised for payment of the fine of £5O which
Gray has been senteneed to fay. A correspondent
writes to us as follows :—€ Mr. Gray's position is now a
very serious one—a wife and nine children 'to support,
and he in durance, under the impression of the judges,
I sincerely believe, that the fine would be a trifling in-
convenience administered as a caution to him and others.
Every reporter will hold his own opinion as to the policy
of the proceedings throughout; but I hope the judges,'
on reconsideration, will reflect that this trifling fine

camel's back."—Advertiser.

BURNING OF A STEAMER IN THE BAY OF BISCAY.—
By the arrival in the London Dock of the Citizen
steamer, Captain Pascoe, from Bordeaux, intelligence
has been received of the total loss by fire •of the Lord
Royston, iron screw steamship, in the Bay of Biscay.
The Lord Royston, which was quite a new vessel, has
only recently been put on the station between Bordeaux
and London. She left Bordeaux on Monday with a full
cargo of merchandise, and, it is reported, some passen-
gers, and was consigned to Messrs. W. S. Lindsay and
Co. The Citizen left Bordeaux on the same day, and
about 4 o'clock in the afternoon, when some 20 miles
out in the Bay of Biscay, she came up with the Lord
Royston, which was on fire from stem to stern, and
burning furiously. The davits were seen to be hanging
over the quarters, as if the boats had bben lowered and
the crew had got away. A huge mass of fire was rising
from the hull, and as it was quite impossible for the
Citizen to render any aid she continued on her course.
A telegram - since received by the agents announces
that the whole of the crew and passengers succeeded ir
escaping, and landed in the vicinity of La Tremblade
It is stated that amongst her cargo were several hun,
dred barrels of the spirit of turpentine, pitch, and resin,
which would readily account for the ' destruction of the
ship. She had also on board a very large quantity 6;
brandies and other goods. The ship and cargo a.rt
insured, but whether to the f:411 extent has not been
•ascertained.

he had heard that I was in want of all the requisites for

—` You have spirits here; I have not tasted any for

of female ascendancy, and making a man feel particularly'
small?' If ever a man thoroughly appreciates the'
personal application of Hamlet's- remark, I could be

ANCIENT SITE OF THE MAMION HOUSE. Stocks•
market, which derived its name from a pair of stocks
anciently set upon the spot - for the punishment of
offenders, was one of the oldest markets in the city of
London, having been established in 128 L,, by Henry de
Waffles, then mayor. Few would imagine that on the
place where the ponderous Mansion-house now stands,
where thousands upon thousands pass and repass, where
the pavement is always inconveniently crowded, and the
street constantly stopped by carriages and public con-
veyances, little more than a century ago there was a
pretty fruit market, planted on the east side with rows of
trees, having an antique conduit at the north end and
surmounted by an equestrian statue, and stalls where
fruit and vegetables of the choicest kind were vended.
An odd story is told about the equestrian statue. It was
designed for John Sobieski, King of Poland, but was left
on the maker's hands, mad the statue of Charles 11.
being wanted by Sir Robert Viner after the restoration,
he availed himself of the image with commendable
thrift, converting the warlike Pole into the Merry
Monarch, and the turbaned Turk, whom his horse was
trampling beneath its feet, into Oliver Cromwell.
Trees, stalls, conduits, and statue were removed in
17'39. On digging the foundation of the proposed
building., the ground proved to be so full of springs that
strong piles were needed for the support of the erection.
Nearly fourteen years were occupied in. the work—the
first Lord Mayor who tenanted the Mansion-house being
Sir Crisp Gasgoigne in 1753,—Ainstoort1ils Lord Mayor
s/ London.

melancholy. I often had to wait a long time with the
old clerk before enough people assembled for a service to
be held. When there was early service no women or
girls came, although, the village was very large. The
school was badly attended, the schoolmaster quite. un-,

honourable .and right-minded man. It was remarked

usually seen in church came regularly, but he sat down
quite carelessly, and as soon as he was on the bench
composed him,self to sleep, and snored so loud th...t he
could even be heard during the singing. A boy to v. hom
and who had a cheerful, open I had sometimes spoken,
countenance, used generally to sit near this man. I
spoke to him, and asked him to sit close behind the
snorer, and to give himn touch sometimes. At first the
boy would not consent, but when I •proraised him a,
groschen he did as I told him. During the whole ser-
vice I saw the contest between the boy and the in .n,

when I offered him again a groschen, told me confiden-
tially that that the peasant had given him two groschen
on condition he would not disturb
man
service was ended, during he
un-

ished at this answer that I did not know what to say;
the hope of influencing the people was quite gone.—. Re.

articles.text:
LATER FROM AMERICA,

NEW YORK, Sept. 26 (Evening.)—No Peden%ls have
yet crossed into Virginia. The • Confederates remain
along the upper line of the Potomac. It is rumoured
that another draught will be proclaimed to increase the
Federal army to 1,000,000 men. The Governors of
sixteen llnion States assembled on the 24th instant at
Altoona (Pennsylvania), and adjourned on the 25th to
waamagton, where they presented an address to Presi-
dent-Lincoln, expressing: their determination to support
his constitutional authority, approving the emancipation
proclamation, and suggesting the expediency of raising a
reserve force of 100,000 men. The Governor of Maryland
objected to sign the address approving the emancipation
proclamation. The New York Republican State Conven-
tion express profound satisfaction at the President's pro-
elamation. The President has been serenaded at Wash-
ingfon, on which occasion he made a speech, saying that
he issued the proclamation after full deliberation, and
under a heavy sense of responsibility. He trusted in
God that he had made no Mistake. It was now for
America and the world, he said, to judge the proclama-
tion, and, it may be, to take action upon it. The
Chicago, Emancipation Committee have published Pre-
sident Lincoln's reply to them, delivered on the
13th of this month. The President therein states
that he did not favour an-emancipation proclamation as
it would be inoperative if issued, and if the slaves
-
were armed 'their arms would fall into the -hands of the
rebels. A-portion of the emancipation proclamation was
•erroneously printed. The proclamation declares that
the presence in Congress on January 14t of the members
from the rebellious States shall be evidence that such
Statesare not then in rebellion, instead of the presence
of such members being evidence that-they have not been
in rebellion. The 'Southern journals sclaim. victory for
'the-Confederates in the battl% Of Antietam -Creek.
The Confederate *Generals, Startel and Branch were
:killed. The Confederate force nunibered 60,000, under
General Lee. To avoid a flank movement by General
McClellan, Lee vithdrew his army across the Potomac.
The Governor of Pennsylvania has discharged the Tani-
'tia lately called out At NeVOrleans General Butler
has ordered all foreigners to present themselves with the
'evidence of their nationality to the nearest provost mar-
shal to be registered, as in the' course of' ten days it may
be necessarrto distinguish disloyal from loyal citizens
and honest 'neutral foreigners. .Islaval expeditions are
fitting out at Port Royal and Pensacola. Correspond-
ents report that the Federal General Ros,,ncrans captured
36 cannon and 500 prisoners in the late battle at Juka,
NEW YORY, Sept. 27, Evening.—General McClellan
has constructed a pontoon bridge, upon which to cross
the Potomac at Harper's Ferry. The .I;ouisville Journal
declares that Kentucky -will never acquiesce in Presi-
dent Lincoln's proclamation.
New 'YORK, Sept. 29, Evening.—The Confederates
have made Winchester, Virginia, the basis of their
operations, but keep a force on the bank of the Potomac
to prevent the Federals from crossing. It is rumoured
that the Federal army is going into winter quarters.
The Northern press strongly condemns this pilcy.
General Daivis shot General Nelson, commanding at
Louisville, this morning, killing him instantly. The
affair occurred through a personal dispute at Galthouse.

One of the most daring and well-planned robberies
that have recently occurred wasecommitted in Sheffield
on the 4th, and was followed by a mostfortunate and

And Taylor' watchful for the opportunity, bolted from

A letter says that Garibaldi was told of the amnesty
on the Ist:
On receiving the intelligence he looked with a smile 1
at his leg, wrapped up in bandages, and said to his
friends, It appears that we are pardoned.' Garibaldi
wishes to return to Caprera, but prudence dictates that 1
he should not be exposed at present to a fatiguing voyage.
He will, I am assured, proceed to Quarto, near Genoa, to
the house of his friend De Vecchi. The villa is situ-
ated on the sea coast, at the very spot where Garibaldi I
embarked for Marsala.
The following is an extract fro= a private letter, dated
Varigrumo, October Ist :
The General improves. ff on.e did not know that a
rascally ball had broken the malleolus ; if the foot could ;
turn on its own pivot; if-the frame were not emaciated
by the fever of the body, which is lessened, and by the 1
fever of the mind, which still burns, the colour of his I
face, his serene eye, and sometimes the hilarity of his i
lip, would tempt one into believing the attempted heroi-
cide of Aspromonte a total failure. But last night he
never slept ; nothing could make him sleep. Ile felt
and feels in his heel the strangest sensation, as though,
with all his might, he was striking it against an anvil.
These are his words.
Several times the ligatures andplasters were unloosed,
and a larger space left between the machine and the heel,
and this was anointed with cold pomade. Still this sen-
sation increases, lasts, goes away, and returns to torment
him. The machine of which I speak was put into opera-.
don. three days ago. It is a'sort of iron cage, ia which'
is suspended- a cradle of ewathes—a sort 'cf hanging
cradle—into which the legis slowly let down on its soft
pillow. Here the leg isextended and the foot of the-
patient supported. This useful piece of mechanism was
brought from London by Dr. Partridge, who ordered it
of the maker, Mr. Matthews, of Lincoln's-inn. I thank
them both. With the •leg suspended in this manner we
easily-dress his wounds, from a bed on the other side, and
we lower him horizontally when he wishes to sleep, and
raise him when he wishes to read or write. In -these
operations he gives his orders in his metallic and sympa-
thetic tones as if hewere giving the word of command on
beard ship. Orders short and precise, a sharp look if the
move gives himpiil, a sweet expression if effected ably
and easily. The-lion now sleeps, and I write, and he
thanks you for the interest youtake. We don't want
nurses or any other women here. They would only make
,a confusion.

A Paris correspondent forwards to a contemporary the
following document, said to bean address from Gari-
baldi to the people of Stockholm:-
4 Varignano, Oct 2.

To the People at .:Stockholm:
When you issue from the manufactories where
manual labour renders still ;more vigorous the temper
of your soul, or when you leave your domestic hearth,
where the, holiest of affections raises your soul to
sublimity, and strong in your numbers, you assemble on
your public places to manifest your feelings, you
never think of stifling your thoughts--your words,
your cheers, are the reward of the kindness shown
to those who suffer from temporary misfortunes, or
those who lie prostrate •by slavery. You also fair-
haired -Scandinavian people, sent me an affectionate
greeting when God gave me strength to wrench the
crown a thorns from the brow of our southern brethren.
Now you assemble once more to offer to a good,
cause the moral support of your good wishes—the real'
unity of the Italian nation; Italy mistressat home. In
the name of my countrymen I thank y0u,,0 noble race,
one of the finest in Eurepe ! Let us all unite to raise
and enforce the great voice of affection and concord-I
The sword is a crime, -as the punishmentof death is an
abuse and conquest an insult. Let us make war an
anachronism, and labour a hymn to the Most
When balls and cannons shall have been turned into
productive instruments, force, disarmed, will return to
the darkness from whence it has escaped for the misfor-
tune of mankind, and the dawn of felicity will whiten
the- horizon, to flood the whole world with. its rays. :From
the-depths of my soul,,zreeting and gratitude, peopls!of
Stockholm. C-AUL6.IILI)I.I

Tikes ZOSTEEA. the Western Annexe of:
the Exhibition during the past ,few days Mr. •llarben has
been exhibiting specimens of ,the fibre extracted from
the Zoatera Marina. The; seaweed from which this
fibre is obtained is found commonly enough on all
the shores of England and Ireltuid, though nowhere
in any very great abundance, It is the common
slimy Sea grass, which, when broken, shows a
few minute shreds of fibre, so thin as to be more
like mucilage. Under no other cireunastances short .01
the total disappearance of the cotton ylant from the flice
of the earth can we imagine v this being resorted to as a
substitute. We believe silk itself would not only be
cheaper but much more easily and abundantly obtained.
The difficulties in first produring the plant and then ex-
tracting the small amount of fibre from it are SO many
and so great that it is needless to enumerate its demerits
further than to say that as a substitute for cotton it
appears to be almost worthless.—Times
BALLINASLOE Fain.—The great annual fair at )3allin-
asloe commenced on Shturday, which was devoted to the
sale of sheep, as the first day of the fair always is.
There was a considerable falling off in the number of
sheep, a fact which tends to p-rove the accuracy of the
agricultural statistics published annually by- Mr.
Donnelly, the Registrar-General, The total number of
sheep in Ireland last year was 3,556,060 ; this year the
total number is 3,455,857; which shows a falling off to
the extent of about 100,000. The number of sheep sold
at Ballinasloo on Saturday was 42,620. The number
sold on the corresponding day last year was. 54,782—a
difference of 12,162. The diminution may not be found
so great after the sales, which are proceeding, to day;
but, as the heaviest part of the business is done on the
erst day, we may conclude that there is a considerable
falling off in the number of sheep at the' fair—amount-
ing to about 10 per cent. This, however, is partly
owing to the foot disease among sheep, and to the suc-
cessful precautions taken to prevent diseased animals
being brought to the fair. Among the thousands that
covered the extensive lawn of Lord Clancarty, it is said
there was not a single tainted sheep from England. The
average prices were from 38s. to 465. for ewes, and 40s.
to 48s. for wethers, while some few first-rate lots brought
60s to 645. Lord Clancarty is building a large hotel
for the accommodation of visitors. It is expected to be
ready next year. The horse fair takes place to-morrow.
It is stated that the Liverpool and Birkenhead Dock
Commissioners have sanctioned an expenditure of £6,000.
on works for the storage of petroleum, and that in case
of necessity they will be extended so as to cost £10,00.0.

articles.text:
A HORRIBLE INSINUATIO7.

Ifany one man were to call any other man what Professor
Huxley calls the whole human race, it would probably
lead to an interchange of co mpliments by which the dignity
of the species would notbe much advanetd. We mustnot
be surprised, therefore, at the indignation which the
Darwinian theory,' represented by the Professor, never
fails to provoke. If the most delicate hint tnat one
resembles some member of the brute creation is resented
as the grossest of insults, how unspeakably offensive
must be the suegeeion that we are lineally descended
from the most hideous animal that can be found in our
menageries or museums. It would not be half so in-
tolerable to most minds to be told that the stock of man-
kind was degenerating, and that the lords of creation,
some thous mds or myriads of years hence, would assume
the form and habits of gorillas.- A civilised man is by no
means so sensitive about the destiny of his posterity as
about the social condition of his progenitors, and the
wonder is that the Chinese system of ennobling the an-
testors of public benefactors has never been adopted by
Europe. Hoot great a value would be set on such a re-
ward is-evident from the horror inspired by the converse
process as applied by certain physivfogis-ts. The --ques=
tion is argued in many a company; both learned and
unlearned, as if it really affected our status in the great
society ot sentient beings,- or as if Professor Owen de-
served the thanks of humanity for giving the alarm and
manfully withstanding the misanthropes who would
sacrifice the aspirations of their kind to th Ar own-vanity.
It is not that any one would suspect Professor Huxley
of a malignant satisfaction in the degradation of his
fellow-creatures such as sullies the pages of Swift. He
has probably no more personal sympathy with his clients
than A Northern nigger- worshipper with a black, and
would altogether decline to ocupy the benches of the
British Association in company with them. Still, he
hasiared to maintain their relationship with us, and no
remoteness of the point of transition or divergence can
reconcile flesh and blood to this. The indefinite exten-
ion of our genealogy cannot be accepted as a set-off
-against the consequences of so ignoble an inception. A.
pedigree with- an ape at the top of it is equally revolting
to faiily prid-k, though it may be measured by geological
epochs instead of generations. So this invasion of our
rights by brutes must bo resisted at -any cost. There
must surely be scientific weapons powerful enough to
repel it, or, if none .such already exist, new ones must be
invented. To give way on this point would be to -sur-
render our prescriptive supremaey, and to confess
ourselves parvenu monarchs of the world.—The

GENETILL M'CLELLAN'S 4Popinaurrr.—.Nevertheless,
too much praise cannot be given to General M'Clellan
and to the generals under him, and specially General
Hooker, for the manner in which they handled as
unpromising.= army as ever took the field. It is idle
to .atterept_to analyse the grounds and arguments which
account for ,General M'Clellant.s popularity. He- is az
much-belovedand trusted by his men as 'the little cor-
poral' himself. Nor can it be denied that, valuable as
is his army's enthusiasm on his behalf, the danger which
would _axis° if anythinghefell him would be proportion-
ably great. If li`Clellan fell either in action, ca- by
disease, his army would become a xope of sand. But if
ever agein there is an attempt to depose him, and he

the 6th an accident occurred in Edmond's (Wombwell's)
Menagerie, now exhibiting In Nottingham, which at
one time wore a most serious aspect. The Royal Lion
Hunter a native African, entered- the performing-pan-
ther's den. He commenced to put one of these animals

in making it leap from one platform to another, the two
elevations being erected at either end of the den. The
instead of taking the proper course, leaped upon

ously from the wound. The keeper, no ways daunted,
notwithstanding a cry of terror from the spectators,

notwithstanding a terrible thrashing which it had re
-

to the programme before the keeper quitted" the den,
though-all this time he himself was bleeding from the
wound inflieted by-the animal on his face The self-
possession of the keeper washighly extolled. The fight
between the panther and his keeper lasted 20 minutes.
The same evening a keeper went into the zebra's den,

articles.text:
SIB JOHN .R,431-ssimilr. SUING A

uRiCKET CLUB.

At the Huddersfield County Court- on- Friday; before
James Staneteld, Esq., judge, Sir J. W. Ramsden, Bart.,
brought an action against Messrs. F. W. J acomn and
J. D. Hardy, to recover-the sum of £5O in respect of
rent due to him by-the Huddersfield Club, for the occu-
pation of a field adjoining Greenhead Park, and now
occupied as the- parade-ground of the Huddersfield
Volunteers.
The facts ef the case are these the year 1352,
on the occasion of Sir John Ramsden airiving at his
majority, the Huddersfield Cricket Club, after having-
played for seven- years on ground that was not
altogether suitable,- made application to Sir John by
letter; requesting at his' hands a suitable plot of
ground, and that he would give such- directions to his
agent, Mr. Alexander Hathorn, as would secure- them
one adapted to their necessities, so that they might 'rank
with neighbouring .towns in the possession of grounds.'
The same letter also requested permission to en-o 1 the name
of Sir John Ramsden as honorary president of the club.
.Sir John replied to this 'application that he eheuld be
glad for the :dal) to have the use of a piece of his
ground for their sports,. and felt gratified at the honour
of being made .the honorary president -of the club.'
This letter was considered by the club as a promise of a
piece of laud free from rent; and they made- application
to the agent for 'the use of the field now occupied by,
the volunteers. The agent, however, informed them
that their impression was .a -wrong one, and that
Sir John would expect them to pay a yearly rental
of from £lO to £l2 for the field, which is four acres
in extent. Disregarding this information, they drew
up a memorial to Sir John Ramsden, and for-
warded it to the residence of the agent for presen-
tation, and meanwhile 'entered into possession of the
--,ground on the understanding that the question of •
'rent was reserved for appeal to Sir John' himself. The
agent, in his discretion, did not forward the memorial to
Sir John, who happened to be abroad. On this becoming
known to the club some time after, they wrote to Sir
John requesting a personal interview. This was de-
clined by Sir -John, on the ground that business ought
to be transacted in writing. The club then forwarded
a full statement of their case, and received in due time
a reply to the effect that he should abide by the letter
of his agent, correcting the' misapprehension- which had
existed in the minds -of the club regarding the tenure of
the cricket field. The club them instructed the 'secre-
tary te 'write to Sir John (at the close-of 1858), pointing
out that the • enforcement of retrospective rent would
lead to a 'dismemberment' -of the club, which they
could not conceive their honorary president' would
permit, and asking Sir -John:, to remit the
rent of the present year; and promising to
pay in future. To this request -Sir John
refused to accede, informing the club that Mr. Hathorn't
-application for rent was duly made according to 'instruc-
tions from himself: The club thereupon refused to pay
any rent, and received notice to quit in February, 1859.
They quitted the ground-in February, 1.860,-their tents,
grass-roller, and other property being retained by the
parties-taking possession in the name of Sir-J. W. Rams-
. den. The matter was allowed to lie over in the hope of
an amicable settlement, but -the club refused to ecome to
terms; .and the case was entered in -the county .court.
After aprolonged hearing the jury -returned a verdict
in favour of the plaintiff of .X 8 .17s. 11d. Mr. Clough,
on behalf of Sir-John, refused this verdict, ,preferringa
nonsuit. A nonsuit avas therefore entered against the
plaintiff, with eosts.

articles.text:
POLAND..
THE GRAND DUKE ,CONSTANTINrS

ADDRESS

The following speech was made by the Grand -Duke I
•Constantineat the opening of the session of the general
assembly of the 'Council of State on October 1. The
speech was delivered inthe Polish language :
Gentlemen,—ln.addressing you for the first time in
this assembly, .1 'wish above all things to assure you that
.the painful circumstances which prevented me from
taking part in the proceedings of your last.session have
not chilled My „good intentions towards the country. •
-Full of faith in the protection of Providence, I reckon
• on the loyal sentiments and attachment of good citizens,
of which the _Council of State has already given proof,
In fulfilling the .duties .which the will of my august
trether, our gracious sovereign, has devolved upon me,
I shall never cease to look forward to the welfare- of the
kingdom of. Poland. The governmentof which I am
the head will.never deviate from the-legal path and will
never permit any departure from it with impunity. I
shall consider myself happy ,in being able to exercise
liberally the noblest •of the prerogatives with which
I am invested—the prerogative of .mercy.; but in its
cmercieo I cannot allow myself to lose sight of .public
justice, the intereal-,5,, and the security of the community.
Out of 499 persons who have been condemned since the
state of siege, 131 have undergone their „punishment,'
289 have been pardoned, 7 have fled,- and 69 are still
undergoing their sentence. The institutions which
were granted last . year are everywhere about to come
into operation. The district councils .in the greater
part of the country have concluded their first ses-
sion. The delegations which h tve issued .from them
will commence their important Itbours regarding the
taxation, and will, no doubt, justify the confidence
twhich the Legislature has reposed in them. The
:municipal- councils are performing their duties with
advantage. The petitions of seventeen towns, re-
cently presented, for the establishment .of similar
councils in them, are .a -new proof that the utility
.of this institution is fully appreciated by the country.
:Simultaneously with your deliberations the opening of a
. superior school and of a polytechnic school has taken
.place, as well as those other educational establishments,
which-you considered to be required by the wants ,of the
country, when you last year voted the law on public
.educatien, the elaboration of which forms one of the great
.merits of my colleague, the chief of thern civil power.
.Since
.your last deliberations, his Majesty, in his paternal
solicitude, has designed to give no v guarantees to the
administrative autonomy ,ofthe country by decreeing the
independence of several branches of service; such as those
of the post-office and public highways. The reforms
,effectedlast year will require some change in our financial
system. The abolition of the tearree, which obliges: the
proprietors of the land to :employ hired labour,, has
exhibited the inconvenience of the tax to which the
tillers of the so and other .agricultural servants are
exposed. The-koszerne tax, inasmuch as it is exclusively
religious, is :not in harmony with the spirit of recent
•leeislatiou as regards the equality of the civil rights of
the Jews, the introduction .of lqich the govern-
ment of his Majesty has received from you such active
co-operation. The abolition of both those taxes is pro-
jected, and„ inorder to replace the deficit which will be
occasioned therf..‘by, it is proposed to increase the duty
,on the .manufacture of spirits. Moral •considerations and
the true interest of the proprietors, os of the cultivators,
equally require these alterations. Besides those projects,
you will have to examine the budget,of the receipts and
; expenditure of the kingdom for the year 18.634 as well as
:the reports of the officials for the year just peat. A bill
on forced expropriation., on the payment of taxes and
treasury rents, on the establishment of a court .of appeal
in the Council of State for business relating, to the
taxes and, lastly, a bill State,
the internal arganisaion ui
the douncil of State, will be submitted 'to your delihera-
tion.
.I now declare the session to be open.

respectabl3 farmer, near Rathfryland, County Down,
was going home on a car with his wife, when the .
horse became unmanageable while passing through a
bog with no fence on either side, The horse and ear

'Tits WORLD IS ON THE Movs.'--A provincial clergy-
man, whose bump of hopefulness must; we should think,
be excessively developed, speaking,
,a few days, ago, at
The dinner of the Dauesbury and Frodsham Farmer's

PHEASANT AND PARTRIDGE SHOOTING—PERTHSHIRE;
—The pheasant shooting season openesi on Tuesday, but
nothing will be done for some time: Pheasants are
scarce this year in all the preserves, many of the eggs
having been destroyed during the hatching, and numbers
of the young birds having perished in consequence of
the inclement season. The cold wet summer was also
injurious to the surviving birds, and they do not grow
well. Their improved, however, very much during
August and September. Owing to the limited number,
it is probable few will be shot this seven. Partridges
have also improved very much in condition, and are now
generally strong and healthy. They have benefited
much from the late harvest, and' by the-time the lelds
are cleared they will afford ordinary sport. They are
not nearly so. numerous as usual, and there are a,lrge
number of late broods.- The coveys average from .six to
seven birds, which is under the usual number.. Little
sport has yet been enjoyel- on the low grounds, but in
the course of this month most of the preserves will be
shot over. Blackcock are scarce, but plantation' game
is plentiful, such as hares, rabbits, and roe deer. Some
good hare and partridge shooting has been obtained on

articles.title: COMMISSIONERS- OF THE EXHIBITiON AND MR. CADOGAN;
articles.text:
THE COMMISSIONERS- OF THE EXHI-
BITiON AND MR. CADOGAN;

TO TAB EDITOR OF THE TIMES.

.
Sir,—l have read this morning the article in the
Times of the Ist inst. retieeting on a letter from Mr.
Frederick Cadogan, in whivh that gentleman explained
the circumstances attending his connexion with Messrs.
Veillard and Martin and the remuneration which he
received, and in which he denies that he exercised any
influence on her Majesty's Commissioners in favour of
Messrs. Veillard and Martin. lam not in a position to
afford any information' on the first tv.o points. lam
aware that Mr. Cadogan gave much of his time to the
business of Messrs. Vei-llard and Martin, and that
he was often the organ of communication between-
them and the persons charged with the superintend-
ence of the refreshment department; but, till Mr. Cade-
gan's letter appeared in the Times, I never knew,
excepting from hearsay and very conflicting reports,
what were the duties he engaged to perform, or the
amount of remuneration he was to receive. I can cor-
roborate Mr. Cadogan's statement that he exercised no
influence on the Commission in favour of the contractors.
I gave my opinion in favour of accepting Messrs. Veil-
' ird and Martin's tender for the following reasons :—Be-
cause their tender was the most advantageous of all the
foreign tenders for the interest of the Exhibition as a
self-supporting institution. Becattse the conditions of
the agreement made it almost impossible, as has proved
to be the case, for the Commission to sustain any pecu-
niary loss. Because a foreign restaurateur was likely to
prove attraetive to the public, andto afford a stimulus to the
English rival. Becaneethecontractors, having both been at
the head of large French eatinghouses—one of them the
most famous in Europe—were likely to possess the skill,
as it would also be-for their interest, to cater well for
the public. I can state that, in joining in the un-
animous decision of the Commission, 1 was not influenced
in the slightest degree by any representations of Mr.
Cadbgan, or by the wish, although I have known him for
many years, of assisting or pleasing him. I should have
preferred making this explanation in common with my
colleague., but the distance at which I am from London
makes it impossible to communicate -with them without
great delay. I have no doubt, however, that the
assertions made in this letter are as applicable to all of
them as to myself.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant,
IGotha, Oct. 4. GRAN VILLE.

articles.title: GLADSTOIVE AT NinrCASTLE.
articles.text:
GLADSTOIVE AT NinrCASTLE.

NEWCASTLE-ON-TYNE, Oct. 7.—The Chancellor of
the Exchequer arrived in this district yesterday. The
right hon. gentleman came from .Brougham Hall- in the
afternoon to Blaydon, where he alighted,- and- drove to
Gibside, the residence of the Right. Hon. J. Hutt,
M.P. To-day the Chancellor arrived in Newcastle' and;
after visiting, the church of St. Nicholas, the High
Level Bridge. the monument recently erected to the.
memory of George Stephenson, and other places of inte-
rest in the town, he attended a banquet, given in his
honour, in the new Town Hall. All the tickets for the
dinner had been purchased several days ago, and there
.was a large number of persons from various parts of the
country who were anxious to be present, but who could
not. getadmission for want- of room. After the dinner
the side elevations and galleries were filled with ladies,
who gave' the hall a lively appearance.
The Right ,Worshiplail the Mayor of Newcastle
(Joseph Armstrong) •occupied tho chair. On his right
sat the guest •of the ovening, the Right Hon. W. E.
Gladstone,-M.P.
After the cloth was removed, the usual loyal toasts
were proposed by the chairman.
The Chairman, in highly eulogistic terms, proposed
the-4 Health of Mr. Gladstone,' referring especially to his
repeal of the paper duty and the furtherance of com-
mercial treatiesewith other nations, from which this dis-
trict had received so much benefit.
Mr. Gladstone, on rising to respond, was received
with loud and protracted cheers. The right hen. gen-
tleman acknowledged the warm compliment paid him.
He contrasted the labours of a public career, its toil and
reeponsibility.; but its reward, though not always in the
present, lay in the future; and to the future it was most
wholesome that .a public man should look. Though a
member of tho Government, he had freedom to speak of
public affairs. As.a memberof the Government he would
take creiit for his own services in promoting the French
treaty. Yet to the Emperor of the French and Mr.
Cobden it was mainly due. They were two distinguished
men, whose position on tilt one hand, and -sagacity and
ability on the other, accomplished it. His noble colleague
and Earl Russell were next in order entitled to the
honour of the meeting on account of the treaty. It had
been a success :beyond all expectations. The commer-
.cial experience of the public knew it as surely as official
documents showed it. The right hon. speaker gave nu-
merical facts as• to the state of trade with France for
twelve months past; the trade foreign and colonial, of
England, which was before the treaty of the value of
nine millions, was twelve months after twenty-one mil-
lions. The increase of the export of British produce
was no less satisfactory. On the average of two years
before the treaty the value of trade in metals and tissues
was two millions- in. .value: Now -it- was- six-millions.
The particular commerce of Newcastle had benefitted
three hundred per cent. The exports to America had
fallen off in twelve -months -nine millions. The treaty
of commerce had supplied this calamitous deficiency.
The hon. speaker • gave the increase of tonnage by sea
resulting from the treaty. Every ten or twelve millions
of increased trade gives us an increase of a million of
duties arising from tax-paying commodities imported.
The treaty has. compensated for all the Ration's
sacrifice on, account of the treaty; besides, the
moral effect of the treaty was greater than its pecu-
niary result. France then took its stand an free trade—
it added its influence th England's, and new treaties else-
where-had arisen; and its effects upmethe future -peace
of the world was very significant and influential. When
Parliament meets, it will be its duty to retrench, as far
.as possible, its expenditure. Considering that the great
industry of the country had been smitten by a blight, it.
was a matter of great satisfaction that the revenue had
increased to -tile amount of £G-00,000. The Chancellor
of the Exchequer must compliment the workmen of the
north thrown out of employ. He doubted if any class of
the community would have borne any similar calamity
with equal fortitude and self-denial. Mr. Gladstone de-
fended the manufacturers generally, but condemned
those who made wealth an object of. worship, and ne-
glected its wise use. The manufacturer who sold his
cotton clandestinely was abusing the rights of property
as much as any condemned aristocrat. Relief ought to
be given to. the workmen without humiliation. The
men were as innocent as children, but have borne
their sufferings like heroes. He hoped that no
man would be deprived of the franchise because
he had accepted parish relief. When. Parliament again
considered the franchise, the conduct of -the men of
Lancashire would be taken into account. He next
referred to the war in America. The slam would be
better of if the States were separqted, as on the basis of
Union the laws against the slaves were enforced by
the whole power of the Federal United Government.
Our neutrality has been More against the South than
the North. We ought to judge tenderly the North;
it has never drunk the cup of bitterness, and it exag-
gerates its feelings. Let us bear with them. Let us
not forget the reception they gave the Prince of
-Wales; it was a proof of the settled goedwill of America
to England. There can be no doubt that Jefferson Davis
has made a nation, of the South. [Mr. Gladstone
treated the South as a successful cause, and the
announcement created great sensation.] Lori Palmer-
ston had been one of the earliest of this country
to recognize the condition of Italy. Earl Russell had
no less faithfully represented the sentiments of the
people of England. The conduct of the people-of Italy
gives them new' claims. to public confidence; they would
not follow' the man it best loved into error for the sake
of a peace in Europe. He hoped- that the question of
Italy would early reach its final stage. Mr. Gladstone
ended by proposing The Health of the .Mayor; on ac-
count of his connection with the press, which he praised
as the friend of the people, the safeguard of liberty, and
check upon ministers.
The other toasts proposed and responded to were Her
Majesty's Ministers," The Members for Newcastle and
for theother Boroughs and Counties of Northumberland
and D urham ".The Consular Representatives of Foreign
Sautes," The Unity and Independence of Italy," The
Tyne Improvement Commissioners," The Mayor and
Corporation of Newcastle,' and The Chamber of. Com-
merce.'

FATAL ACCIDENT ON TEE RIVER.-011 the 6th a
young man named Peter Moss, a compositor, with
another young man, were sailing on the river in a skiff,
with a main and fore sail set. When off Deptford a
squall capsized the biat, in consequence of the main
sheet having been made fast, and.the boat being with-

body was not found.

THE THEATRES IN HOLY WEEK.---Some time since
a petition was presented to Lord Sydney, the Lord
Chamberlain, by the Hon. Colin Lindsay, and other
members of the Church of England, praying that in the
licences about to be granted to the managers of metropo-
litan taeatres for next year, a clause should be inserted
restrictine, them from opening for public performances
during Holy Week, as was formerly the case. The Hon.
Spencer Ponsonby, acting for the Lord Chamberlain, has
addressed a letter to Mr. Lindsay, declining to grant the
prayer of the memorial, on the ground that other places
of public amusement are allowed to be open during the
season. The Lord Chamberlain suggests that a bill
should be introduced into parliament by those anxious to
maintain the TeStriCtiOD, as being the best way of carry-
iug old their wishes.

PALACE AND PRISON.
In the fort of Varignano,
On a hard and narrow bed,
Brooding thoughts, as a volcano
Brooded), lava floods unshed,
Lies a chained and crippled hero
310 i. d and baffled, not subdued,
Though his fortune's sunk to zero,
At blood heat still stands his mood.

In his sumptuous sea side palace,
Where Biarfrita looks e'er sea,
With all splexdour, for such solace
As from splendour wrung may be,
Sits a crowned and sceptred sovereign,
Strong in arms, more strong in art,
Wrapped in thoughts past men's discovexing,
With a marble stone for heart.

From her centuries', sleep arisen,
Clenching half Unfettered hands,
'Twixt that palace and that prison,
Flushed and fierce Italia stands.
Brave words she has owed that ruler,
Brave words and brave deeds as well;
Now she doubts he fain would fool her,
Of the hopes he helped to swell.
So with visage dark and lowering
She that palace-threshold spurns,
And v.ith tenderness o'er-powering-
To the fortress-prison turns. .
Ne'cr a doubt of the devotion
Of that chained and crippled chief,
Clouds her love's profound emotion,
Stays the passion of her grief.
What's an Emperor's word, whose action
To his utterance gives the lie?
But this chief for love bade faction;
Prudence, policy stand by—
Blind may-be, but blind for brightness..
Of the goal to which he strove,
All his live is one long witness
Life to him is less than love.
Then what wonder to the prison
From the palace if she turn?
'Tis her star th:t newly risen
O'er that fortress-cell doth burn.. .
The true prison is that palace,
And that prisoner is true King !'
Were his pallet, bed a gallows, -
There Italia's heart would cling,.
Not to you man dark and callous,
Girt by his base courtier-ring.

articles.title: FOLLOW MY LEADER.
articles.text:
FOLLOW MY LEADER.

A Grand ball was held the other day at the Imperial
Villa at Biarritz, and according to a letter from that
place :
'The toilettes of the ladies were richer than ever.
Hair powder seems to be coming into vogue again, for
many of the ladies used it on this occasion.'
Very probably. The admirable revival of hoops
should naturally be followed by a return to hair-powder.
The sequacious gregariousness with which the French
ladies follow their leader, and the English ladies them,
is, though a goose-like, a gratifying attestation of their
attachment to the Crinoline Dynasty. Venus forbid
that the Empress of the French should wear rings in her
nose; but if she were to adopt such ornaments her
example would doubtless be followethby our wives and
daughters.

articles.text:
DEVOTION TO SCIENCE.

At one of the meetings of the British Association last
week, Dr. Edward Smith said—
'ln certain cases tobacco acts as a stimulant, and may
supply to the literary man the state of system at night
which would be induced by a moderato quantity of
alcoholic stimulants, but when the body is.of full habit
it must lead to disturbed sleep and may lead to apo-
plexy.'
Dr. Punch said that as a literary man of full habit
(applause) he should like to ask his friend Dr. Smith
'whether the unpleasant consequenceshe indicated might
not be obviated by taking both the cigar and a moderate
quantity of alcoholic stimulants.
Dr. Edward Smith said that he had not directed his
attention to that question, and thought that experiments
bearing upon it might be conducted with interest and
with advantage.
Dr. Punch, in the most liberal manner, immediately
undertook to prosecute them, and departed. to hishotel with
that view. Ile was shortly joined by Dr. Smith, and the
distinguished philosophers pursued their investigations
until a late hour.

SERIOUS CHARGE OF FORGERT.—At the public office
at Birmingham, on the 7th, a young man named John
Howard Baker was brought up on the charge of forging
the name of Mr. Thomas Howell, an auctioneer of that
town, to a valuation of certain leasehold property, and
thereby obtaining the loan of a large sum of money.
The case was remanded, but it was understood that the
accused has obtained money from a bank in the town

way he has defrauded solicitors of considerable sums of

AN limn ADDRESS TO GARIBALDI.—An Irish ad-
dress to Garibaldi has been prepared, and is in course of
signature in Dublin. It is to be accompanied by e
testimonial from the people of Ireland.' The address
hails him as- a successful deliverer of his countrymen
from the most miserable of all bondage—that which, as
one of our own statesmen has well described it; confines
the intellet and enslaves the soul;' and the glorious
liberty which marks his path has not been tarnished. or
sullied by selfish ambition or boastful pride. Expressing
sympathy with the Liberator in this season of temporary
failure, the signers of the address pray for his restora-
tion to health, and his future happiness; and they con-
clude by observing that his will not be the least illu-
minated pages of Italy's historic annals, and of her en-
during chronicles of the great and good, having revived
in his own person, and exemplified in his conduct and
character, the martial energy of aNsztr with the Ohristaag
devotedness of Constantine.'
